claims.claim: RunLoopGeneric exists in WTF and is used by the JSCOnly and PlayStation ports, so no GLib is needed
claims.evidence: Source/WTF/wtf/generic/RunLoopGeneric.cpp (363 lines). PlatformPlayStation.cmake:4 'generic/RunLoopGeneric.cpp' (always). OptionsJSCOnly.cmake:30-36 EVENT_LOOP_TYPE values GLib|Generic, DEFAULT_EVENT_LOOP_TYPE "Generic"; :102-111 Generic => SET_AND_EXPOSE_TO_BUILD(USE_GENERIC_EVENT_LOOP 1) + WTF_DEFAULT_EVENT_LOOP 0; PlatformJSCOnly.cmake:169 adds generic/RunLoopGeneric.cpp in the non-GLib branch. PlatformUse.h:210-226: when WTF_DEFAULT_EVENT_LOOP is 1 the choice is GLIB > WINDOWS > COCOA > GENERIC.

claims.claim: RunLoopGeneric is portable to Windows and macOS (doc says the RunLoopGeneric portability patches should go upstream)
claims.evidence: RunLoopGeneric.cpp only uses WTF::Lock, Condition, RedBlackTree and MonotonicTime. It has no POSIX calls. PlatformJSCOnly.cmake adds it for WIN32 and APPLE builds too, because the Generic branch at :160-170 has no OS check. The JSCOnly Windows build therefore already uses it, together with win/MainThreadWin.cpp (:16). The Apple build uses generic/MainThreadGeneric.cpp (:36).
claims.implication: The run loop itself needs no OS porting work. The real portability problems are in WebCore code keyed on OS(WINDOWS) rather than the event-loop USE() macros (see MainThreadSharedTimer below), plus a missing timer-deadline/wakeup API.

challenge.reasoning:
I tried to show the reviewer wrong and could not. The doc implies RunLoopGeneric needs portability patches that would then go upstream. The source says it already builds on Windows and macOS with no changes. It has no OS(), PLATFORM() or USE() guards and no POSIX calls. Its only OS-dependent piece is getCurrentProcessID(), and ProcessID.h already has OS(WINDOWS) branches for it. The JSCOnly port already selects it on WIN32 and APPLE, because the Generic branch of PlatformJSCOnly.cmake has no OS check. So the "patches to go upstream" part is mostly unfounded for the run loop itself.

The doc is right that real porting work exists, but it is elsewhere, so PARTIAL stands. The reviewer missed several gotchas:
(1) Generic is not the default on Windows or macOS. PlatformUse.h picks WINDOWS_EVENT_LOOP for OS(WINDOWS) and COCOA_EVENT_LOOP for PLATFORM(COCOA) unless WTF_DEFAULT_EVENT_LOOP=0. The ZeroG port has to copy what OptionsJSCOnly.cmake:108-110 does: SET_AND_EXPOSE_TO_BUILD USE_GENERIC_EVENT_LOOP 1 and WTF_DEFAULT_EVENT_LOOP 0.
(2) PlatformLegacy.h works out PLATFORM() from BUILDING_<PORT>__. JSCOnly avoids PLATFORM(MAC)/COCOA/WIN only through its explicit BUILDING_JSCONLY__ branch. Without a matching BUILDING_ZEROG__ branch, ZeroG on macOS gets PLATFORM(MAC) and PLATFORM(COCOA), which turns on USE(CF), plus Cocoa-only code in RunLoop.h and WebCore. On Windows it gets PLATFORM(WIN). Fixing this means editing PlatformLegacy.h (an upstream patch), or reusing BUILDING_JSCONLY__.
(3) MainThreadGeneric.cpp uses pthread, so Windows needs win/MainThreadWin.cpp. The JSCOnly cmake already does this split.
(4) WebCore's MainThreadSharedTimer checks OS(WINDOWS), not the event-loop macro. On Windows it expects platform/win/MainThreadSharedTimerWin.cpp, which uses an HWND message window plus SetTimer and PostMessage, so it needs a Windows message pump. Getting the generic RunLoop timer path on Windows needs an upstream guard change, e.g. switching to USE(WINDOWS_EVENT_LOOP).
(5) setWakeUpCallback does exist for GENERIC_EVENT_LOOP, so a wakeup hook is there. There is no public way to ask for the next timer deadline, though, so a host loop has to poll cycle() or build its own deadline export.

claims.claim: Windows ports use RunLoopWin
claims.evidence: PlatformWin.cmake:19 win/RunLoopWin.cpp. RunLoopWin.cpp:161-166: each RunLoop creates an HWND_MESSAGE window. :77-95 run() is a PeekMessage/MsgWaitForMultipleObjectsEx loop. :215-227 cycle() runs PeekMessage(&message, nullptr, 0, 0, PM_REMOVE), which pumps every message of the thread, including the host's windows. Threading.cpp:511-513 registers the window class in WTF::initialize().
claims.implication: Don't use RunLoopWin for game or own-loop mode, because cycle() would steal and dispatch the host's Win32 messages. Use Generic on Windows as well.

claims.claim: An embedder can drive the loop step by step (zg_runtime_update) and get a wakeup handle (zg_runtime_wakeup_handle)
claims.doc_section: Integrazione con il loop dell'applicazione; Loop
claims.evidence: RunLoop.h:116-123: static run(), stop(), wakeUp(), static CycleResult cycle(RunLoopMode). RunLoopGeneric.cpp:277-281: cycle() = runImpl(RunMode::Iterate), always returns Continue. :139-174: Iterate mode does not wait, fires expired timers once and calls performWork() once. :148-150: Drain mode blocks on Condition m_readyToRun.waitUntil(m_loopLock, nextTimer) (WTF::Condition/ParkingLot, no fd or HANDLE). RunLoop.h:147-149 + RunLoopGeneric.cpp:240-243: a static setWakeUpCallback(Function) exists for GENERIC and WINDOWS. :262-269: the callback runs inside wakeUpWithLock(), i.e. with m_loopLock held, on any thread. TimerBase::start (:321-328) and dispatch (RunLoop.cpp:160-173, only when the queue was empty) call it. The next-timer time (m_schedules.first()->scheduledTimePoint()) is private (RunLoop.h:391-417). There is no public 'time until next timer'.
claims.implication: zg_runtime_update maps to RunLoop::cycle() on the main thread. zg_runtime_wakeup_handle can be built on setWakeUpCallback without patching: the callback writes an eventfd/pipe (Linux/macOS) or SetEvent (Windows). It must not call back into RunLoop (that deadlocks on m_loopLock) and must be thread-safe. A small WTF patch is still needed to expose the next timer deadline (e.g. RunLoop::secondsUntilNextTimer()), because the callback fires when a timer is armed, not when it expires. Without that, the host can't compute its idle-wait timeout.

challenge.reasoning:
I tried to find a public "next deadline" API or a native waitable handle in the generic RunLoop and found neither, so the reviewer's PARTIAL stands. Step-by-step driving is already there: RunLoop::cycle() runs one non-blocking iteration. A wakeup notification can be built on setWakeUpCallback without patching. It is a callback, though, not a handle. It fires when work is queued or a timer is armed, not when a timer expires. The time until the next timer is private. So the doc's line "signaled ... timer in scadenza" (signaled when a timer is due) cannot be met without a small WTF patch, or a host-side timeout from some other source.

The reviewer's line numbers and semantics all match the tree. I add four things the review missed or blurred:
(1) There is already an upstream example of exactly this pattern. RemoteInspectorSocketEndpoint::workerThread sets a wakeup callback that writes to a socket, calls RunLoop::cycle(), and then polls with its own pollingTimeout(). That timeout does not include RunLoop timers, which shows the same deadline gap.
(2) On Windows the default build selects USE_WINDOWS_EVENT_LOOP (PlatformUse.h:217-219), not RunLoopGeneric. The doc claims RunLoopGeneric everywhere, which is only true if ZeroG forces it the way OptionsJSCOnly.cmake:109-110 does (USE_GENERIC_EVENT_LOOP=1, WTF_DEFAULT_EVENT_LOOP=0).
(3) The Windows loop behaves differently. wakeUp() calls the callback without holding the lock and also posts PerformWorkMessage. TimerBase::start never calls the callback; it only posts SetTimerMessage, which is a no-op in wndProc. RunLoop timers fire only inside fireTimers(), called from run() or cycle(). cycle() drains every message for the thread (PeekMessage with a null HWND), so it also dispatches the host's own window messages. msTillNextTimer() is private.
(4) WebCore's main-thread shared timer, which drives DOM timers, uses RunLoop::Timer on generic builds. On Windows it uses Win32 SetTimer/PostMessage on its own message-only HWND. So on Windows those wakeups come through the host message queue, while on generic builds they need the deadline patch.

The reviewer's warning about re-entering RunLoop from the callback is right: on generic builds the callback runs inside wakeUpWithLock with m_loopLock held, from any thread. setWakeUpCallback sets one slot on currentSingleton(), so it must be called on the engine thread and it replaces any earlier callback.

claims.claim: WTF registers the main thread once per process and global state can't be torn down, so zg_runtime is a process singleton

claims.implication: Make zg_runtime_create idempotent-or-fail, and make destroy effectively a no-op. All JSC::Options and the GC signal must be fixed before the first VM is created.

claims.claim: The main thread can be whatever thread creates the runtime
claims.evidence: MainThreadGeneric.cpp:42-55: s_mainThread = pthread_self(), and a comment says it need not be the OS main thread. MainThreadWin.cpp:41-50 uses Thread::currentID(). But MainThread.cpp:47 has RELEASE_ASSERT(!isMainThread() || Thread::currentSingleton().uid() == 1). Threading.cpp:136-141 (non-Cocoa): s_uid starts at 0 and the first lazily created WTF::Thread gets uid 1. ThreadingPOSIX.cpp:550-563 / ThreadingWin.cpp:275-289: any Thread::currentSingleton() on any thread calls WTF::initialize() and takes a uid. WebCoreMainThread.cpp:45-50 calls JSC::initialize() and then WTF::initializeMainThread().
claims.implication: The thread that calls zg_runtime_create must be the first thread in the process to touch WTF in any way. If any host thread touches WTF first (zg_* call, static init, another WebKit), the process crashes at a RELEASE_ASSERT. Call JSC::initialize(), WTF::initializeMainThread() and WebCore::populateJITOperations() (ScriptController::initializeMainThread) back to back on the creating thread.

challenge.reasoning:
I tried to prove the reviewer wrong and could not. Their evidence is correct for the generic (POSIX) and Windows main-thread code. On those platforms WTF lets any thread become the "main thread", as long as that thread creates the first WTF::Thread object in the process.

I also found two points the reviewer missed. One makes the uid-1 rule stricter. The other makes the claim false on macOS.

1. It is not only Thread::currentSingleton() that uses up a uid. Thread::tryCreate()/Thread::create() also builds a new Thread with IsMain::No, which runs ++s_uid (Threading.cpp:271-275, Threading.h:322). So if the creating thread, or any other thread, spawns a WTF thread before the creating thread's own Thread object exists, uid 1 is gone. Then the RELEASE_ASSERT in initializeMainThread fails (MainThread.cpp:47). The real rule: the thread calling zg_runtime_create must be the first to construct any WTF::Thread object, by either path. WTF::initialize() does not spawn WTF threads itself (Threading.cpp:489-515). JSC::initialize() calls Thread::currentSingleton() on the calling thread (InitializeThreading.cpp:131), and WebCore's helper runs JSC::initialize(), WTF::initializeMainThread() and populateJITOperations() back to back (WebCoreMainThread.cpp:45-50). So the reviewer's advice to call these in sequence is correct.

2. On macOS the claim fails outright, unless ZeroG defines its own port macro. PlatformLegacy.h:49-58 sets PLATFORM(MAC) for any OS(MACOS) build without BUILDING_GTK__/BUILDING_HAIKU__/BUILDING_WPE__/BUILDING_JSCONLY__, and PLATFORM(COCOA) follows from it (line 80-81). A new port without its own BUILDING_ZEROG__ branch therefore builds with Cocoa semantics:
- MainThreadCocoa.mm:155-157 defines isMainThread() as pthread_main_np(), so the main thread is hard-wired to the OS main thread.
- initializeMainThreadPlatform logs a fault and ASSERTs when called from a secondary thread (MainThreadCocoa.mm:58-62).
- uid 1 is reserved for the pthread_main_np() thread (Threading.cpp:132-135, ThreadingPOSIX.cpp:554-555).
- WebCore::initializeMainThreadIfNeeded under WEB_THREAD_DISABLEMENT moves init onto CFRunLoopGetMain when not on the OS main thread (WebCoreMainThread.cpp:54-62).

The RELEASE_ASSERT at MainThread.cpp:47 does not fire there, because !isMainThread() is true. But isMainThread() is false on the creating thread, so every main-thread assertion and RunLoop::main use breaks. To make "any thread" work on macOS, ZeroG would need its own PLATFORM branch in PlatformLegacy.h and the generic MainThread/RunLoop sources. Even then, AppKit window work has to stay on the OS main thread.

Overall verdict: PARTIAL. The claim holds on Linux (MainThreadGeneric) and Windows (MainThreadWin) with the strict first-WTF-Thread ordering rule. It does not hold on macOS under the default Cocoa platform selection.

claims.claim: The JSC GC uses a signal to suspend threads: SIGUSR1 by default, configurable with JSC_SIGNAL_FOR_GC
claims.evidence: ThreadingPOSIX.cpp:195-208 Thread::initializePlatformThreading: if !g_wtfConfig.isUserSpecifiedThreadSuspendResumeSignalConfigured then sigThreadSuspendResume = SIGUSR1, overridden by getenv("JSC_SIGNAL_FOR_GC") via sscanf. Called from WTF::initialize (Threading.cpp:507). Thread::suspend/resume use pthread_kill and a global sem_t (:575-625). Callers: MachineStackMarker.cpp:165 (GC conservative scan of other threads), SamplingProfiler.cpp:391, VMTraps.cpp:309.
claims.implication: The host's main thread (and worker threads) will receive this signal during GC and VM traps.

claims.claim: WebKit checks that nobody else handles the GC signal, and a host that already uses it (Ruby) crashes
claims.evidence: ThreadingPOSIX.cpp:227-237: if an old handler exists it only logs WTFLogAlways("Overriding existing handler for signal %d. Set JSC_SIGNAL_FOR_GC ...") and then installs its own handler over it. It RELEASE_ASSERTs only if sigaction() fails. The old handler is not saved and not chained.
claims.implication: The failure mode is now the reverse: the host's SIGUSR1 handler is silently replaced. If the host later re-installs its own handler, or blocks the signal with pthread_sigmask, Thread::suspend waits forever on globalSemaphoreForSuspendResume (:592) and the GC deadlocks. Choosing a free signal is still required.

challenge.reasoning: The claim has two parts. Part 1, "WebKit checks whether anyone else handles the GC signal", is still literally true. Thread::initializePlatformThreading still reads the old disposition with sigaction(signal, nullptr, &oldAction) and checks whether it is non-default (ThreadingPOSIX.cpp:227-231). Part 2, "a host that already uses it (Ruby) crashes", is false at the pinned commit. The check now only logs a warning, then installs JSC's handler over the host's. The old handler is not saved or chained. The only RELEASE_ASSERT (:237) fires when sigaction() itself fails, not when a handler already exists. The Ruby crash in bug 223069 (2021) came from an older version that asserted on an existing handler; that behaviour is gone. So the reviewer is right on the substance, and the doc's stated failure mode is out of date. But "checks that nobody else handles it" is still accurate, which makes PARTIAL more precise than a flat REFUTED. The reviewer's implication also holds up. If the host later reinstalls its own SIGUSR1 handler, that handler never posts globalSemaphoreForSuspendResume. If the host blocks the signal on a mutator thread with pthread_sigmask, pthread_kill succeeds but the signal stays pending. Either way Thread::suspend blocks forever in globalSemaphoreForSuspendResume->wait() (:592), so the GC hangs. initializeCurrentThreadEvenIfNonWTFCreated unblocks the signal only once, when a thread is registered (:248-256), so later re-blocking by the host is not prevented. One remaining crash path: an invalid value in JSC_SIGNAL_FOR_GC or JSConfigureSignalForGC makes sigaction fail and hits RELEASE_ASSERT(signalIsInstalled). Facts the doc misses: (a) there is already a supported API for the doc's "choose the signal in zg_runtime_config" proposal. JSConfigureSignalForGC(int) is in JSBasePrivate.h:58 (non-Apple, non-Windows), implemented at JSBase.cpp:186-193. It sets g_wtfConfig.sigThreadSuspendResume and isUserSpecifiedThreadSuspendResumeSignalConfigured, which takes precedence over the env var (ThreadingPOSIX.cpp:197). It must be called before JSC/WTF initialization, otherwise it returns false. ZeroG can call it directly, or set the WTFConfig fields before WTF::initialize, with no patch. (b) Upstream already handles the alternate-signal-stack case the doc credits to Bun's fork. The handler backs off when the stack pointer is outside the thread stack (:150-160), and suspend retries after a yield (:593-597). Verify this is equivalent to the Bun fix before carrying a patch. (c) Signals.cpp:588 removes the GC signal from the sa_mask of JSC's trap handlers, which interacts with the doc's point about chaining handlers.

claims.claim: The GC signal can be set programmatically (zg_runtime_config) instead of via env var
claims.evidence: JavaScriptCore/API/JSBase.cpp:185-193 bool JSConfigureSignalForGC(int) (only !OS(DARWIN) && !OS(WINDOWS)). It returns false if isThreadSuspendResumeSignalConfigured is already set, and otherwise sets g_wtfConfig.sigThreadSuspendResume and isUserSpecifiedThreadSuspendResumeSignalConfigured. It is declared in the private header JSBasePrivate.h:50-59 ('Call this function before any of JSC initialization starts').
claims.implication: zg_runtime_create must call JSConfigureSignalForGC(cfg.gc_signal) before anything that triggers WTF::initialize(), and check the return value. A user-specified value also turns off the JSC_SIGNAL_FOR_GC env override. For a real-time default, compute SIGRTMIN+n at runtime: glibc's SIGRTMIN is not a compile-time constant.

claims.claim: Bun fixed a GC hang when the host installs an alternate signal stack (sigaltstack)
claims.evidence: Upstream already handles this at this revision. ThreadingPOSIX.cpp:150-160: if the handler's stack pointer is not inside thread->m_stack (alt stack), it sets m_platformRegisters = nullptr, posts the semaphore and returns. Thread::suspend (:586-598) retries with Thread::yield() until it succeeds. Upstream code never uses sigaltstack or SA_ONSTACK (suspend handler flags SA_RESTART|SA_SIGINFO at :221; trap handlers SA_SIGINFO only at Signals.cpp:590). I could not check the Bun PR (external).
claims.implication: There is no hang, but there can be a busy retry loop while a thread runs a host handler on its alt stack. JSC's SIGSEGV handler has no SA_ONSTACK, so a stack-overflow SIGSEGV that reaches JSC first cannot run. CI should run with a crash handler plus sigaltstack, as the doc says.

challenge.reasoning:
The reviewer said "there is no hang" because upstream already backs off and retries when the handler runs on an alternate stack. That reading is wrong, and the retry loop is the cause of the bug. Upstream tests currentStackPointer(), which is the handler's own stack pointer, not the stack pointer the thread had when the signal arrived. If the GC suspend handler ends up with SA_ONSTACK and the target thread has a sigaltstack, the handler runs on the alternate stack every time. The check `!thread->m_stack.contains(sp)` then fails on every attempt, and Thread::suspend loops forever (pthread_kill, wait, yield, repeat). The GC hangs on a live-lock.

Upstream does not set SA_ONSTACK itself, and the reviewer was right about that. But a host can add it: the Go runtime's initsig calls setsigstack on every handler it did not install, and other c-shared libraries do the same. The alternate stack itself comes from ASan (always), sanitizers, libbacktrace, or the host's crash handler. Bun's fix reads the interrupted stack pointer from the ucontext instead (interruptedStackPointer()). It was proposed in oven-sh/WebKit PR #235 and merged through oven-sh/WebKit PR #817. The pinned upstream checkout does not have it.

So the doc's core claim is correct, with two small inaccuracies:
1. PR #235, the one the doc cites, is still open. The fix actually landed in #817, merged 2026-10-21.
2. The SIGUSR1-to-SIGPWR default change came from a separate Bun commit (ceb3e74), not from PR #235. The doc's "in the same work" (nello stesso lavoro) is loose.

The doc also leaves out the precise trigger: an alternate stack alone is not enough. The GC handler must also carry SA_ONSTACK.

- Backport the #817 change to ThreadingPOSIX.cpp, which reads the stack pointer from registersFromUContext(ucontext) under HAVE(MACHINE_CONTEXT).

challenge.reasoning:
I tried to prove the reviewer wrong and could not. The verdict holds, and I have a few additions.

What the doc gets right: JSC does handle CPU fault signals on Linux, through SIGSEGV and SIGBUS (Signal::AccessFault), for WebAssembly fault-based bounds checks and for signal-based VM traps. Chaining to the host's handler matters.

What the doc gets wrong:
(1) SIGILL is listed, but the library never registers it. Only the jsc shell does (jsc.cpp:4292-4305, alongside SIGFPE, SIGTRAP and SIGABRT, plus SIGUSR2 at :3762). In libJavaScriptCore the only fault signal registered is AccessFault, in VMTraps.cpp:215 and WasmFaultSignalHandler.cpp:160.
(2) The doc says the handlers "must be chained" as if ZeroG has to add that. JSC already chains, but only one way. JSC saves the old sigaction when it installs its own handler in SignalHandlers::finalize (Signals.cpp:592-594). That happens once, from Config::finalize (WTFConfig.cpp:190-198), which runs during the first VM construction (VM.cpp:568). Signals JSC does not handle go to oldAction.sa_sigaction, or to SIG_DFL if there is none (Signals.cpp:536-543). A host crash handler installed after the first VM must chain back to JSC itself.

Corrections and additions to the reviewer's evidence:
- The signal-based VM trap path is a compile-time choice as well as a runtime option. ENABLE_SIGNAL_BASED_VM_TRAPS needs DFG_JIT, HAVE(MACHINE_CONTEXT), and an x86_64, ARM64 or RISCV64 CPU (PlatformEnable.h:969-971). Without it, Options.cpp:653-655 forces usePollingTraps=true.
- Turning the JIT off also forces usePollingTraps=true (Options.cpp:749).
- !ENABLE(WEBASSEMBLY) forces useWasmFaultSignalHandler=false and useWasmFastMemory=false (Options.cpp:657-660).
- The install itself is gated at InitializeThreading.cpp:144-148. So a JIT-less or Wasm-less profile installs no SIGSEGV/SIGBUS handler at all, and the reviewer's conclusion holds even more strongly.

Gotchas the doc misses:
- The handler list lives in g_wtfConfig, which is permanently frozen after Config::finalize (WTFConfig.cpp:195-196). Nothing can be added to it after the first VM.
- The chaining code calls oldAction.sa_sigaction without checking SA_SIGINFO or SIG_IGN. If the host had set SIG_IGN, that is a call to address 0x1, which crashes.
- The GC suspend/resume signal (SIGUSR1 by default, or JSC_SIGNAL_FOR_GC) is a separate mechanism. It is installed by Thread::initializePlatformThreading (ThreadingPOSIX.cpp:194-238), which overwrites any existing handler with only a log message and does not chain. JSC's fault handler is installed with the GC signal removed from its blocked mask (Signals.cpp:586-589). There is also a hook, isUserSpecifiedThreadSuspendResumeSignalConfigured, that can carry the doc's zg_runtime_config proposal without an environment variable.
- On Windows, a vectored exception handler is registered first in the chain (SignalsWin.cpp:146-157). Unhandled faults return EXCEPTION_EXECUTE_HANDLER (SignalsWin.cpp:110-121); for a VEH, any value other than EXCEPTION_CONTINUE_EXECUTION means continue search. That return-value behaviour is from Windows documentation, not the checkout.
- On Darwin, Mach exception ports are used. disableAllSignalHandlerBasedOptions (Options.cpp:765-772) can turn the whole mechanism off.

challenge.reasoning:
I tried to show the reviewer was wrong and could not. Their verdict holds.

GC and JIT: confirmed. JSC exposes thread-count options, and an embedder can set them from code. The customization callback runs after the defaults, the env-var override and the heuristic override, so the embedder gets the last word. Options are finalized right after that.

Image decoding: refuted as a "count". No WebCore setting, option or env var controls how many decode threads exist. ImageFrameWorkQueue::start creates its own WorkQueue for each BitmapImageSource. On generic WTF, which Windows and GTK both compile, every WorkQueue is a new RunLoop thread. The worker loop blocks on a SynchronizedFixedQueue until stop() closes it, so you get one live thread per image that is currently decoding asynchronously, with no upper limit.

Nuances the reviewer did not mention:
1. Async decoding can be switched off completely through the preferences LargeImageAsyncDecodingEnabled and AnimatedImageAsyncDecodingEnabled. Decoding then happens on the main thread. That is an on/off switch, not a count.
2. The Skia painting worker pools are sized only by env vars (WEBKIT_SKIA_CPU_PAINTING_THREADS, 1-8; WEBKIT_SKIA_GPU_PAINTING_THREADS, 1-4) inside CoordinatedTileManager, which belongs to the coordinated-graphics code. If ZeroG reuses it, these are more threads with no API for setting their count.
3. The JSC_* scan of the environ array only exists on Cocoa and Linux. On Windows the per-option getenv("JSC_<name>") heuristic path still runs, because it is guarded by !PLATFORM(COCOA). So the host environment can change engine behaviour on every platform until the callback overrides it.
4. The concurrent GC collector thread is separate from the marker pool. It is turned off with useConcurrentGC=false, not counted by numberOfGCMarkers.

So: GC/JIT confirmed, decode needs a WebCore patch (a shared or bounded queue, or a WorkerPool), and the overall verdict is PARTIAL.

challenge.reasoning:
I tried to prove the reviewer wrong and could not. PARTIAL is the right verdict. The reviewer's evidence is accurate, but I would add three corrections.

What holds:
(1) Dedicated workers always get their own OS thread. WorkerMessagingProxy hard-codes WorkerThreadMode::CreateNewThread, and that mode makes WorkerThread::createThread call Thread::create(..., ThreadType::JavaScript).
(2) Each worker has its own run loop. It is WebCore::WorkerDedicatedRunLoop, built on WTF::MessageQueue, not WTF::RunLoop.
(3) The process malloc heap and the allocator really are shared with the host, which is what the sentence at line 183 literally says.

What is wrong or missing:
(a) The JS heap is not shared. WorkerGlobalScope gives a worker scope the main VM only if it is created on the main thread; otherwise it calls JSC::VM::create(HeapType::Medium). So every dedicated worker has its own VM, GC heap and GC thread activity. That contradicts doc line 135 ("Una sola VM JavaScript", one JS VM shared by all views) and line 590 (all views share the same JS VM), and memory accounting and limits must cover the worker VMs too.

Correction 1 (nuance the reviewer missed): service workers can use WorkerThreadMode::UseMainThread when serviceWorkerPageIdentifier() is set or in testing. In that case they run on the main thread through WorkerMainRunLoop and DO share commonVM(). So "each worker runs on its own engine thread" is not universal.

Correction 2 (gotcha the reviewer missed): the "own run loop" is not self-sufficient. WorkerDedicatedRunLoop::runInMode pumps the native per-thread loop only behind USE(GLIB) (g_main_context_iteration), USE(CF) (CFRunLoop timer deadline) and OS(WINDOWS) (RunLoop::cycle() plus vm.deferredWorkTimer->timeUntilFire()). JSC's JSRunLoopTimer-based timers on a worker thread (GC activity, deferred work) are backed by that thread's WTF::RunLoop. If ZeroG picks a non-GLib, non-CF RunLoop backend on Linux or macOS, it must add an equivalent pumping branch, or those timers will never fire on workers.

Correction 3 (implication confirmed): workers need nothing from WebKit2. For dedicated workers, loader tasks go through postTaskToLoader to the document context on the main thread, so worker script and fetch loads stall if the host stops pumping the main loop.

On the "terminate with the view" part: Worker::stop() calls terminate(), which is consistent with the doc. Shared and service workers additionally need a SharedWorker server and an SWServer plus context connection, which WebKit2 normally provides. In-process ports would have to supply these.

PlayStation instead adds -DWTF_PLATFORM_PLAYSTATION=1 (OptionsPlayStation.cmake:10).

WebCore's main-thread shared timer (it drives all DOM timers) is chosen by OS, not by event loop. MainThreadSharedTimer.h:33,41,71 and .cpp:49 use '#if !USE(CF) && !OS(WINDOWS)' to choose RunLoop::Timer, so on Windows WebCore always uses platform/win/MainThreadSharedTimerWin.cpp. That file creates an HWND_MESSAGE window (:86-87), uses SetTimer/PostMessage (:95) and timeBeginPeriod for timers under 16 ms. With RunLoopGeneric on Windows, DOM timers only fire if the host pumps Win32 messages on the main thread. Patch the condition to !USE(WINDOWS_EVENT_LOOP), or don't add MainThreadSharedTimerWin.cpp in the ZeroG WebCore platform cmake.

WebCore::RunLoopObserver is a stub on non-CF/non-GLib loops (RunLoopObserver.cpp:52-67: schedule/invalidate do nothing, isScheduled returns false). OpportunisticTaskScheduler uses it, and so do the commonVM GC activity callbacks (CommonVM.cpp:70-73 set FullGC/EdenGC callbacks; OpportunisticTaskScheduler.cpp:186-221 fall back to m_runLoopObserver->schedule() when the page is busy). On Generic those deferred GCs never run from the timer path. Implement RunLoopObserver for the generic loop (before/after-cycle hooks in RunLoop::cycle) or have the embedding layer handle it. Rendering updates also need the embedder to schedule them (ChromeClient), because nothing in Generic observes loop activity.

The generic wakeup callback runs while RunLoop::m_loopLock is held (RunLoopGeneric.cpp:262-269), on arbitrary threads: network, JIT, GC timers (JSRunLoopTimer), workers. It must only signal an OS primitive. Calling RunLoop::wakeUp/dispatch/timer APIs from inside it deadlocks. setWakeUpCallback is static and applies to RunLoop::currentSingleton(), so call it on the main thread after initializeMainThread.

The GC suspend signal is configured and installed inside WTF::initialize() (Threading.cpp:507 -> ThreadingPOSIX.cpp:195-238). WTF::initialize() runs lazily from the first Thread::currentSingleton() (ThreadingPOSIX.cpp:550-553). So JSConfigureSignalForGC must be the very first WebKit call in the process. If the host blocks that signal in a thread that has entered JSC (pthread_sigmask), GC/VMTraps/SamplingProfiler suspension deadlocks in sem_wait (ThreadingPOSIX.cpp:592). initializeCurrentThreadEvenIfNonWTFCreated (:248-256) unblocks it only once, at thread registration.

POSIX trap chaining calls oldAction.sa_sigaction whenever it is non-null (Signals.cpp:530-541). If the host had set SIG_IGN (value 1) for SIGSEGV/SIGBUS before the first VM, JSC jumps to address 1. Old handlers installed without SA_SIGINFO get called with 3 args (usually harmless). JSC installs with sa_mask = all signals except the GC signal and without SA_ONSTACK (:584-590).

Trap handlers and the config freeze happen at FIRST VM creation (VM.cpp:568 Config::finalize), not at JSC::initialize. A host crash handler (Crashpad/Breakpad/Sentry) installed after the first zg_view/VM replaces JSC's SIGSEGV handler unless it chains. VMTraps and Wasm OOB then turn into crashes. Document the init order, or reinstall/verify after the host's crash-reporter init.

Options::usePollingTraps (OptionsList.h:551, default false) controls whether VMTraps uses SIGSEGV-based halt instructions plus a 'JSC VMTraps Signal Sender' WorkQueue thread that suspends the mutator (VMTraps.cpp:208-216, 309, 358). InitializeThreading.cpp:144-148 installs VMTraps signals only when !usePollingTraps. Setting usePollingTraps=true removes one SIGSEGV user and one suspend user; Wasm disabled removes the other.

Env vars prefixed JSC_ are applied to any JSC option at init (Options.cpp:1105-1112 on Linux/Cocoa, plus overrideOptionWithHeuristic getenv for all options on non-Cocoa, Options.cpp:395-420, 1118-1121). A host environment can therefore change the engine (JIT, GC threads, etc.). zg_runtime_config values should be applied in the Options customization callback, which gets the last word (Options.cpp:1141).

On Windows the config pages are NOT frozen (WTFConfig.cpp:228-233 FIXME, no VirtualProtect), so that hardening is missing there. WebConfig::g_config is an extern "C" global named 'g_config' (WTFConfig.cpp:89, WTFConfig.h:51, also GigacageConfig.h:39). It collides with any other JSC/WebKit in the host process unless symbols are localized.

RunLoopWin (if it were used) creates a message-only window per thread RunLoop, including every WorkQueue thread (RunLoopWin.cpp:161-166). Its cycle() dispatches every thread message through TranslateMessage/DispatchMessage. Avoid it for embedding.

RunLoopGeneric's RunLoop::cycle() ignores RunLoopMode and always returns CycleResult::Continue. Each call fires timers and drains m_nextIteration exactly once (RunLoopGeneric.cpp:277-281, RunLoop.cpp:128-158). Work dispatched during the cycle runs on the NEXT cycle, so zg_runtime_update may need to loop until idle or a time budget runs out.

Image decoding creates a new WorkQueue and therefore a new OS thread per async-decoded image source (ImageFrameWorkQueue.cpp:64; WorkQueueGeneric.cpp:44 RunLoop::create -> Thread::create, RunLoop.cpp:108-120). That is unbounded and conflicts with the doc's 'pool di worker' and configurable decode thread count.

Each Web Worker gets a separate JSC::VM (WorkerGlobalScope.cpp:117, HeapType::Medium). That VM has its own GC threads and timers, and its own worker thread is added to the threads that GC/VMTraps suspend with the GC signal.

Linux thread-name truncation keeps the RIGHTMOST 15 characters (Threading.cpp:196-199), so long engine names become unreadable. Windows naming only works with a debugger attached (ThreadingWin.cpp:129-154, MS_VC_EXCEPTION). WTF also names the host's thread 'Main Thread' on Windows (MainThreadWin.cpp:44).

On macOS with a custom (non-Cocoa) port, OS(DARWIN) code still turns on: HAVE_MACH_EXCEPTIONS (PlatformHave.h:227), a Mach exception handler thread, thread_suspend, and pthread_main_np. RunLoopGeneric does not drain the libdispatch main queue (drainDispatchMainQueue exists only for GLib/Windows, RunLoop.h:315-319). In window mode on macOS the NSApplication/CFRunLoop must stay in charge and call RunLoop::cycle() from a CFRunLoopSource that the wakeup callback signals.

challenge.reasoning:
I tried to show the reviewer was wrong and could not. The literal claim holds. WebCore's platform/network/curl directory exists, Curl.cmake builds it into WebCore, and it includes an SQLite-backed cookie store (CookieJarDB). But the doc implies that "networking" and "cookies" come ready-made from WebCore, and that does not hold at this revision.

What WebCore provides is low-level plumbing:
- curl request/stream scheduling (CurlRequest, CurlRequestScheduler, CurlStream, CurlStreamScheduler, CurlMultipartHandle)
- TLS handling (CurlSSLHandle, CurlSSLVerifier, OpenSSLHelper)
- cookie parsing and storage (CookieUtil, CookieJarDB)
- public suffix lookup (PublicSuffixStoreCurl) and DNS (DNSResolveQueueCurl)

Everything that turns these into a working network stack lives in WebKit2:
- NetworkDataTaskCurl does redirects, auth, and cookie header injection and Set-Cookie handling.
- The curl cookie session (the class that owns the CookieJarDB) is now WebKit/Shared/NetworkStorageSession.h plus NetworkStorageSessionCurl.cpp.

The reviewer missed one thing, and it makes the problem worse, not better. WebCore still has a base class, platform/network/CookieStorageSession.{h,cpp}, but its cookie API exists only under PLATFORM(COCOA). It has no USE(CURL) members and no CookieJarDB.

Also, WebCore's own loader/CookieJar.cpp only does real work on Cocoa. In the `#else` branch, cookies() and setCookies() (and the other non-Cocoa methods) are just ASSERT_NOT_REACHED() stubs. So document.cookie and the cookie header only work if ZeroG writes its own CookieJar subclass that overrides those virtual methods (CookieJar.h:63-85) and talks to CookieJarDB/CookieUtil, porting the logic of NetworkStorageSessionCurl.cpp.

The reviewer's link-dependency point is also confirmed. Curl.cmake links CURL::libcurl, LibPSL::LibPSL and OpenSSL::SSL, so BoringSSL has to provide an OpenSSL::SSL CMake target, and libpsl is a hard requirement.

The legacy curl ResourceHandle is gone. platform/network has only the generic ResourceHandle and BlobResourceHandle, and there is no ResourceHandleCurl. ZeroG therefore has to write its own loader (a LoaderStrategy) that drives CurlRequest, which matches doc line 63.

On WebSocket (doc lines 299 and 758): CurlStream and CurlStreamScheduler still exist in WebCore. The WebSocket logic built on them, however, is in WebKit/NetworkProcess/curl/WebSocketTaskCurl.cpp, so that also has to be ported.

challenge.reasoning:
I tried to show the reviewer was wrong and could not. The doc's layer description is accurate in direction: the embedder does create Page and LocalFrame, and it does implement ChromeClient, EditorClient, LocalFrameLoaderClient and ContextMenuClient. But it is far from complete. The real PageConfiguration constructor at the pinned commit takes about 20 required positional arguments, plus guarded ones for CONTEXT_MENUS, APPLE_PAY and WEB_AUTHN. Four RefPtr fields are dereferenced unconditionally in Page.cpp, so they are also mandatory. I confirmed every item the reviewer listed and found no flag renamed and no guard misread.

Two refinements to the reviewer's evidence:
(a) ContextMenuClient is the one client the doc names that is conditional. It exists only under ENABLE(CONTEXT_MENUS).
(b) "Resource loader" in the doc does not mean a page client. In this design it means a WebCore::LoaderStrategy that the port supplies through the process-global PlatformStrategies (setPlatformStrategies). The same object must also provide PasteboardStrategy, MediaStrategy, BlobRegistry and PushStrategy. Neither the doc nor the reviewer mentions these.

Things that matter for ZeroG's implementation:

challenge.reasoning:
I tried to prove the reviewer wrong and could not. The PARTIAL verdict holds, with three corrections.

What is right in the doc's line 82 ("Port PlayStation e JSCOnly: build CMake senza GLib, RunLoopGeneric, rete curl, Skia previsto"):
- Both are CMake ports.
- Both use RunLoopGeneric. PlayStation always does; JSCOnly does by default.

What is wrong or too broad:
1. JSCOnly has no WebCore at all, so it cannot have curl networking or Skia. It is only a reference for WTF and JSC. The doc lumps the two ports together and that is misleading.
2. JSCOnly is not strictly GLib-free. GLib is an option: EVENT_LOOP_TYPE can be set to GLib, and ENABLE_JSC_GLIB_API forces it.
3. JSCOnly does not build JSC statically by default (ENABLE_STATIC_JSC is OFF). PlayStation does (ON).

On PlayStation, curl is correct and always on whenever WebCore is built. "Skia previsto" (Skia planned) undersells it: Skia is already a working path on PlayStation, just off by default. Cairo is the default, and USE_SKIA defaults OFF globally. There is real Skia support:
- PlatformPlayStation.cmake includes platform/Skia.cmake.
- It adds the GLFence sources when Skia is on.
- PlatformDisplaySkia.cpp has PLATFORM(PLAYSTATION) branches.
So the reviewer is right that the default is OFF, but Skia is supported now, not just planned.

Corrections to the reviewer's evidence and advice:
- (a) The reviewer calls WinCairo "WebKit2-only" as if that set it apart. PlayStation is also a multi-process WebKit2 port: it never turns ENABLE_WEBKIT off, it builds WebKit as a SHARED library, and it uses a ProcessLauncher. Neither port is a single-process WebCore-only model.
- (b) "Base OptionsZeroG.cmake on OptionsPlayStation.cmake" needs a strong caveat. That file is tied to the Sony SDK:
  - it turns pkg-config off and replaces pkg_check_modules with an empty macro;
  - it requires WebKitRequirements;
  - it adds Sce* library names to the dependency lookups;
  - it adds -sce-stdlib=v2;
  - it defines WTF_PLATFORM_PLAYSTATION.
  Much of it would have to be rewritten. Skia on PlayStation also assumes EGL/OpenGLES2 and TextureMapper/CoordinatedGraphics.
- (c) Not copying libwpe is correct but not enough on its own. WebCore links WPE::libwpe unconditionally, and EditorLibWPE, GLContextLibWPE and PlatformDisplayLibWPE are listed unconditionally too. ZeroG will need its own replacements for the editor, pasteboard, keyboard-event and platform-display code.

Facts the doc misses that matter for implementation:
- PlayStation turns JIT, DFG and FTL off, and IsoMalloc too.
- It builds bmalloc, WTF, PAL and WebCore as OBJECT libraries. This is how it emulates --whole-archive, which matters for ZeroG's static linking.
- It detects BoringSSL with an OPENSSL_IS_BORINGSSL symbol check, which is reusable for ZeroG.

challenge.reasoning:
I tried to prove the reviewer wrong and couldn't. WebCore does contain a SQLite cookie store, CookieJarDB, built into WebCore for curl ports. But nothing in WebCore connects it to the cookie jar the page actually calls (WebCore::CookieJar) on non-Cocoa builds. The code that does connect them (NetworkStorageSessionCurl.cpp) lives in Source/WebKit/NetworkProcess/curl, which is WebKit2, and ZeroG excludes WebKit2. So the doc is right that the store exists, but it reads as if it works out of the box, and it doesn't. ZeroG has to write that glue itself.

Every guard the reviewer cited checks out:
- In CookieJar.cpp, the Cocoa branch covers lines 126-200. The `#else` branch at 202-244 stubs cookies, setCookies, the 4-arg cookieRequestHeaderFieldValue, cookieRequestHeaderFieldValueDigest, getRawCookies, setRawCookie and deleteCookie with ASSERT_NOT_REACHED.
- getCookiesAsync and setCookieAsync (246-254) do nothing useful on any platform: they return nullopt or false.
- On non-Cocoa, CookieStorageSession has no cookie methods at all.

Corrections and additions to the reviewer's notes:
1. There is no WebCore::NetworkStorageSession any more. It has moved to Source/WebKit/Shared/NetworkStorageSession.h, and its curl version is in Source/WebKit/NetworkProcess/curl/. Porting it means copying WebKit2 code, not reusing WebCore code.
2. The reviewer's override list leaves out cookieRequestHeaderFieldValueDigest. WebCore's cache code calls it (CacheValidation.cpp:399) to handle `Vary: Cookie`. If ZGCookieJar doesn't override it, the base stub asserts in debug builds and returns nullopt.
3. The reviewer listed cookieRequestHeaderFieldValue without saying which one. Only the 4-arg version is virtual. The (Document&, URL) version isn't, and it simply calls the 4-arg one.
4. Override cookiesEnabled too, unless the StorageSessionProvider returns a real session. The base version asserts and returns false when storageSession() is null.
5. The constructor is protected and takes a Ref<StorageSessionProvider>. ZeroG needs its own provider; returning a plain CookieStorageSession (sessionID plus credentials) or nullptr is enough.
6. The jar is handed to the page through PageConfiguration::cookieJar (a Ref<CookieJar>), so ZeroG's Page setup must create a ZGCookieJar.
7. CookieJarDB has its own extra dependencies:
   - it pulls in WebCore's SQLite wrapper (SQLiteDatabase/SQLiteStatement/SQLiteFileSystem);
   - it calls PublicSuffixStore::singleton().isPublicSuffix, so PublicSuffixStoreCurl.cpp and LibPSL must be linked, as Curl.cmake already does with LibPSL::LibPSL;
   - CookieUtil.cpp only compiles under `#if USE(CURL)`.
8. CookieJarDB has two setCookie flavours: Source::Network for HTTP responses and Source::Script for document.cookie. Picking the right one is how HttpOnly cookies are enforced, so the loader and the JS path must not mix them up.
9. For private sessions, upstream passes ":memory:" as the database path (NetworkStorageSessionCurl.cpp:93). ZeroG can reuse that for an in-memory store.
10. CurlRequest.cpp never mentions cookies. The curl loader must add Cookie headers and save Set-Cookie headers itself, through the same store; upstream does this with cookieRequestHeaderFieldValue and setCookiesFromHTTPResponse.

challenge.reasoning:
I tried to clear the doc and could not. The text says bindings are synchronous by default in three places. ZeroG.md:364 says "Chiamate sincrone ... È il caso di default". :403 says "const msg = App.greet(\"Daniele\"), senza await". :634 says "Le binding sono sincrone di default ... i metodi marcati come asincroni girano su un thread di lavoro e lato JS diventano Promise". The Zig struct at :615-616 gives greet and listFiles the same shape: a plain method returning an error union (`![]const u8` and `![]FileEntry`). Nothing marks listFiles as async. Yet :620 calls it with `await App.listFiles("/tmp")`.

There are only two ways to defend the doc, and neither holds.
(1) listFiles is meant to be one of the "marked" async methods and the marker was left out. The doc never defines a marking mechanism. Zig has no method attributes. Zig 0.16 (the target, :604) also has no async keyword: async/await was removed after 0.10, and the new std.Io `io.async` is a runtime call, not something visible in a signature that @typeInfo can read. So any marker has to be a framework convention (a wrapper return type, or a decl listing method names), and the doc specifies none.
(2) The `await` is harmless. That is true at runtime: in JS, `await` on a non-thenable just returns the value. But the doc is still inconsistent. The generated bindings.d.ts would type listFiles as `FileEntry[]`, not `Promise<FileEntry[]>`. With type-aware linting, typescript-eslint's await-thenable rule would flag the call. Strictly that is a lint rule, not a tsc error, so the reviewer's wording "TS lint" is accurate.

So the doc's internal consistency is REFUTED, which matches the reviewer.

The reviewer's secondary point holds too. :634 says the per-call arena is freed at the end of the call ("liberato a fine chiamata"). For an async method, that arena has to live until the worker finishes and the result has been turned into JS values on the main thread, then be freed at resolve/reject. Freeing it when the JS call returns would be a use-after-free. Async error sets also need defining: :632 maps them to a rejected Promise with a typed error code.

The engine side is feasible as described (:365). JSC's public C API has JSObjectMakeDeferredPromise, which returns resolve/reject functions. Because JSC is single-threaded per VM, a worker thread must not call those functions. It has to post back to the main thread, which matches the doc's zg_promise_resolve "eseguito sul thread principale". The doc does not name JSObjectMakeDeferredPromise. Its availability annotation is macOS/iOS-only, but the function is plain C in JSObjectRef.cpp and is also used by the glib port, so other ports can use it. Two things are missing from the doc: zg_promise_resolve has no matching reject, and a resolver must be kept alive (JSValueProtect) across threads until the work completes. Both affect the API design.

challenge.reasoning:
I tried to find somewhere in the doc that defines ownership or lifetime for zg_value, zg_call_arg_string or zg_value_string, and found nothing. I searched ZeroG.md for zg_value, zg_call, zg_result, zg_last_error and the Italian words for ownership, lifetime, exception, throw, free and copy. zg_value appears only in the object table at L352 ("Valore JavaScript visto dall'host, con conversioni verso i tipi C"). zg_call appears only in the example at L374-379. The doc never says:
- whether zg_value_string copies its input;
- who frees the zg_value it returns;
- how long the `name` pointer stays valid, or whether it is NUL-terminated;
- what happens when argument 0 is missing or is not a string.

Passing `call` to zg_value_string hints that the value is scoped to the call, but that is an inference, not something the doc states. So the claim that ownership is "well defined" is false, and the reviewer's REFUTED verdict holds.

One nuance against the reviewer: L632 (the Zig framework error-mapping table) says Zig error sets become a JS exception in sync calls. So the design does intend exceptions to be thrown from native callbacks. What is missing is the C-level primitive for it (for example zg_call_throw). The reviewer is right that the C API as written has no such function.

The reviewer is also right about the conflict with L340. That rule says fallible functions return zg_result, but in the example zg_runtime_create, zg_context_create and zg_window_create return handles, and none of them is checked. The doc has to pick one rule: either creators return a handle (NULL on failure, details from zg_last_error), or they return zg_result with the handle as an out-parameter.

The JSC C API in the checkout adds two facts that confirm these gaps are real and must be specified:
(a) JSStringGetUTF8CString writes into a buffer the caller supplies, sized with JSStringGetMaximumUTF8CStringSize. So zg_call_arg_string can only return a `const char*` if the engine allocates and owns a per-call scratch buffer. Its lifetime has to be documented: valid until the callback returns.
(b) JSStringCreateWithUTF8CString copies its input and needs it NUL-terminated (the "Create Rule"). It is the only public UTF-8 constructor; the other one, JSStringCreateWithCharacters, takes UTF-16 plus a length. So a stack buffer like `reply` is safe only if zg_value_string copies right away. A length-taking variant (to honour L341, "explicit length where needed") would have to go through WTF::String::fromUTF8 internally, or convert to UTF-16 first.

The JSObjectCallAsFunctionCallback signature has a `JSValueRef* exception` out-parameter. That gives a direct path to implement zg_call_throw, which the doc never exposes.

Two smaller defects in the example: snprintf is used without including <stdio.h>, and `embedded_assets` / `embedded_assets_len` are never declared.

challenge.reasoning:
I tried to show the reviewer was wrong and couldn't. The source tree backs their verdict, and it actually understates how many JS VMs exist. One part of the doc is correct: every page and frame on the main thread uses one VM, the leaked process singleton returned by WebCore::commonVM(). So the JSC heap, the GC and any heap limit are process-wide for page content, and a per-view or per-context JSC heap limit can't be done. The literal claim "Una sola VM JavaScript" (L135) is wrong, though. A dedicated Web Worker off the main thread gets its own VM with HeapType::Medium. The reviewer missed that worklets also get their own VMs. A PaintWorklet runs on the main thread with a Document, yet gets a separate VM from VM::tryCreate() rather than commonVM(). An AudioWorklet also gets its own VM. IndexedDB serialization lazily creates another private VM on its thread. So the doc should say "one shared VM for page and frame JavaScript". Workers and worklets have separate heaps and GCs, but they share the allocator (system malloc) with the host. That matters for L183, which says workers "condividono heap e allocatore con l'host": the allocator is shared, the JSC heap is not.

The reviewer's other findings also hold. MemoryCache is a process singleton. LegacySchemeRegistry is all static, covering the secure, CORS-enabled, local, no-access, CSP-bypass, handled-by-scheme-handler and cache-partitioned flags. So scheme security properties can't differ between two zg_contexts, even though L348 lists "schemi custom" as a per-context responsibility. Only the dispatch to handlers can be per-context. One small correction to the reviewer: FontCache isn't strictly global. It is per-thread (FontCache::forCurrentThread). In practice all views share the main-thread instance, and workers or other threads have their own. So "effectively global for views" is fine, but font registration for a single context (L348, L252) would need ZeroG-side filtering. Conclusion: put all memory and cache limits in zg_runtime_config. If the doc keeps any per-view or per-context limit or font/scheme setting, it promises something WebCore doesn't support.

challenge.reasoning:
I looked for anything that would let the JS JIT be switched per view, per context or after startup: a renamed flag, a per-VM or per-JSGlobalObject switch, or a WebCore Setting. None exists in this checkout. Every JS JIT control lives in process-global JSC config, and that config is write-protected for good once the first VM finishes construction.

1. Where the switch lives: the only kill switch is `g_jscConfig.jitDisabled` together with `Options::useJIT()`. All JSC options are stored inside `g_jscConfig` (`OptionsStorage options;`), so they are one global for the whole process.
2. When it locks: `VM::VM` calls `Config::finalize()` at the end of construction. That calls `permanentlyFreeze()`, which marks the config pages read-only. After that, `Options::setOptions` hits a `RELEASE_ASSERT` that the config is not frozen, so it crashes even in release builds.
3. Ordering: `ExecutableAllocator::disableJIT()` asserts that the executable memory pool does not exist yet. Its own comment says it is "always called extra early in the process bootstrap".
4. What upstream does: WebKit2 turns the JIT off only at process launch, through a `-disable-jit` command-line flag in the auxiliary process main. It has no per-page JS JIT control. Its JIT setting is per process pool (`APIProcessPoolConfiguration::setJITEnabled`).
5. One shared VM: WebCore's main thread uses a single VM (`commonVMSlow` → `JSC::VM::create`), shared by every view. Worker VMs read the same global options.
6. WebCore preferences: the only per-page JIT preference is `CSSSelectorJITCompilerEnabled`, and it covers CSS selectors only, not JS. Even that code checks the global `JSC::Options::useJIT()` (`SelectorCompiler.cpp:673`). So there is no partial per-view JS JIT knob.

What this means for the design:
- "Allow external content" must be a `zg_runtime_config` field fixed at `zg_runtime_create`, and setting it must force `jit=off` at that point. It cannot be a view or context option, and it cannot change at run time.
- It must be applied before `JSC::initialize()` and before the first VM is created, i.e. the main-thread VM or any worker VM.
- The doc does not literally say "per view" at L582. But its wording "se abilitato" (if enabled) leaves open a later or per-view toggle, which the code rules out. L590 already says the JIT is a process-level choice; L582 should say the same thing explicitly.
- There is a real inconsistency: L578 says the JIT can be turned off ("JIT disattivabile") as a mitigation, while L177 makes the default "auto". A runtime created with the default that later enables external iframes would already be running with the JIT on, and it cannot be turned off.
- Turning off `useJIT` also turns off the regex JIT and the Wasm JIT tiers. That lowers performance for any app content loaded in the same runtime.

challenge.reasoning:
The PARTIAL verdict holds. I could not refute the reviewer's core points, but three of them go too far and they missed some important gotchas.

What I confirmed:
(1) Turning wasm off does not remove the trap handlers. VMTraps registers an AccessFault (SIGSEGV/SIGBUS) handler, and InitializeThreading.cpp:144-146 calls it whenever !usePollingTraps, with no dependence on wasm. On Linux, SignalHandlers::finalize installs a sigaction for every signal that has at least one registered handler (Signals.cpp:573-594). So tying the chaining rationale to wasm (L153) is wrong.
(2) Signals.cpp already chains trap signals to handlers that existed earlier, saving them in oldActions at :592 and calling them at :528-538. Handlers can only be added while initState==Initializing (:74). Config::finalize freezes them (WTFConfig.cpp:191-197). Init order therefore matters.
(3) The GC suspend signal is installed in every build (ThreadingPOSIX.cpp:195-238). It only logs 'Overriding existing handler' (:231-232) and is never chained (:233 passes a null old-action).
(4) useWasmFastMemory defaults to true (OptionsList.h:595). It is forced off when !ENABLE(WEBASSEMBLY) (Options.cpp:657-660), so it only matters for the standard profile.

Where the reviewer is wrong or overstated:
(a) 'Every profile' is too strong. disableAllJITOptions forces usePollingTraps=true (Options.cpp:737-749), and this runs whenever useJIT is false (:881-882). With zg_runtime_config jit=false and wasm off, there is no SIGSEGV/SIGBUS handler on Linux at all, only the GC suspend signal. The accurate scope is 'every JIT-enabled or wasm-enabled configuration'.
(b) Calling L151 'outdated' is only half right. The mechanism changed: there is no check anymore, only a log. The crash outcome is still real. signalHandlerSuspendResume dereferences targetThread without a null check (ThreadingPOSIX.cpp:133,138). targetThread is nullptr until the first suspend (:585,619) and is never reset afterwards. A SIGUSR1 sent by the host before the first GC suspend therefore dereferences a null pointer. Later stray signals act on a stale thread pointer, which can corrupt the suspend semaphore or leave a thread stuck in sigsuspend.
(c) The macOS 'real conflict with crash reporters' is overstated. WebKit sets exception ports per thread, only on threads it has registered (thread_set_exception_ports at Signals.cpp:387, registerThreadForMachExceptionHandling at :406-415). When no handler claims an exception it returns KERN_FAILURE (:285), and the kernel then falls back to the task-level ports. Those are what Crashpad and Breakpad use, so normally they coexist. There is only a conflict with tools that set ports per thread. Also, when JIT is off and the sandbox policy is unknown, Darwin turns off all signal-based options (Options.cpp:752-760, 883-889). L155 is still incomplete, though. Windows does install trap handling: a first-in-chain vectored exception handler (SignalsWin.cpp:146-156, AddVectoredExceptionHandler(1,...)). It sees every access violation in the host process, but it chains by OS design because the unhandled return value is not EXCEPTION_CONTINUE_EXECUTION (:91-107). So 'Linux only' is correct for the GC suspend signal, but not for trap handling as a whole.

Gotchas missed by both the doc and the reviewer:
- Linux trap sigaction uses sa_flags = SA_SIGINFO only, with no SA_ONSTACK (Signals.cpp:590). A SIGSEGV from stack overflow on a JIT-enabled thread therefore runs WebKit's handler on the overflowed stack. That defeats the host crash handler's sigaltstack before chaining can ever reach it.
- Chaining calls oldAction.sa_sigaction whenever it is non-null (:530-536). It ignores the old handler's sa_flags and sa_mask, and would jump to address 1 if the old disposition was SIG_IGN.
- JSC already has a hook to pick the GC signal programmatically, JSConfigureSignalForGC (JSBasePrivate.h:58, JSBase.cpp:186-193, non-Darwin and non-Windows only). It returns false once the signal has been configured, so zg_runtime_create must call it before JSC/WTF initialization. The getenv path is skipped when it is used (ThreadingPOSIX.cpp:197).
- The alternate-signal-stack GC hang that L152 attributes to Bun's fork appears to be handled upstream already, by backing off and retrying (ThreadingPOSIX.cpp:151-161).

I tried to show the reviewer was wrong and could not. Their evidence holds, and on two points the doc is in worse shape than they said.

1) The arithmetic is right. The 'Tenere' rows at L459-472 add up to 16 libraries, and ANGLE (L492) makes 17. So the number matches the table, but the table leaves things out.

2) SDL3 is missing from the count. It is named for window mode at L477 and in the license table at L554, but it is not counted. The same goes for zstd (L272 lists 'zlib, brotli, zstd' for response decompression), which does not appear in the decisions table at all. These are omissions, not real contradictions: SDL3 is only for window mode, and zstd is optional in curl.

3) Fontconfig: the reviewer is right. On every non-Windows, non-PlayStation target, the in-tree Skia CMake hard-requires Fontconfig and builds SkFontMgr_fontconfig. Dropping it needs a CMake patch that adds SkFontMgr_custom_* sources. The doc says Fontconfig is replaced (L476) and lists dropping it among the things that 'si toglie o si sostituisce' (L445), but it never says this requires patching Skia's CMakeLists.

4) HarfBuzz 'senza ICU' (L460) is wrong. Three WebCore files include hb-icu.h under USE(HARFBUZZ) and call hb_icu_script_to_script, and every port's find_package asks for the ICU component. The fix is small: build HarfBuzz with hb-icu, or patch those calls (e.g. to hb_script_from_iso15924_tag). But as the code stands, the doc's statement is false.

5) libwebp 'escludibile' (L470): this is worse than the reviewer said. They suggested that setting USE_SKIA_ENCODERS=OFF would be enough. It is not. WebCore's ImageDecoders.cmake always compiles WEBPImageDecoder.cpp and links WebP::demux, with no guard. WEBPImageDecoder.h includes webp/decode.h and webp/demux.h without any #if. ScalableImageDecoder.cpp creates the WebP decoder unconditionally. So libwebp cannot be dropped without patching WebCore, whatever USE_SKIA_ENCODERS is set to.

6) A gotcha the reviewer missed, which affects the '17 su Windows' number: upstream Skia on WIN32 uses DirectWrite (SkFontMgr_win_dw, SkScalerContext_win_dw) and does not link FreeType. OptionsWin.cmake has no find_package(Freetype). If ZeroG follows upstream on Windows, the Windows count would be 16 (minus FreeType, plus ANGLE). If it wants FreeType on Windows for the same rendering on every OS, it needs a Skia CMake patch. The doc does not say which.

The PARTIAL verdict holds. Having ANGLE in minimal while WebGL is off is not a contradiction. Upstream already supports building ANGLE only as an EGL/GLES provider: Source/CMakeLists.txt:30 adds ANGLE when `ENABLE_WEBGL OR USE_ANGLE_EGL`, and ANGLE/CMakeLists.txt:163 does the same. Skia links ANGLE::EGL when USE_ANGLE_EGL is set (skia/CMakeLists.txt:859-866). The real conflict is L200, which says 'WebGL incluso' for Windows while L435/L500 turn WebGL off in minimal. Two of the reviewer's points are wrong or misdirected.
(1) D3D9 is not needed. PlatformWin.cmake still says 'ANGLE will not compile without it' and appends ${d3d9_backend_sources} / ANGLE_ENABLE_D3D9 / d3d9. (2) 'Override ANGLE to STATIC/OBJECT' is aimed at the wrong file. WEBKIT_INCLUDE_CONFIG_FILES_IF_EXISTS (WebKitMacros.cmake:234-242) only includes Platform${PORT}.cmake. claims.doc_section: Struttura L420-424; Cosa resta dinamico L518-519; Simboli L161
claims.evidence: WebKit requires C++23: Source/cmake/OptionsCommon.cmake:1-3 (CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 23, REQUIRED, no extensions). It requires GCC >= 13.1: Source/cmake/WebKitCommon.cmake:134-137. Clang < 19 is only tolerated through a workaround: Source/cmake/WebKitCompilerFlags.cmake:243-252 ('Remove once Clang 18 does no longer need to be supported'). MSVC is dropped, clang-cl only: Source/cmake/OptionsMSVC.cmake:1. Upstream uses /MD, not /MT: OptionsMSVC.cmake:58 `set(CMAKE_MSVC_RUNTIME_LIBRARY MultiThreadedDLL)`. Code is built with -fno-exceptions/-fno-rtti and /GR- (WebKitCompilerFlags.cmake:198-203, OptionsMSVC.cmake:91-92). CMake >= 3.20 (CMakeLists.txt:9). WTF calls statx (Source/WTF/wtf/posix/POSIXExtras.h:130), which needs glibc 2.28, so 2.28 is the hard floor.
claims.implication: Decide which compiler builds WebKit on Linux. If zig does the final link with its bundled libc++/libc++abi, WebKit must be compiled against the same libc++ headers: use `zig c++` as CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER (WebKit flag compatibility is untested), or clang -stdlib=libc++ from the same LLVM version. Mixing objects built against libstdc++ fails. On Windows, /MT means overriding OptionsMSVC.cmake:58, and it forces every host that links the static archive to also use /MT (LNK2038 RuntimeLibrary mismatch). Document that, or ship the static archive in both variants. Localizing libc++ (L161) must also cover the unnamespaced libc++abi symbols (__cxa_*, operator new/delete), which clash with a host's libstdc++/libsupc++.

challenge.reasoning:
The reviewer's PARTIAL verdict holds. One piece of their evidence is wrong and has to be corrected.

What I re-confirmed in the checkout:
- C++23 is required.
- GCC must be 13.1 or newer. There is no hard minimum for Clang; only a workaround path for Clang below 19.
- MSVC is no longer supported; only clang-cl.
- Upstream Windows builds use the DLL CRT (MultiThreadedDLL), not /MT.
- Builds use -fno-exceptions / -fno-rtti, or /GR- and /EH- on clang-cl.
- CMake 3.20 or newer is required.

So "clang everywhere, clang-cl on Windows" matches upstream. A static C++ runtime is possible but not the upstream default, and the doc does not mention what it costs.

Where the reviewer is wrong: statx does not make glibc 2.28 a hard floor. WTF uses statx only when a configure-time check finds it. In OptionsCommon.cmake:378, WEBKIT_CHECK_HAVE_FUNCTION(HAVE_STATX statx sys/stat.h) sets HAVE_STATX. All uses are guarded by `#if OS(LINUX) && HAVE(STATX)` (POSIXExtras.h:127,176; FileSystemPOSIX.cpp:98,103). Without it, fileCreationTime() just returns std::nullopt. WebKit would build against an older glibc too. With 2.28, statx is found and used, so the doc's choice of 2.28 is fine. The reviewer's "hard floor" wording should be dropped.

What the reviewer missed: upstream explicitly supports libc++ on non-Apple targets. OptionsCommon.cmake:273-316 checks for libc++ (_LIBCPP_VERSION), then for libc++ 19 or newer, then libstdc++ (_GLIBCXX_RELEASE), and picks a hardening/assertion macro for each. Clang plus libc++ on Linux is therefore a supported path, not untested ground. The real limits are: libc++ should be 19 or newer (else the old _LIBCPP_ENABLE_ASSERTIONS path is used), and every object, WebKit included, must be compiled against the same libc++ headers that zig links. Mixing libstdc++-built objects with zig's libc++ fails, as the reviewer says. Their Windows point also stands: /MT must override OptionsMSVC.cmake:58, and a static /MT archive forces the same CRT on the host (LNK2038). Their point about libc++abi symbols for L161 also stands. Upstream sets MultiThreadedDLL only because Swift ships just a release-CRT swiftrt.obj. Nothing else in Source/cmake requires /MD, so overriding it to /MT looks mechanically feasible, but that needs a build to confirm.

Overall: the toolchain direction fits WebKit's requirements. The doc leaves out the libc++ header/version matching, the CRT override and the host-compatibility consequence, and the libc++abi symbol-localization detail. The statx/glibc floor is not a real constraint.

challenge.reasoning:
I tried to refute the reviewer and could not. PARTIAL holds, and checking SDL3 upstream makes it lean toward REFUTED. The reviewer left SDL3's feature coverage as 'to be checked externally'. I checked it against upstream SDL main.

What SDL3 covers:
- Open, save and folder dialogs (SDL_dialog.h).
- Message boxes (SDL_messagebox.h), which are enough for alert and confirm.
- Clipboard with MIME types, file drop events, display enumeration, borderless and fullscreen windows.
- IME on Linux through IBus/Fcitx over D-Bus.
- IME on macOS through an NSTextInputClient implementation.

What it does not cover:
1. TSF (L319). SDL3's Windows IME (src/video/windows/SDL_windowskeyboard.c) is IMM32 only. It loads imm32.dll with SDL_LoadObject and uses ImmGetContext, ImmSetCompositionWindow and related calls, guarded by SDL_DISABLE_WINDOWS_IME. There are no ITfThreadMgr or ITfUIElementSink references, so the TSF requirement is not met.
2. Menus (L645). There is no application-menu or context-menu API. include/SDL3 has no SDL_menu.h; only SDL_tray.h exists, and the system tray is deferred past v1 in the doc.
3. Single instance (L649). SDL3 has no API for it.
4. prompt() (L325). WebCore's ChromeClient::runJavaScriptPrompt (WebCore/page/ChromeClient.h:278) is synchronous and needs a text field. SDL message boxes have only buttons, so prompt() needs native code.
5. Composition quality on macOS. SDL's NSTextInputClient strips the attributes and sends only text plus cursor and selection. validAttributesForMarkedText returns an empty array, attributedSubstringForProposedRange returns nil, and characterIndexForPoint returns 0. WebCore's Editor::setComposition (WebCore/editing/Editor.h:434) expects CompositionUnderline and CompositionHighlight vectors. Through SDL the clause underlines are lost and reconversion does not work.

Corrections to the reviewer:
- L319 does not say the NSTextInputClient has to be the engine's own. It just lists NSTextInputClient. However, SDL's implementation is too thin (point 5), so the conclusion that it should be implemented natively still stands.
- Native dialogs are mostly covered by SDL, apart from prompt. The reviewer implied dialogs were unverified.

Their other points hold:
- L477 leaves the choice open between SDL3 and a custom window layer.

claims.doc_section: Cosa fa il motore per la conformità L561-564; Simboli L160
claims.evidence: The doc never mentions LTO, but WebKit supports it (Source/cmake/WebKitCompilerFlags.cmake:350-366 LTO_MODE, -flto=thin/full, lld-link /opt:lldlto). With LTO, the objects are LLVM bitcode tied to the exact LLVM version, and the 'archivio unico prelinkato e localizzato' (L160) is a derived artifact that the LGPL user must be able to regenerate.

challenge.reasoning:
I tried to refute the reviewer and couldn't. Their evidence holds, with one correction to how it reads.

1. The relink kit described at L561 is the standard way to meet LGPL static linking, and it is workable in principle. WebCore is "GNU Library General Public License version 2 or later" (Source/WebCore/dom/Document.cpp:12-15), and Source/JavaScriptCore/COPYING.LIB exists. Under LGPL v2 §6 the app's object code must be supplied so the user can relink with a changed library. The doc also has a real point in its favor that the reviewer did not mention: the public API is pure C99 with opaque handles and no exposed WebKit types (L333-337). So the app's object files contain no inlined LGPL code, which keeps them a "work that uses the Library".

2. The LTO facts are accurate but slightly overstated. Source/cmake/WebKitCompilerFlags.cmake:350-366 adds -flto=${LTO_MODE} and lld-link /opt:lldlto=2 only when the user sets LTO_MODE. OptionsCommon.cmake:30 switches to lld when LTO is on. The only CMake preset that enables it is mac-performance (CMakePresets.json:149-160, LTO_MODE=thin). Tools/Scripts/webkitdirs.pm:3156 passes it only when asked. Thin LTO is the default only in the Xcode xcconfig files (Source/WTF/Configurations/Base.xcconfig:125), which are not used for a CMake PORT. So LTO is opt-in for ZeroG. It is a rule to state ("app objects in the kit must be native objects, not LLVM bitcode"), not something the build forces. LTO inside the engine can still work if the prelink step (ld.lld -r) turns the bitcode into one native object. Either way, regenerating the archive needs the same toolchain.

3. The doc does leave out what makes the kit usable. L160 says the engine ships as one prelinked archive with all symbols made local except zg_*. That archive is built from the LGPL code, so whoever modifies WebCore must be able to rebuild it. The corresponding source (L564) must therefore include:
- the partial-link and symbol-localization scripts;
- the build scripts for the dependency sysroot (L421);
- the pinned versions of clang, zig, lld and objcopy.

The relink "script" is in practice a zig build call (L423), so the Zig version must be pinned too. The doc says none of this, and it never mentions LTO.

4. A gap neither the doc nor the reviewer covers: the localize-symbols approach is easy on ELF (ld -r plus objcopy --localize-hidden or a version script) and on Mach-O (ld -r -exported_symbols_list). lld-link has no relocatable (-r) output for COFF, so on Windows the prelinked, localized single archive, and with it the kit's rebuild recipe, needs another mechanism. The checkout can't settle this.

Net: the reviewer's PARTIAL and their three rules stand. One clarification: LTO is off by default in WebKit's CMake, so the risk only appears if ZeroG turns it on.

claims.evidence: ELF works with `ld.lld -r` followed by `objcopy --localize-hidden` and -fvisibility=hidden builds. Mach-O can use `ld -r -exported_symbols_list`, which demotes the rest to private extern; this needs checking with the new Apple linker. COFF has no relocatable link (link.exe and lld-link have no -r) and no hidden visibility for static libs. Upstream already struggles with large static WebCore archives: Source/cmake/OptionsPlayStation.cmake:368-373 'The size of a libWebCore.a is too much for ranlib' (it uses OBJECT libs). claims.implication: On Windows, prefix the C dependencies at build time (BORINGSSL_PREFIX, zlib Z_PREFIX, libpng PNG_PREFIX, a renamed SQLite amalgamation, curl via a CURL_STATICLIB rename header) and keep the WebKit C++ symbols as they are, since their mangled namespaces rarely clash. Alternatively make the DLL profile the default on Windows. Spell out the per-OS procedure in the doc.

challenge.reasoning:
I tried to show the reviewer was wrong and could not. The claim says one prelinked archive with only zg_* left global works "on every OS". That holds for ELF and Mach-O. It fails on COFF/Windows: link.exe and lld-link cannot do a relocatable (-r) link, and a COFF static symbol is private to the single .obj it is in. So symbols used across WebKit's thousands of objects cannot be made local without first merging them into one object, and the normal tools cannot do that merge. The only theoretical route is merging the whole engine as LLVM bitcode (llvm-link + internalize + llc), which is impractical at WebCore size. PARTIAL stands.

Some of the reviewer's details need correcting, and the doc misses a few things:

(1) ELF: "ld -r + objcopy --localize-hidden + -fvisibility=hidden" is not enough. WTF_EXPORT_PRIVATE, JS_EXPORT_PRIVATE and WEBCORE_EXPORT give default visibility (visibility("default")) when STATICALLY_LINKED_WITH_* or BUILDING_* is defined. --localize-hidden would leave thousands of WebKit symbols global. Two fixes work: predefine those macros as empty (each header checks `#if !defined(...)` first, so a predefinition wins), or use `objcopy --keep-global-symbols=<zg list>` (-G), which localizes every defined non-listed symbol whatever its visibility. Statically linked libc++ must also be built hermetic/hidden, or be covered by -G.

(2) Mach-O: by default `ld -r` turns private-extern (hidden) symbols into static (local) ones. Only -keep_private_externs keeps them private-extern. So `ld -r -exported_symbols_list` does localize; the reviewer's "demotes to private extern" undersells it. Behaviour of the new Apple linker (ld-prime) still needs testing: UNVERIFIABLE without a build.

(3) Windows has extra blockers beyond the missing -r. With USE(DECLSPEC_ATTRIBUTE), the export macros become __declspec(dllexport) in a static build. The .lib would then carry /EXPORT directives (in its .drectve sections), and the host .exe would export WebKit symbols. The macros must be predefined as empty. Upstream also never builds static JSC/WebCore on Windows: OptionsWin.cmake makes them SHARED. And the MSVC runtime is fixed to MultiThreadedDLL (/MD), so a host that uses /MT gets a RuntimeLibrary mismatch at link time.

(4) The doc's BoringSSL-prefix sub-claim is CONFIRMED, and upstream already does it. libwebrtc's CMakeLists sets BORINGSSL_PREFIX for its static build on non-Apple, for exactly this collision reason. The prefix_symbols.h headers come pregenerated in the tree. This supports the reviewer's advice to prefix the C dependencies on Windows instead of localizing.

(5) The ranlib / OBJECT-library evidence for PlayStation is correct. The 4 GB COFF archive limit (4-byte offsets in the linker members) comes from the PE/COFF spec, not this tree: plausible, but I did not check it here.

Net: PARTIAL. ELF and Mach-O are feasible once the export macros are dealt with; COFF is not feasible as written. The doc should spell out a procedure per OS.

L227 says the engine renders 'sul proprio thread' while L225 says the engine draws on the runtime-owner thread, which is ambiguous. WebCore hooks: Source/WebCore/page/ChromeClient.h:484 displayRefreshMonitorFactory(), :527 triggerRenderingUpdate(), :529 scheduleRenderingUpdate(). Source/WebCore/page/RenderingUpdateScheduler.cpp exists. On the generic event loop, WebCore RunLoopObserver is a no-op: Source/WebCore/platform/RunLoopObserver.cpp:52-66 (schedule/invalidate empty when !USE(CF) && !USE(GLIB_EVENT_LOOP)).
