Texture/CPU mode: an explicit `zg_view_render(view, frame_timestamp)` or `zg_view_vsync()` from the app. Implement it through a ZeroG DisplayRefreshMonitorFactory, and drive rendering updates from the embedding layer, since RunLoopObserver does nothing on RunLoopGeneric. Fix L227 to say 'on the runtime thread'. Also, 'same device, fence is enough' (L232) is false for D3D11: the immediate context is not thread-safe, so the engine needs its own device/context, or ID3D11Multithread protection, or shared NT handles with a keyed mutex. With triple buffering and damage-only redraw, the engine must also track buffer age or copy forward.

challenge.reasoning:
REFUTED is too strong. The design itself is not contradictory, but it leaves things out, and one sub-claim (L232, for D3D11) is wrong without more synchronization.

1) "Presentation advances rAF" is a real pattern in WebKit upstream, and it already works with a separate render thread. In WPE/GTK, ThreadedCompositor composites on its own thread. AcceleratedSurface takes a frameCompleteHandler, and that frame-done signal is what lets the main thread schedule the next rendering update. So rendering on a different thread from the one that runs the rendering update does not conflict with presentation pacing. In ZeroG's texture mode, the natural signal is the app's zg_surface_acquire/release (or its zg_view_render call). Using it is a design gap, not a logical contradiction.

2) L227's "sul proprio thread" reads most naturally as "the engine's own thread", which is the runtime-owner thread from L225. That is ambiguous wording, not an inconsistency.

3) CPU mode has no hardware vsync, but L215 says "il vsync dell'applicazione". In CPU/texture mode the app's zg_view_render cadence is the app's vsync, so the claim still holds if the tick is defined that way.

4) What WebCore does by default supports the reviewer's main warning: nothing ties rAF to presentation unless the port builds it. With no DisplayRefreshMonitorFactory (ChromeClient default returns nullptr), WebCore falls back to its built-in monitor. On Windows that is DisplayRefreshMonitorWin, a 16ms RunLoop timer the reviewer missed. On other non-Cocoa platforms it returns nullptr, and RenderingUpdateScheduler then uses a one-shot Timer set to preferredRenderingUpdateInterval. Either way, rAF is clock-driven, not presentation-driven.

The reviewer's RunLoopObserver point is correct: on generic, non-GLib/non-CF loops it does nothing. That matters because upstream LayerTreeHost relies on a RunLoopObserver to schedule rendering updates.

5) L232 ("same device, fence is enough") does not hold for D3D11. The immediate context is not thread-safe; that comes from Microsoft's documentation and cannot be checked in this tree. ANGLE can wrap an app-supplied D3D11 device (Renderer11 mCreatedWithDeviceEXT on EGL_PLATFORM_DEVICE_EXT), but the ANGLE source has no ID3D11Multithread use. So if the engine and the app share one device across threads, you need ID3D11Multithread protection, separate devices with shared NT handles plus a keyed mutex/fence, or all submissions on one thread.

Corrected statement: the claim is feasible and has upstream precedent, but the doc leaves the rAF clock undefined for each mode. Nothing in WebCore provides presentation-driven rAF out of the box, and the D3D11 same-device sub-claim needs extra synchronization.

Missing gotcha: PLATFORM() macros come from the OS unless BUILDING_<PORT>__ is defined. A new ZeroG port would therefore silently get PLATFORM(WIN) or PLATFORM(MAC) code paths, including DisplayRefreshMonitorWin and LegacyDisplayRefreshMonitorMac, unless it adds its own BUILDING_ZEROG__ / PLATFORM(ZEROG) branch in WTF/wtf/PlatformLegacy.h.

JSCOnly forces the generic loop with SET_AND_EXPOSE_TO_BUILD(USE_GENERIC_EVENT_LOOP 1) and WTF_DEFAULT_EVENT_LOOP 0 (Source/cmake/OptionsJSCOnly.cmake:109-110), but still uses per-OS WTF sources such as win/MainThreadWin.cpp and win/SignalsWin.cpp (Source/WTF/wtf/PlatformJSCOnly.cmake:5-30). RunLoop has the hooks ZeroG needs: cycle() (RunLoop.h:123) for zg_runtime_update and setWakeUpCallback (RunLoop.h:147-148) for the wakeup handle. PlayStation uses the default loop, which resolves to generic, so L69 is confirmed for it.
claims.implication: The ZeroG Options file must force the generic loop the way JSCOnly does. On macOS, building WebCore without PLATFORM(COCOA)/USE(CF) is uncharted, and zg_runtime_run has to integrate with NSApp/CFRunLoop for AppKit, IME and display link. Treat macOS as its own risk item, which the CI order (L703, macOS third) already implies.

challenge.reasoning:
I tried to refute the reviewer and could not. Everything they cited checks out at the stated lines. Two things in the doc are factually true: RunLoopGeneric is already used by JSCOnly and PlayStation, and a single Options file can cover several OSes, as OptionsJSCOnly.cmake shows with its WIN32 and APPLE branches. The claim that "the same configuration applies to Linux, Windows and macOS and the per-OS differences live only in the platform layer" is not true as written, for three reasons.
(1) The event loop is chosen per OS unless the port overrides it. The port has to force USE_GENERIC_EVENT_LOOP=1 and WTF_DEFAULT_EVENT_LOOP=0, the way JSCOnly does.
(2) The WTF source lists stay per OS even inside one port: win/*.cpp on Windows; posix/* plus MainThreadGeneric elsewhere; Mach exception MIG generation and cocoa/TimeZoneCocoa.cpp on Apple.
(3) The reviewer missed two things, and both make the claim weaker.
(a) PlatformLegacy.h derives PLATFORM() from the OS unless a BUILDING_<PORT>__ macro is defined. A new port with no branch there gets PLATFORM(MAC), and with it PLATFORM(COCOA), USE(CF) and USE(FOUNDATION), on macOS, and PLATFORM(WIN) on Windows. Only JSCOnly is excluded today. ZeroG therefore needs an upstream patch adding its own branch, or it will silently pick up the Cocoa/CF or Win code paths.
(b) WebCore's MainThreadSharedTimer, the timer behind every DOM timer, is guarded by OS(WINDOWS), not by the event-loop type. On Windows the header drops the RunLoop::Timer member, and the implementation is the hidden-HWND WM_TIMER version. So even with the generic loop forced, WebCore on Windows needs a running Win32 message pump on the main thread, or a patch to the guard. That is a per-OS difference inside upstream WebCore, not in the project's platform layer.
The reviewer's macOS caveat is sound. The RunLoop hooks they cite, cycle() and setWakeUpCallback, do exist and setWakeUpCallback is available under the generic loop.
challenge.evidence:

claims.claim: System malloc (USE_SYSTEM_MALLOC=ON) gives 'no virtual memory reservations'; a hardened allocator such as mimalloc would replace libc malloc (L144-146).
claims.evidence: WebKit already vendors mimalloc as an alternative to bmalloc/libpas: Source/bmalloc/mimalloc, option USE_MIMALLOC at Source/cmake/WebKitFeatures.cmake:366, and bmalloc.cpp:145-163 (mi_free, mi_theap_collect). The JIT still reserves a fixed executable pool of 1 GB on x86_64 and 128/512 MB on ARM64 (Source/JavaScriptCore/jit/ExecutableAllocator.cpp:93-105).
claims.implication: Evaluate USE_MIMALLOC, which is supported upstream, gives WebKit-only heaps and does not interpose on the host's malloc, rather than relinking libc malloc. Reword L144: the JIT pool reservation stays unless jit=off, and so does wasm fast memory in standard.

challenge.reasoning:
I checked the reviewer's evidence and it is correct: upstream ships mimalloc as a third allocator, and the JIT pool is reserved at a fixed size. But PARTIAL is too generous, because the claim fails in more ways than the reviewer found.

(1) USE_SYSTEM_MALLOC=ON does not compile on Windows. BPlatform.h has a hard #error for that case, and the doc targets Windows (L7, L86). On Windows the only choices are libpas, the default for x86_64/ARM64, or mimalloc.

(2) "No virtual memory reservations" is false on every 64-bit platform, whatever the allocator. JSC always reserves a 4 GB Structure heap. This is guarded only by CPU(ADDRESS64), not by the allocator choice. JIT on adds 1 GB on x86_64 (128/512 MB on ARM64) of executable pool. Wasm fast memory reserves about 4 GB plus a redzone per memory through OSAllocator when Gigacage is off.

(3) The mitigation in the doc, "link a hardened mimalloc in place of libc malloc without huge reservations", does not match upstream either. Upstream's USE_MIMALLOC builds mimalloc as an object library with MI_OVERRIDE=OFF, so it never replaces libc malloc. That part is actually good for an embedded engine. It leaves MI_SECURE at its default OFF, so you get no hardening unless you turn it on yourself. mimalloc reserves arenas 1 GiB at a time by default on 64-bit. With mimalloc Gigacage is disabled at compile time. With system malloc it is disabled at run time.

What it means for ZeroG: the realistic option for all three OSes is USE_MIMALLOC, optionally with MI_SECURE and a smaller arena_reserve. You cannot avoid the virtual memory reservations, but you can shrink them: the structureHeapSizeInKB option, FIXED_EXECUTABLE_MEMORY_POOL_SIZE_IN_MB or JIT off, and useWasmFastMemory=false. L144 and L146 need rewording to say that.
challenge.evidence:
Checkout: C:/Users/dzonerzy/CppProjects/ZeroG/third_party/webkit/Source/

- **System malloc is blocked on Windows:** bmalloc/bmalloc/BPlatform.h:430-432 says `#if BOS(WINDOWS) #error "System malloc configuration is not supported in Windows since aligned memory cannot be freed via ::free. Use mimalloc instead"`. bmalloc/bmalloc/SystemHeap.cpp:110-112 says "SystemHeap unimplemented on Windows".
- **Allocator options and defaults:** cmake/WebKitFeatures.cmake:365-366 defines USE_SYSTEM_MALLOC and USE_MIMALLOC. Lines 112-118 set both to OFF on x86_64/ARM64, which means libpas. BPlatform.h:400 enables libpas on Windows, and lines 420-436 make libpas, mimalloc and system malloc mutually exclusive.
- **Structure heap reservation:** JavaScriptCore/heap/StructureAlignedMemoryAllocator.cpp:107-111 calls `OSAllocator::tryReserveUncommittedAligned(mappedHeapSize, ...)`. Line 271 sets `baseSize = 4 * GB` (the non-iOS, non-PlayStation default). The whole block is guarded only by CPU(ADDRESS64) (line 84). It can be overridden with runtime/OptionsList.h:99 `structureHeapSizeInKB`.
- **JIT pool:** JavaScriptCore/jit/ExecutableAllocator.cpp:93-104 sets the fixed pool size: FIXED_EXECUTABLE_MEMORY_POOL_SIZE_IN_MB override, 512 MB / 128 MB on ARM64, 1 GB on x86_64, 32 MB otherwise.
- **Wasm fast memory:** JavaScriptCore/runtime/BufferMemoryHandle.cpp:73 gives `maxMemory32Bytes + fastMappedRedzoneBytes()`. Line 91 reserves it with `OSAllocator::tryReserveUncommitted` (no Gigacage). It is on by default via OptionsList.h:595 `useWasmFastMemory, true`.
- **Gigacage is off in both alternatives:**

  - With system malloc: bmalloc/bmalloc/Gigacage.cpp:278-280 returns early when `shouldBmallocAllocateThroughSystemHeap()`.
- **How upstream builds mimalloc:** bmalloc/mimalloc/CMakeLists.txt sets `MI_OVERRIDE OFF`, `MI_BUILD_OBJECT ON` and static/shared OFF, and requires CMake >= 3.25 (fatal error otherwise). It does not set MI_SECURE. bmalloc/CMakeLists.txt:3-5 and :653 link `$<TARGET_OBJECTS:mimalloc-obj>` into bmalloc. bmalloc/mimalloc/mimalloc/CMakeLists.txt:7 shows `MI_SECURE ... OFF` by default.

- **JSC already uses mimalloc arenas:** StructureAlignedMemoryAllocator.cpp:90-94 and :137-141 (`mi_manage_os_memory_ex`), and bmalloc/bmalloc.cpp:145-172 (mi_free, mi_theap_collect, mi_collect).
- **Doc targets Windows:** ZeroG.md L7 and L86, which conflicts with the USE_SYSTEM_MALLOC=ON decision at L144.

claims.claim: The WebSocket backend question (L299, L758) is still open.
claims.doc_section: Dev mode L299; Questioni aperte L758
claims.evidence: WebCore now has only the abstract channel: Source/WebCore/Modules/websockets/ThreadableWebSocketChannel.h, with no WebSocketChannel.cpp. The legacy implementation lives in Source/WebKitLegacy/WebCoreSupport/WebSocketChannel.cpp and SocketStreamHandleImpl.cpp, with the CFNet backend in SocketStreamHandleImplCFNet.cpp. The curl primitives remain: Source/WebCore/platform/network/curl/CurlStream.cpp and CurlStreamScheduler.cpp, used by Source/WebKit/NetworkProcess/curl/WebSocketTaskCurl.cpp. CurlContext uses CURLOPT_CONNECT_ONLY with curl_easy_send (CurlContext.cpp:706, 979), so curl's ws protocol is not needed. The frame and handshake helpers (WebSocketHandshake, WebSocketFrame, WebSocketDeflater) are still in WebCore.
claims.implication: Close the question: port WebKitLegacy's WebSocketChannel (BSD) plus a CurlStream-based SocketStreamHandleImpl, and serve it through a SocketProvider. curl can stay built with http/https only. Note that CurlContext.cpp:555 also enables the 'file' protocol.

challenge.reasoning:
I agree with PARTIAL. The doc does leave the question open (L758 is an unchecked box, and L299 says "va verificato presto", i.e. it still needs checking), so the claim is literally true. But the checkout answers most of the question, so it no longer needs to be open. The doc asks whether WebCore's curl code is still there or whether the embedding layer must do the work. The answer is both:
(a) The low-level curl socket code is still in WebCore: CurlStream and CurlStreamScheduler.
(b) WebCore no longer has a concrete WebSocketChannel. Only ThreadableWebSocketChannel is left, and Modules/websockets/ has no WebSocketChannel.cpp.
(c) The upstream curl glue class SocketStreamHandleImplCurl is gone.

Every file and line the reviewer cited checks out. I could not find a renamed or hidden curl SocketStreamHandle anywhere in Source/.

The reviewer's plan underestimates the work in four places:
1. WebKitLegacy's SocketStreamHandleImpl is CFNetwork-specific, not a portable base you can drop curl into. Its header uses CF types throughout (CFHTTPMessageRef, CFReadStreamRef/CFWriteStreamRef, RetainPtr<CFURLRef>, PAC handling). SocketStreamHandleImpl.cpp is wrapped in #if PLATFORM(COCOA) (L28 to L188). A curl SocketStreamHandleImpl has to be written from scratch on top of CurlStreamScheduler, not adapted.
2. The legacy WebSocketChannel.cpp:124 calls SocketStreamHandleImpl::create with a Cocoa-flavoured signature: SessionID, credentialPartition, SourceApplicationAuditToken, StorageSessionProvider*, shouldAcceptInsecureCertificates (SocketStreamHandleImpl.h:50). That call has to be changed or shimmed.
3. LegacySocketProvider is Objective-C++ (LegacySocketProvider.cpp uses #import). WebKitLegacy as a whole is only built for Cocoa (CMakeLists.txt lists WebViewGroup.mm; only PlatformCocoa.cmake exists). It will not compile unchanged in a non-Cocoa CMake port. The C++ rewrite is small.
4. SocketProvider (WebCore/page/SocketProvider.h) has two pure virtual methods: createWebSocketChannel and createWebTransportSession. The legacy provider handles the second by delegating to WebCore::emptySocketProvider() (EmptyClients.cpp:1270-1279), and ZeroG can do the same.

The reviewer missed one alternative: WebKit/NetworkProcess/curl/WebSocketTaskCurl.cpp already runs the full client handshake and frame handling with WebCore::WebSocketHandshake on CurlStreamScheduler. It is a working curl reference that is easier to adapt than the CFNet code.

The reviewer is right that curl's own ws:// support is not needed. CurlStream.cpp:48 rewrites ws/wss to http/https before CONNECT_ONLY. So the doc's L299 suggestion ("sopra curl (che supporta WebSocket nelle versioni recenti)", i.e. build on curl, which supports WebSocket in recent versions) is unnecessary, though not wrong. CurlContext.cpp:555 setting CURLOPT_PROTOCOLS_STR to "file,http,https" is also confirmed. The legacy WebSocketChannel.cpp is under a Google BSD 3-clause licence (header L2-L29), so porting it is fine licence-wise.

claims.claim: Security policy (bindings only for app:// origins, navigation outside app:// blocked, L579-581) is compatible with dev mode loading http://localhost:5173 (L299).
claims.doc_section: Dev mode L299; Superficie d'attacco L579-581; Esempio L394
claims.evidence: L579 limits bindings to the declared app:// origins and L581 blocks navigation outside app://, while L299 has dev mode load the Vite dev server over http. zg_view_bind (L394) and zg_context_config (L384-387) have no origin allowlist parameter.
claims.implication: Add an `allowed_origins` list to zg_context_config. The framework would put the dev-server origin into it only in dev builds, and the same list would drive both binding installation (at dispatchDidClearWindowObjectInWorld, Source/WebCore/loader/LocalFrameLoaderClient.h:292) and the navigation policy. Define the frame rule as well: main frame only, or every same-origin frame.

challenge.reasoning:
The core gap the reviewer found is real. As written, L579 says bindings are installed only for "the declared app:// origins". So a page served from http://localhost:5173 (L299) would get no App.* bindings, and in dev mode the app would not work. The public C API also has no way to declare any other origin: zg_context_config at L384-387 has only size and app_id, and zg_view_bind at L394 takes no origin argument. The document never says how dev mode is exempted.

Calling the doc a flat contradiction (REFUTED) overstates it, though, for three reasons:
(1) L581 says navigation outside app:// is blocked "di default" (by default). That makes it a configurable default, not a fixed rule, and the reviewer's paraphrase dropped the qualifier.
(2) L366, which is the normative description of how bindings are installed, uses the generic phrase "solo per le origini autorizzate" ("only for the authorized origins"), not "app:// only". So the design already implies an allowlist idea; it just never defines it.
(3) L581 is aimed at an app page being carried off to an external site. An embedder-initiated zg_view_load_url to the dev server is not that case in intent. In WebCore, however, every load does pass through FrameLoaderClient::dispatchDecidePolicyForNavigationAction. A naive "scheme != app → ignore" check would therefore block the initial dev-server load and Vite full reloads too, so the policy must be written with this in mind.

Correct verdict: the doc is under-specified and internally inconsistent (L579 vs L366/L299), but not irreconcilable. The fix is small, and there are two valid designs:
(a) The reviewer's proposal: an allowed_origins list in zg_context_config that drives both binding installation and the navigation policy. The framework adds the dev-server origin only in the dev profile.
(b) The Wails approach: in dev mode the app:// handler proxies requests to the Vite server, so the page origin stays app:// and the policy needs no exception. The catch is that HMR WebSocket and absolute URLs then go to ws://localhost cross-origin.

Option (a) also benefits from WebKit treating http://localhost as potentially trustworthy, so crypto.subtle and other secure-context APIs work in dev mode without app://. Either way the doc must also state the frame rule: does window-object-cleared install bindings only in the main frame, or in every frame whose origin is allowed? This matters because dispatchDidClearWindowObjectInWorld fires per frame and per world. It must also state where the per-call origin check from L579 gets its origin: the lexical global object's document origin.
challenge.evidence:
Doc:

- L366: bindings are installed "solo per le origini autorizzate" (generic, not limited to app://).

It is called per frame and per world from FrameLoader.cpp:5227-5245 (dispatchDidClearWindowObjectsInAllWorlds iterates every world, guarded by canExecuteScripts and existingJSWindowProxy).

claims.claim: Dev tooling: the inspector opens 'in una seconda finestra' (L409) in the dev profile, which is 'per lavorare sul motore stesso' with assertions on (L437), and the CLI `dev` command uses that profile (L658).
claims.doc_section: Diagnostica L409; Profili L437; Parità Wails L643; CLI L658; Funzioni da spegnere L508
claims.evidence: L643 defers 'Più finestre' to after v1, but the inspector needs a second window in v1. L437 defines dev as debug/assert builds for engine work, while L658 runs app developers on it. In the L508 table, the 'standard' column says 'Solo nel profilo dev'. With a single process, a JS breakpoint pauses the main thread in a nested loop (Source/WebCore/inspector/FrameDebugger.cpp:132-153 runEventLoopWhilePaused), and that loop must keep the inspector's own view rendering. In zg_runtime_update mode the host's loop freezes during the pause. Sync dialogs (alert/confirm/prompt as host callbacks, L325) behave the same way in texture mode.
claims.implication: Split the profiles into `dev` (release engine plus inspector) and `debug` (assertions). Allow a second internal window for the inspector, or serve the frontend to an external browser over the remote-inspector socket (Win uses USE_INSPECTOR_SOCKET_SERVER, Source/cmake/OptionsWin.cmake:130). Document the nested-loop semantics for breakpoints and modal dialogs in both loop modes.

challenge.reasoning:
REFUTED is too strong. The doc does say all three things: the inspector opens in a second window in the dev profile (L409), dev means full symbols, assertions on, Web Inspector, "per lavorare sul motore stesso" (L437), and the CLI `dev` command uses the `dev` engine profile (L658). The design can also be built: the single-process WebKitLegacy port already runs an in-process inspector frontend in a second view, with a nested event loop during breakpoints. Some of the reviewer's points hold and some do not.

Points that hold:
(1) L437 and L658 really disagree. L437 defines dev as an assert/debug build for engine work, while L658 runs app developers' `dev` loop on it. The Wails table (L653) also ties Devtools to that profile. App developers would end up on a slow assert build just to get devtools. Splitting it into `dev` (release engine + inspector) and `debug` (assertions) is a sound fix.
(2) Breakpoints pause the main thread inside a nested loop, and the doc never says so. On non-Mac platforms that loop is `while(!m_doneProcessingDebuggerEvents) RunLoop::cycle()`. ZeroG's RunLoop therefore has to keep the inspector's own view loading, painting and taking input while JS is paused. In zg_runtime_update/texture mode the host's frame loop is frozen for the whole pause. Sync JS dialogs (L325) cause the same kind of freeze in texture mode.

Points that are weak or wrong:
(a) "Più finestre — Dopo" (L643) is a framework/API parity item for app developers. An engine-internal inspector window is not the public multi-window feature, and WebCore handles several Pages in one process without trouble. This is a doc-consistency issue at most, not a refutation.
(b) The L508 cell "Solo nel profilo dev" under the standard column just means off in standard. It matches L409 and contradicts nothing.

Facts the doc misses:
- The second window does not need ENABLE_REMOTE_INSPECTOR or a local port. WebKitLegacy uses WebCore::InspectorFrontendClientLocal directly. Tying the second window to "inspector remoto su una porta locale" mixes two different mechanisms.
- To use the socket path, a port must set USE_INSPECTOR_SOCKET_SERVER itself. Only Win and PlayStation do this today. JSCOnly picks GLib if USE_GLIB, Cocoa (XPC/webinspectord, not a TCP port) on APPLE, and Socket otherwise. So on macOS a "porta locale" means forcing the Socket backend.
- The socket frontend-side client (RemoteInspectorClient, RemoteInspectorProtocolHandler) and the HTTP+WebSocket server that serves the UI to an external browser (RemoteInspectorHTTPServer, GLib/libsoup only) all live in Source/WebKit/UIProcess. That is WebKit2, which ZeroG drops, so they must be rewritten.
- WebInspectorUI already ships BrowserInspectorFrontendHost.js, which opens a WebSocket. That makes the reviewer's "external browser" alternative realistic.
- On Windows, RunLoop::cycle() runs PeekMessage(nullptr...) and dispatches every message on the thread, so the host's windows keep getting wndproc calls during a pause. On the generic RunLoop (Linux), X11/Wayland events are processed only if ZeroG wires the display fd into the RunLoop.

claims.claim: Rendering 'uguale per tutti gli OS' (L687, L694) with FreeType everywhere by default (L247).
claims.doc_section: Stack testo L247; Testing L687, L694; Backend GPU L197-201
claims.evidence: In-tree Skia on WIN32 compiles DirectWrite ports instead of FreeType (Source/ThirdParty/skia/CMakeLists.txt:815-826). The FreeType and Fontconfig path is non-Windows only (:827-853). GPU backends also differ by OS (GL/ANGLE, Metal, Vulkan).
claims.implication: The 'FreeType everywhere' default requires patching the Skia CMake on Windows. Restrict pixel-identical reference tests to CPU mode with FreeType and embedded fonts, and use a tolerance for GPU modes.

challenge.reasoning:
The PARTIAL verdict holds, and the evidence is stronger than the reviewer showed. I could not find anything that would make the reviewer wrong: no option or flag selects FreeType on Windows, and nothing was renamed.

1. The doc itself (L247, L751) calls this a proposed default and an open question, not a fact. As a design goal it is technically possible: Skia's FreeType scaler and the custom embedded/directory font managers are all in the tree. Upstream does not do it today, so it is extra work.

2. The block on Windows is not only in the Skia CMake. On WIN32 the Skia CMake does not even look for FreeType or Fontconfig. It compiles the DirectWrite sources and sets SK_TYPEFACE_FACTORY_DIRECTWRITE. WebCore's FontCacheSkia.cpp also hardcodes the font manager per OS: DirectWrite on Windows, Android on Android, Fontconfig everywhere else. Fallback-font lookup (SkiaSystemFallbackFontCache) uses Fontconfig directly. So "FreeType everywhere" means patching both the Skia CMake and WebCore's FontCacheSkia.cpp / SkiaSystemFallbackFontCache.cpp, plus compiling SkFontMgr_custom*.cpp, which no build currently includes.

3. Missed fact: the in-tree Skia CMake has no Apple branch at all. On macOS the non-WIN32 path would pull in FreeType plus Fontconfig. The CoreText sources (SkFontMgr_mac_ct, SkScalerContext_mac_ct, SkTypeface_mac_ct) exist on disk but are never compiled. So the "native CoreText option" also needs new CMake work.

4. GPU side (L197-201): the in-tree Skia CMake only enables Ganesh with OpenGL (SK_GL, SK_GANESH) and assumes OpenGL ES (SK_ASSUME_GL_ES=1). No Vulkan or Metal defines are set. The ganesh/mtl, vk and d3d source directories exist, but none of their files are listed. GPU output therefore cannot be pixel-identical across Linux GL/Vulkan, ANGLE/D3D11 and Metal, and the Metal and Vulkan backends need CMake work first.

5. Correction to the reviewer's suggestion: L694 already says "confronto con immagini di riferimento con tolleranza" (comparison against reference images with tolerance) for both CPU and texture modes, so the doc already has a tolerance. The real conflict is with L687, which promises the same page rendered "allo stesso modo" (the same way) on every OS. That is only realistic in CPU raster mode, with the same FreeType/HarfBuzz build, embedded fonts and identical hinting/gamma settings. One remaining risk: Skia's CPU paths are chosen per processor (SSE/AVX vs NEON, see the skcms Hsw/Skx files), so even CPU output can differ slightly between x86_64 and arm64 machines. A small tolerance is still needed.

claims.claim: The runtime is a process singleton that cannot be recreated (L165-166), and this fits the test plan and the dynamic profile.
claims.doc_section: Runtime e main thread L165-166; Livelli di test L693, L697; Profilo dinamico L562
claims.evidence: Main-thread init runs once: Source/WTF/wtf/MainThread.cpp:40-48 (std::call_once, plus RELEASE_ASSERT that the main thread is WTF thread uid 1 when isMainThread). Config is frozen after the first VM (WTFConfig.cpp:190-197). L693 plans 'creazione e distruzione' unit tests.
claims.implication: Every C-API test that creates a runtime has to run in its own process, so pick a test runner that forks per test. In the dynamic profile, dlclose/FreeLibrary must be documented as unsupported. Specify what zg_runtime_destroy actually does (flush cookie and localStorage SQLite, stop network threads, return without freeing) and that a second zg_runtime_create returns an error.

challenge.reasoning:
I tried to show the claim was fully right or fully wrong and could do neither, so PARTIAL stands.

The first half of the claim is CONFIRMED, and the evidence is stronger than the reviewer's. (1) Main-thread init runs once per process through std::call_once. (2) WTF config pages are permanently frozen read-only, via mprotect/vm_protect, the first time any JSC::VM is built. (3) The reviewer missed this one: WebCore's shared VM is created with leakRef() and kept in a global pointer. Nothing ever destroys it, so WebCore global state truly cannot be torn down and rebuilt. I found nothing in the tree that undoes any of this. The only escape is the testing-only disabledFreezingForTesting flag, and it must be set before the freeze and only skips the page protection.

The second half, "fits the test plan and the dynamic profile", is only partly true. L697 talks about create/destroy cycles of *views*, which a singleton runtime handles fine. L693 says "Creazione e distruzione" at the C-API level without saying which objects, so it is ambiguous. If it means the runtime, it conflicts with the singleton rule. L562 (dynamic library) is fine for normal load-time linking. Unloading at runtime (dlclose/FreeLibrary) and loading again cannot work, because the main-thread state, the frozen config pages and the leaked VM all live in the library's globals. The doc does not say this.

The reviewer goes too far in two places. First, not every C-API test needs its own process: one runtime can be shared per test process through a global fixture. Only tests of runtime create/destroy, of a second create, and of wrong-thread init need their own process. Second, "a second zg_runtime_create returns an error" and "destroy returns without freeing" are design choices, not facts from the source. They are sensible ones, though.

A gotcha the doc and the reviewer both miss: off Apple platforms, the main thread is detected only by order. The first WTF::Thread object created gets uid 1 (s_uid starts at 0), and then a RELEASE_ASSERT requires the main thread to hold uid 1. So if any WTF thread object is created before zg_runtime_create runs on the main thread, the process aborts. That could happen by calling a zg_* function or touching a WTF-backed static from another thread first. On Apple platforms, init must also happen on the real OS main thread (pthread_main_np), so there the engine's main thread cannot be a secondary thread.

claims.claim: Version and profile matrix: the standard profile has WebGL (L436, L500) while the compositor 'serve per WebGL' only in v2 (L207-208).
claims.evidence: The AcceleratedCompositingEnabled preference still exists (Source/WTF/Scripts/Preferences/UnifiedWebPreferences.yaml:140-144, status embedder), so v1 without compositing is possible. The doc never says whether standard with WebGL ships before v2.
claims.implication: Make profiles and versions orthogonal in writing: standard plus WebGL requires the v2 compositor, or v1 WebGL uses a slow non-composited readback path.

challenge.reasoning:
PARTIAL is the right verdict. I tried to prove the reviewer wrong and found more evidence for it.

What the doc says:
- L436 and L500 put WebGL in the standard profile.
- L207-208 say v1 turns accelerated compositing off, and that the v2 compositor "serve per WebGL".
- No line says whether standard plus WebGL can ship before v2, so the profile/version matrix is unresolved. The reviewer is right on that.

Runtime: is the compositor needed? No. If a canvas has no compositing backing, HTMLCanvasElement::paint takes a software path: prepareForDisplay, then a GPU-to-CPU readback (surfaceBufferToImageBuffer / copyNativeImage, then paintToCanvas), then drawImageBuffer into the page's GraphicsContext. AcceleratedCompositingEnabled is still an embedder preference. So WebGL can be shown in v1, slowly, through a readback every frame. The reviewer's "slow readback path" option is real.

Compile time: the reviewer missed a harder point. WebKit has no non-Apple GraphicsContextGL that works without the compositing infrastructure:
- GraphicsContextGLEGL is the only non-Cocoa createWebProcessGraphicsContextGL. Its .cpp and .h are both guarded by `ENABLE(WEBGL) && (USE(GRAPHICS_LAYER_WC) || USE(COORDINATED_GRAPHICS))`.
- Without COORDINATED_GRAPHICS it holds a TextureMapperGCGLPlatformLayer, so it needs USE(TEXTURE_MAPPER). That is how Win (WC) works: OptionsWin.cmake sets GRAPHICS_LAYER_WC and TEXTURE_MAPPER on.
- With COORDINATED_GRAPHICS it goes through GraphicsContextGLCoordinated.
- ChromeClient::createGraphicsContextGL calls createWebProcessGraphicsContextGL directly.

So with ENABLE_WEBGL=ON and none of those USE flags, a ZeroG port gets no GraphicsContextGL backend at all. It must either turn on a compositing USE flag (bringing in the WebCore-side layer code while still painting non-composited), or write its own GraphicsContextGLANGLE subclass that implements the pure virtuals platformInitializeContext, readCompositedResults and reshapeDrawingBuffer. "WebGL needs v2" is wrong at runtime but close to right at build time. That is why the claim is PARTIAL, not REFUTED or CONFIRMED.

Side fact the doc gets wrong (L208): TextureMapper is no longer the default compositor for GTK/WPE at this revision. OptionsGTK.cmake and OptionsWPE.cmake define USE_TEXTURE_MAPPER as "Whether to use TextureMapper for compositing instead of Skia", PRIVATE, default OFF. Both force USE_COORDINATED_GRAPHICS on and default to the Skia compositor: SkiaCompositingLayer*, guarded by `USE(COORDINATED_GRAPHICS) && USE(SKIA) && !USE(TEXTURE_MAPPER)`. The thing that drives these layers (LayerTreeHost, ThreadedCompositor, CompositingRunLoop, DrawingAreaCoordinatedGraphics) lives in Source/WebKit, which ZeroG excludes, so it has to be rewritten. The layer and backing-store classes themselves are in WebCore and can be reused.

Fix for the doc: say explicitly that standard+WebGL either (a) requires the v2 compositor, or (b) ships in v1 using the readback path plus a custom or flag-enabled GraphicsContextGL backend. Also replace "TextureMapper, il compositor dei port GTK e WPE" with the upstream Skia compositor (USE(COORDINATED_GRAPHICS) + USE(SKIA)).

Inferred from the text: Phase 0 = toolchain/bootstrap, i.e. a static WTF+JSC build from the JSCOnly config on Linux and Windows plus measured build/iteration times (L526, L683 'durate ... dopo la fase 0'). Phase 1 = the critical gate: WebCore renders a page through the custom embedding layer without WebKit2, with Skia (L679), and first metrics are taken (L664-672: size, RSS, startup to first frame, CSS animation frame time, so phase 1 probably includes basic presentation). The Windows GPU prototype is probably a gate in phase 1 or 2 (L735). Phase 2 = stable C API plus JS bindings (L673 binding latency 'dopo la fase 2', L683 'API C della fase 2'). Phases 3 and 4 run in parallel with 5 and are probably network/storage/app:// (curl, BoringSSL, cookies, WebSocket, dev mode) and input/IME/clipboard/window mode/fonts/GPU backends, in an unknown order. Phase 5 = the Zig framework (it can start once the phase 2 API is stable). JSC/WTF configuration is permanently frozen at first VM creation (Source/WTF/wtf/WTFConfig.cpp:190-197, Source/JavaScriptCore/runtime/VM.cpp:568), and signal handlers can only be added during init (Source/WTF/wtf/threads/Signals.cpp:74). Every JIT, signal, GC-thread-count and wasm option must be fixed in zg_runtime_create before any view exists.

Upstream GC signal API: JSConfigureSignalForGC (Source/JavaScriptCore/API/JSBase.cpp:185-193) must be called before WTF threading init. Without it, WTF defaults to SIGUSR1 and only logs on conflict (Source/WTF/wtf/posix/ThreadingPOSIX.cpp:198-232).
On macOS, WTF traps go through Mach exception ports (Signals.cpp:126-141, 381-387), which conflicts with Crashpad and Breakpad on macOS. The doc's L155 'riguarda Linux' is incomplete.

Web Workers each create their own JSC VM (Source/WebCore/workers/WorkerGlobalScope.cpp:117), so 'una sola VM' (L135) holds only for page JS, and the per-runtime heap limit must account for worker VMs.

WebCore RunLoopObserver does nothing on the generic event loop (Source/WebCore/platform/RunLoopObserver.cpp:52-66). The embedding layer must schedule rendering updates itself through ChromeClient::scheduleRenderingUpdate / triggerRenderingUpdate (Source/WebCore/page/ChromeClient.h:527-529) and supply a DisplayRefreshMonitorFactory (:484) for rAF.
Upstream Windows uses the /MD CRT (Source/cmake/OptionsMSVC.cmake:58). The doc's /MT (L519) needs an override, and it forces the host to also use /MT when linking the static archive.

WebKit needs C++23 (Source/cmake/OptionsCommon.cmake:1-3), GCC >= 13.1 (Source/cmake/WebKitCommon.cmake:134-137), effectively Clang >= 18 with a workaround and >= 19 cleanly (Source/cmake/WebKitCompilerFlags.cmake:243-252), clang-cl only on Windows (OptionsMSVC.cmake:1), and CMake >= 3.20. glibc 2.28 is the hard floor because of statx (Source/WTF/wtf/posix/POSIXExtras.h:130).

In-tree Skia CMake builds only Ganesh GL (Source/ThirdParty/skia/CMakeLists.txt:423-452, 856-866), hard-requires Fontconfig and FreeType on non-Windows (:4-7, 846-852), uses DirectWrite on Windows (:815-826), and needs WebP::mux when USE_SKIA_ENCODERS is on (:9-11, 879) plus JPEG and PNG always (:972-975). Vulkan, Metal, an embedded font manager and FreeType-on-Windows all require CMake patches.

Upstream Windows ANGLE is SHARED and includes the D3D9 backend unconditionally (Source/ThirdParty/ANGLE/PlatformWin.cmake). The doc's Windows runtime DLL list (L519) misses d3d9, d3dcompiler_47, dxguid/dwrite (if native fonts), imm32/msctf (IME), winmm, dbghelp, shlwapi and synchronization (from Source/WTF/wtf/PlatformJSCOnly.cmake:24-29).

HarfBuzz must be built with hb-icu: Source/WebCore/platform/graphics/skia/ComplexTextControllerSkia.cpp:35 and Source/WebCore/platform/text/LocaleICU.cpp:48. The doc's 'senza ICU' (L460) will not link.

The executable JIT pool reserves 1 GB of virtual address space on x86_64 (Source/JavaScriptCore/jit/ExecutableAllocator.cpp:101-102), and FIXED_EXECUTABLE_MEMORY_POOL_SIZE_IN_MB can shrink it. Wasm fast memory (OptionsList.h:595) reserves more in the standard profile.
WebKit vendors mimalloc with a USE_MIMALLOC option (Source/bmalloc/mimalloc, Source/cmake/WebKitFeatures.cmake:366). That is the obvious 'hardened allocator' candidate for L146/L754.

Large static WebCore archives are a known upstream problem: Source/cmake/OptionsPlayStation.cmake:368-373 ('libWebCore.a is too much for ranlib'), so PlayStation uses OBJECT libraries. COFF .lib archives use 32-bit offsets, which matters for the dev and debug profiles.

A WebSocket implementation is available to reuse: Source/WebKitLegacy/WebCoreSupport/WebSocketChannel.cpp, SocketStreamHandleImpl.cpp and LegacySocketProvider.cpp, plus Source/WebCore/platform/network/curl/CurlStream.cpp. In-process storage is also available: Source/WebKitLegacy/Storage/InProcessIDBServer.cpp, StorageAreaImpl.cpp, StorageNamespaceImpl.cpp. Both are BSD and support L303 and L758.

The scheme registry is static and process-global (Source/WebCore/platform/LegacySchemeRegistry.h:49,85), and MemoryCache is a singleton (Source/WebCore/loader/cache/MemoryCache.h:98). Per-context schemes, caches and fonts are not isolatable.

The design has no origin allowlist API, no JS-exception-throwing API for C callbacks, no zg_promise creation API, no definition of zg_value ownership, no list of thread-safe functions, and no specification for view/window ownership (does destroying zg_window destroy the view from zg_window_view?).
macOS: AppKit, NSTextInputClient and Metal display links need the process main thread. The runtime-creating thread must be the process main thread in window mode, which the doc does not state.

challenge.reasoning: I tried to show the reviewer was wrong and couldn't. All four named ports can build with Skia, but upstream only turns it on by default for three of them: GTK, WPE and Win. PlayStation ships a working Skia build path, yet the option is off by default there, so it builds with Cairo unless someone passes -DUSE_SKIA=ON. "Uses" is ambiguous. Read as "supports", the claim is true for all four ports. Read as "defaults to", it is false for PlayStation. Either way the verdict is PARTIAL. One thing the reviewer understated: PlayStation is a real Skia target, not just an option nobody wired up, because both its WebCore and WebKit platform files include the Skia sources when USE_SKIA is set. I also checked for a renamed or relocated flag (Options*.cmake, PlatformUse.h, WebCore/Configurations, webkitdirs.pm, FeatureList.pm) and found nothing that changes the picture. For ZeroG this means the Windows Skia path (Skia with HarfBuzz) is the one upstream builds by default. macOS with Skia and Metal would be a combination no upstream port builds, so ZeroG would carry it alone. The PlayStation port, being Skia-capable, curl-based and GLib-free, is a good reference for a single-process port without GLib.

claims.evidence: Reusable: WebCore/platform/Skia.cmake and SourcesSkia.txt (about 50 files in platform/graphics/skia). Hard-coded platform choices that need patching: (1) PlatformDisplaySkia.cpp:370-382 `PlatformDisplay::skiaGLContext()` returns a GL context only `#if PLATFORM(GTK) || PLATFORM(WPE) || (PLATFORM(PLAYSTATION) && !USE(COORDINATED_GRAPHICS))` and returns nullptr otherwise, so a new PLATFORM gets no GPU Skia at all. challenge.reasoning:
The reuse half of the claim is correct. WebCore has a Skia painting layer that any port can pull in (platform/Skia.cmake, SourcesSkia.txt). The "only adds GPU context creation per OS" half is false, and the situation is a bit worse than the reviewer said. I tried to refute each of their four points and all of them hold. Precise corrections:

(1) The skiaGLContext() guard at PlatformDisplaySkia.cpp:370-382 is exactly as described. There is an injection API, PlatformDisplay::setSkiaGLContextForCurrentThread (PlatformDisplaySkia.cpp:398-407, PlatformDisplay.h:123), and the only caller is WebKit2's ThreadedCompositor.cpp:139. It sets s_skiaGLContext, which is enough for skiaGrContext() (:409-413). But skiaGLContext() still returns nullptr on a platform outside the guard, and about 20 WebCore files call skiaGLContext(). So the guard does need a PLATFORM(ZEROG) branch, or the GL-context setup has to be rewritten.

(2) The reviewer was slightly imprecise about FontCacheSkia. The include at :47 is gated on PLATFORM(WIN), but the code at :66 is gated on OS(WINDOWS). A new PLATFORM built on Windows would include SkFontMgr_fontconfig.h and then call SkFontMgr_New_DirectWrite without dwrite.h or SkTypeface_win.h, so it would not compile. Line 457 (`!OS(ANDROID) && !PLATFORM(WIN)`) and SkiaSystemFallbackFontCache.cpp:29-31 (fontconfig include) pull FontConfig in as well. A ZeroG build on Windows would hit both. On macOS there is no CoreText branch at all.

(3) Skia's CMakeLists is correct as quoted. Lines 4-6 make Freetype and Fontconfig REQUIRED unless the target is WIN32 or PLAYSTATION. Lines 855-867 always link either libepoxy or EGL/ANGLE. The doc misses something more important. Lines 1065-1074 compile only the GL Ganesh backend (SK_GL and SK_GANESH, with "FIXME: Support other combinations"). The vendored Skia does ship the Metal, Vulkan and D3D sources (src/gpu/ganesh/mtl, vk, d3d; also src/ports/SkFontMgr_mac_ct.cpp, SkFontMgr_custom_embedded.cpp), but CMake never builds them.

(4) The doc's plan of Metal on macOS and Vulkan on Linux (ZeroG.md:195-203) clashes with WebCore's Skia GPU code, which is GL-only throughout. The Ganesh context is created with GrDirectContexts::MakeGL (PlatformDisplaySkia.cpp:354). Textures are wrapped with GrBackendTextures::MakeGL in SkiaUtilities.cpp:70, SkiaBackingStore.cpp:339 and the coordinated-graphics buffers. The GPU context type is WebCore::GLContext (EGL). Metal or Vulkan would mean new WebCore code plus Skia build changes, not just context creation. ANGLE-on-D3D11 for Windows and EGL for Linux fit the existing path. Metal does not.

challenge.reasoning:
I could not find anything that contradicts the reviewer's evidence. WebKit's Skia build compiles Ganesh only, assumes GLES only, and gets its GL interface only through EGL. WebCore creates a Skia GPU context in exactly one way, GrDirectContexts::MakeGL. I found no Ganesh Vulkan/Metal/D3D or Graphite sources in the Skia CMakeLists.txt, and WebCore never refers to GrVk, GrMtl, GrD3D, MakeVulkan or MakeMetal. I checked for a renamed flag or a hidden alternative path and found none.

Calling the whole table REFUTED goes too far, though. The table has three rows, and they come out differently:
(1) Linux "OpenGL (EGL)": CONFIRMED. This is the only GPU path that is actually wired up (GTK/WPE).
(2) Linux "o Vulkan": REFUTED as an option that works today. Skia's Vulkan backend source is in the tree (src/gpu/ganesh/vk has 70 entries), but WebKit's CMake does not build it and WebCore has no code to use it. USE_VULKAN, which only builds when experimental features are on, adds WebCore/platform/graphics/vulkan helpers for GL interop, not a Skia backend.
(3) Windows "OpenGL tramite ANGLE su D3D11": CONFIRMED at the build level. OptionsWin.cmake sets USE_ANGLE_EGL ON, USE_ANGLE ON and USE_SKIA ON. Skia then links ANGLE::EGL, and ANGLE's PlatformWin.cmake compiles the D3D11 backend with ANGLE_ENABLE_D3D11. Skia goes through GLES 3 via ANGLE EGL, so this is exactly the path the doc describes. Whether the Win port actually turns on Skia GPU painting at runtime, and how direct D3D11 texture sharing with games would work, cannot be settled without a build.
(4) macOS "Metal": REFUTED as a Skia backend. Skia's Ganesh Metal source is present (src/gpu/ganesh/mtl has 51 entries, .mm files), but WebKit does not build it and WebCore has no Metal Skia path. The Metal that is reachable is ANGLE's Metal backend: ANGLE/CMakeLists.txt:27 includes Metal.cmake, PlatformCocoa.cmake sets ANGLE_ENABLE_METAL, and OptionsCocoa.cmake:231 sets USE_ANGLE_EGL ON. So the realistic macOS option is Skia GL(ES) over ANGLE over Metal, or CPU raster.

"Il backend Metal di Skia è maturo" is a statement about Skia upstream (Chromium ships Ganesh Metal), and the source in the tree backs it up. It is just not usable from WebKit.

Missed gotchas:
- "Driver caricati dal sistema con dlopen" depends on libepoxy. With USE_LIBEPOXY on (which GTK/WPE force via SET_AND_EXPOSE_TO_BUILD), epoxy dlopens EGL/GL. Without it, Skia links ${EGL_LIBRARIES} or ANGLE::EGL directly.
- SK_DISABLE_LEGACY_GL_MAKE_NATIVE_INTERFACE is PUBLIC, so the GL interface has to come from the EGL/epoxy factories.
- The Skia CMake uses GCC-style flags (WEBKIT_ADD_TARGET_CXX_FLAGS with -Wno-*) and DirectWrite on WIN32, and is shared across ports, so any extra backend means editing that shared file.

Net result: Linux EGL and Windows ANGLE/D3D11 hold; Linux Vulkan and macOS Metal-as-Skia-backend would be new port work. That is PARTIAL, not REFUTED.

challenge.reasoning:
The reviewer's PARTIAL verdict holds. I tried to show it was wrong and found nothing that does.

1. skiaGLContext() really does return nullptr on Windows. The guard in PlatformDisplaySkia.cpp:372 is `#if PLATFORM(GTK) || PLATFORM(WPE) || (PLATFORM(PLAYSTATION) && !USE(COORDINATED_GRAPHICS))`, and the #else at 378-381 returns nullptr. WIN is not in the guard and no flag was renamed. The only other line in that file that mentions PLATFORM(WIN) is makeSkiaGLContextCurrentIfExists (387). It calls skiaGLContext(), which is still nullptr, so it does nothing on Windows.

2. Nothing outside PlatformDisplaySkia.cpp gives Windows a Skia GL context. The one caller of setSkiaGLContextForCurrentThread is CoordinatedGraphics/ThreadedCompositor.cpp:139. That compositor is CoordinatedGraphics only (GTK/WPE). Windows uses the GraphicsLayerWC/TextureMapper path instead. DrawingAreaWC.cpp:415 asks for DOM image buffers with RenderingMode::Unaccelerated. So in upstream WebKit on Windows, Skia always draws on the CPU, and ANGLE is used only for TextureMapper compositing and WebGL.

3. One detail the reviewer missed actually backs the doc's choice, though not its wording. WebKit's own Skia CMake (Source/ThirdParty/skia/CMakeLists.txt:1066-1086) builds only Ganesh with SK_GL and SK_ASSUME_GL_ES=1, marked 'FIXME: Support other combinations'. Lines 856-866 compile the EGL GL interface and link ANGLE::EGL when USE_ANGLE_EGL is on. In-tree there is no Direct3D, Vulkan or Graphite backend. So on Windows, GL over ANGLE isn't the 'most tested' Skia GPU path in WebKit. It is the only one the build supports, and no WebKit port has ever turned it on at runtime.

4. Outside WebKit (from my own knowledge, not checked in the tree), Ganesh GL over ANGLE/D3D11 has long been the main Skia GPU path in Chromium on Windows. Chromium is now moving to Graphite on Dawn, which this tree doesn't build. So the phrase is true of Chromium, not of WebKit.

Correction to the reviewer: the parenthetical in their quote of PlatformDisplaySkia.cpp:379-380 is the comment about PlayStation coordinated graphics. It does not explain why Windows is excluded. Windows is excluded only because it is missing from the #if.

Implication for ZeroG: ZeroG will be the first WebKit code to give WebCore a Skia GrDirectContext on ANGLE/D3D11. It will need to add PLATFORM(WIN), or a ZeroG port flag, to the guard at line 372, or call setSkiaGLContextForCurrentThread from its own compositor. Every WebCore Skia call site that uses skiaGLContext()/skiaGrContext() (ImageBufferSkiaAcceleratedBackend, GraphicsContextSkia, SkiaPaintingEngine, NativeImageSkia, etc.) will then run on Windows for the first time. The doc's risk line (doc line 735, 'Prototipo Windows presto', i.e. build a Windows prototype early) is the right mitigation. CPU Skia plus a texture upload, which is what upstream Windows does, is the proven fallback. Side note: on WIN32 the in-tree Skia build sets SK_TYPEFACE_FACTORY_DIRECTWRITE (CMakeLists.txt:1088-1092). That conflicts with the doc's proposed 'FreeType everywhere' default and will need a CMake override.

claims.doc_section: Backend GPU per piattaforma / Render thread separato

challenge.reasoning:
I tried to prove the reviewer wrong and couldn't. Their verdict holds. One detail needs fixing: they said no WebCore code touches ANGLE on Windows. WebCore does create an ANGLE display on Windows. It just never uses the device-injection or D3D-texture-sharing extensions.

1) Capability: confirmed in the vendored ANGLE. On Windows, WebKit's ANGLE CMake builds the D3D11 backend (and also D3D9, which ANGLE needs to compile). Renderer11 always advertises EGL_ANGLE_d3d_texture_client_buffer and EGL_ANGLE_image_d3d11_texture. It also advertises the keyed-mutex extension, and the share-handle client buffer when share handles are supported. Display.cpp turns on device creation (eglCreateDeviceANGLE) whenever ANGLE_ENABLE_D3D11 is defined. ANGLE's own tests already exercise the path the doc needs (eglCreateDeviceANGLE on an outside ID3D11Device, then eglCreatePbufferFromClientBuffer with EGL_D3D_TEXTURE_ANGLE).

2) Use in WebKit: refuted. The only Windows ANGLE display WebKit creates is PlatformDisplayWin::create(). It calls eglGetPlatformDisplayEXT(EGL_PLATFORM_ANGLE_ANGLE, EGL_DEFAULT_DISPLAY, ...) and passes only the debug-layers attribute. It never injects an outside D3D11 device and never wraps a D3D texture. A search of WebCore, WebKit, WebKitLegacy, WTF and JavaScriptCore finds no EGL_D3D_TEXTURE_ANGLE, eglCreateDeviceANGLE, EGL_D3D11_DEVICE_ANGLE, IDXGIResource or CreateSharedHandle. The nearest existing pattern is on Cocoa: GraphicsContextGLCocoa.mm calls eglCreatePbufferFromClientBuffer with EGL_IOSURFACE_ANGLE. ZeroG can copy that structure for D3D on Windows.

So "direct texture sharing with D3D11 games via ANGLE" is technically supported by the ANGLE in the tree. All the integration is new ZeroG code with no upstream WebKit precedent, and "most battle-tested" only describes ANGLE itself, not this sharing path. PARTIAL is right.

Gotchas the doc misses:
(a) WebKit's ANGLE PlatformWin.cmake forces GLESv2_LIBRARY_TYPE and EGL_LIBRARY_TYPE to SHARED. That breaks the doc's "everything static" goal on Windows unless ZeroG overrides it, and static ANGLE on Windows is not a configuration upstream tests. The same file links d3d9, dxgi, dxguid and synchronization, and D3D9 can't be dropped.
(b) If ANGLE runs on the game's own ID3D11Device, ANGLE and the game share that device's single immediate context. ANGLE on the engine thread and the game's render thread would both issue commands on it, so the doc's separate render-thread design would need ID3D11Multithread::SetMultithreadProtected or careful serialization. Otherwise two separate devices are needed.
(c) The doc's cross-device plan uses NT handles (IDXGIResource1::CreateSharedHandle). ANGLE's share-handle client buffer (EGL_D3D_TEXTURE_2D_SHARE_HANDLE_ANGLE) takes legacy share handles. For NT handles, ZeroG must open the resource on ANGLE's device (ID3D11Device1::OpenSharedResource1, device obtained through eglQueryDeviceAttribEXT with EGL_D3D11_DEVICE_ANGLE) and wrap it with EGL_D3D_TEXTURE_ANGLE.
(d) ANGLE's keyed-mutex extension is available as a sync option, but no D3D11 fence (ID3D11Fence) export/import through ANGLE was found. The doc's "D3D11 fence" step therefore means ZeroG talks to ID3D11Device5/ID3D11DeviceContext4 directly, beside ANGLE. That last part is my inference, not found in source.
(e) ENABLE_WEBGL is ON for Windows in one branch of OptionsWin.cmake (line 100) and OFF in another (line 89). The doc's "WebGL included" depends on which options ZeroG picks.

The Skia CMake links `${EGL_LIBRARIES}` when epoxy is not used (:865). WebCore egl/GLContext.cpp:31-39 and GLDisplay.cpp:32-37 call EGL and GLES directly (<EGL/egl.h>, <GLES2/gl2.h>) when USE(LIBEPOXY) is off. libepoxy is the component that actually dlopens.
claims.implication: Without libepoxy, the binary gets link-time dependencies (DT_NEEDED) on libEGL.so and libGLESv2.so, which breaks the 'only dlopen' promise and fails to start on machines without libEGL. ZeroG needs a dlopen shim: either its own tiny epoxy-like loader exporting the egl* and gl* symbols WebCore uses, or a custom GrGLInterface built with GrGLMakeAssembledInterface plus a dlopen'd eglGetProcAddress (public API in include/gpu/ganesh/gl/GrGLAssembleInterface.h) together with a patch to PlatformDisplaySkia.cpp:83-94.

challenge.reasoning:
I tried to show the reviewer was wrong and could not. The first half of the claim is a design goal: GPU drivers should be loaded from the system with dlopen (ZeroG.md:199, 414, 518). That goal is reasonable. The justification for replacing libepoxy (ZeroG.md:478) is wrong at the source level.

1. Skia's non-epoxy GL path does not load core GL functions with eglGetProcAddress. In GrGLMakeEGLInterface.cpp, egl_get_gl_proc returns `(GrGLFuncPtr) X` for every entry in GR_GL_CORE_FUNCTIONS_EACH, which takes the address of a link-time symbol. Only names outside that list fall through to eglGetProcAddress. The file includes <EGL/egl.h> and <GLES2/gl2.h> with GL_GLEXT_PROTOTYPES. The epoxy variant does the same thing using epoxy_X symbols, so in both cases the actual dlopen is done by libepoxy, not Skia.
2. Skia's CMake links `${EGL_LIBRARIES}` (or ANGLE::EGL) whenever USE_LIBEPOXY is off. That gives the binary a direct DT_NEEDED on libEGL and, through the core GLES symbols, on libGLESv2.
3. WebCore also calls EGL and GLES directly in its #else (non-epoxy) branches. About 33 files include EGL or GL headers directly, including GLContext.cpp, GLDisplay.cpp, GLFence*, BitmapTexture.cpp, PlatformDisplaySkia.cpp, SkiaUtilities.cpp, SkiaBackingStore.cpp and TextureMapperGLHeaders.h. So replacing libepoxy affects all of these files, not only Skia's interface factory.
4. Every upstream Linux port has USE_LIBEPOXY forced TRUE (GTK and WPE). The non-epoxy path is only exercised on PlayStation and Windows, where EGL comes from ANGLE or the platform. On Linux, the "no epoxy" path is untested.

Where I'd adjust the reviewer: their two shim options are valid but incomplete. A third option is cheaper. libepoxy is MIT-licensed, can be built as a static library, and already dlopens libEGL, libGL and libGLESv2 at runtime with no DT_NEEDED. Keeping libepoxy statically linked meets the "dlopen only" goal with zero WebCore or Skia patches, so "Sostituire" (replace) is arguably the wrong decision. If ZeroG still replaces it, the shim must export every egl* and gl* symbol used by both Skia (GR_GL_CORE_FUNCTIONS_EACH) and the WebCore files above. Alternatively, it can supply epoxy-compatible headers, i.e. a mini-epoxy.

If SDL3 is used (ZeroG.md:477), SDL_EGL_GetProcAddress / SDL_GL_GetProcAddress can feed GrGLMakeAssembledInterface. That still does not help WebCore's direct egl* calls.

Note that resolving core GL functions through eglGetProcAddress is only guaranteed with EGL 1.5 or EGL_KHR_get_all_proc_addresses. Mesa and NVIDIA support it, but a custom loader should prefer dlsym on the dlopen'd libGLESv2 for core functions.

Other things the doc misses: PlatformDisplaySkia.cpp includes <xf86drm.h> under USE(LIBDRM), and the GTK/WPE ports link GBM::GBM and LibDRM::LibDRM directly. These are further link-time system dependencies the doc does not list. ZeroG must either turn off USE_GBM and USE_LIBDRM (losing DMABuf and GPU-process paths) or dlopen them as well. The Vulkan half of the claim (vkGetInstanceProcAddr) was outside this check.

challenge.reasoning:
PARTIAL is still the right verdict. GPU Skia in WebCore is only partly tied to coordinated graphics. The GrDirectContext/SkiaGLContext machinery, the accelerated ImageBuffer backend and GraphicsContextSkia have no USE(COORDINATED_GRAPHICS) guard. The Skia tile painting/replay engine and the Skia compositor do. The reviewer got that part right.

Their stated implication has a serious error, though. GPU Skia also has a second gate that they missed: a check on the platform macro, not on coordinated graphics. PlatformDisplay::skiaGLContext() creates and returns a context only when PLATFORM(GTK) || PLATFORM(WPE) || (PLATFORM(PLAYSTATION) && !USE(COORDINATED_GRAPHICS)). On every other platform it returns nullptr unconditionally. That includes PLATFORM(WIN) and any new PLATFORM(ZEROG).

This breaks their advice that the embedder can inject a context with setSkiaGLContextForCurrentThread. That function stores the context in s_skiaGLContext, but on a non-GTK/WPE platform skiaGLContext() never reads it. All GPU entry points check skiaGLContext() first; for example, ImageBufferSkiaAcceleratedBackend::create returns nullptr when it gets no GL context. So on a new port, GPU Skia stays silently off (CPU fallback) until ZeroG patches that guard or builds as WPE.

There is a related trap the reviewer did not mention. WTF picks the platform at compile time. If no BUILDING_*__ define is set, a Windows build automatically becomes PLATFORM(WIN), a macOS build becomes PLATFORM(MAC) (Cocoa, pulling in CA/Cocoa code paths), and a Linux build gets no PLATFORM at all. So ZeroG needs its own BUILDING_ZEROG__/WTF_PLATFORM_ZEROG define plus patches wherever GTK/WPE are hard-coded. Otherwise on Windows it inherits the hard-coded ANGLE PlatformDisplayWin singleton, which has no setSharedDisplay, and skiaGLContext() returns nullptr.

On compositing without coordinated graphics: the only GraphicsLayer for ZeroG is GraphicsLayerTextureMapper (the Win configuration). The Skia compositor (SkiaCompositingLayer*) needs COORDINATED_GRAPHICS && SKIA && !TEXTURE_MAPPER. CoordinatedPlatformLayer (not reviewed here) is the only file outside skia/ that references it.

The rest of the reviewer's evidence checks out:
- the protected PlatformDisplay(Ref<GLDisplay>&&) constructor, the pure virtual type() and m_eglDisplay;
- setSharedDisplay exists only when !PLATFORM(WIN);
- the LIBDRM guards; it uses Skia's EGL GL interface (MakeEGL, or MakeEpoxyEGL when libepoxy is used), so it is EGL-only.

challenge.reasoning:
I tried to refute the reviewer and could not. Their findings hold up, and I found a nuance that helps them.

Supporting the claim: upstream already does CPU-only Skia rasterization. ImageBufferSkiaUnacceleratedBackend.cpp exists. PlatformDisplay::skiaGLContext() gives a real GL context only under `PLATFORM(GTK) || PLATFORM(WPE) || (PLATFORM(PLAYSTATION) && !USE(COORDINATED_GRAPHICS))`. Every other platform hits the `#else` branch and gets `return nullptr` (PlatformDisplaySkia.cpp:370-382). That means the Windows port and PlayStation with coordinated graphics never give Skia a GL context today: Skia paints on the CPU there, and only compositing uses GL. A new PLATFORM(ZEROG) would also land in the nullptr branch by default unless that guard is changed. So the in-memory raster path is real and has upstream precedent.

Against the claim (the reviewer's point): the CPU mode does not free you from EGL/GL at build or link time. It also compiles skiaGLInterface(), which calls GrGLInterfaces::MakeEGL(), plus the SkiaGLContext class, under `#if !(PLATFORM(PLAYSTATION) && USE(COORDINATED_GRAPHICS))` (line 82). For a new port that condition is true, so this code gets compiled. When USE(LIBDRM) is on, the file also calls eglGetCurrentDisplay, eglQueryString, eglQueryDisplayAttribEXT and eglQueryDeviceStringEXT directly (lines 98-115). Runtime gotcha: some paths dereference the GL context without a null check. SkiaPaintingEngine.cpp:169 calls `PlatformDisplay::sharedDisplay().skiaGLContext()->makeContextCurrent()` and then RELEASE_ASSERTs grContext. challenge.reasoning:
I tried to prove the reviewer wrong and couldn't. Every fact they cited checks out, so PARTIAL stands. Here is each part of the claim in turn.

(1) "No Skottie": true. modules/skottie exists in the tree, but the CMakeLists never names it.

(2) "No SVG": already the default unless USE_SKIA_OPENTYPE_SVG is set. That flag defaults to ON in GTK and WPE, so ZeroG's own Options file just has to define it OFF or leave it out. The flag also pulls in expat, skshaper (HarfBuzz), skresources and SkXML. Its only consumers are the WebProcess main files, which call SkGraphics::SetOpenTypeSVGDecoderFactory.

(3) "No PDF": not achievable without patching the CMakeLists. src/pdf/*.cpp sits in the unconditional add_library(Skia STATIC ...) list, and SkDeflate.cpp includes <zlib.h>. One nuance the reviewer missed: Skia is a STATIC archive, and the only SkPDF consumer is the GTK print code (WebPrintOperationGtk.cpp), which ZeroG won't build. So the linker won't pull the PDF objects into the final binary unless whole-archive linking is used. The binary-size goal is mostly met anyway. The real cost is compile time and needing zlib headers. Excluding PDF entirely still takes a one-block CMake patch.

(4) "Only the needed GPU backends": the doc implies a choice, but WebKit's Skia CMake builds exactly one backend: Ganesh GL with SK_GL, SK_GANESH and SK_ASSUME_GL_ES=1. The interface comes from libepoxy, or from EGL/ANGLE::EGL when USE_LIBEPOXY is off. No Vulkan, Metal, D3D or Graphite sources are compiled, though src/gpu/ganesh/{vk,mtl,d3d} and src/gpu/graphite are in the tree. So the doc's own backend table ("Linux: OpenGL (EGL) o Vulkan", "macOS: Metal") is the bigger problem. Vulkan and Metal will not exist until ZeroG adds those source lists and defines (SK_VULKAN, SK_METAL) to the Skia CMakeLists. "Only what's needed" is therefore wrong in the other direction: today, less than what's needed is built. Also, GL always goes through EGL. There is no WGL or CGL path, so on macOS GL only works through ANGLE.

(5) The reviewer's point about build order holds. JPEG::JPEG and PNG::PNG are linked unconditionally, and the Jpeg/Png codec .cpp files are in the base source list. The Skia CMakeLists does not call find_package for them; it expects the port's Options file to do it (OptionsGTK.cmake:21,24,27 finds JPEG, PNG and ZLIB). So libjpeg-turbo, libpng and zlib are needed at step 2 of "Ordine di lavoro", not step 3. libwebp is only needed when USE_SKIA_ENCODERS is on, which defaults ON (WebKitFeatures.cmake:364), so it should be turned OFF until step 3.

Gotcha the doc misses: on any non-WIN32, non-PlayStation platform (so Linux and macOS), the Skia CMakeLists hard-requires Freetype 2.9 and Fontconfig 2.13 (lines 4-7) and compiles SkFontMgr_fontconfig (lines 844-851). Expat is required too, but only on Android or with OpenType SVG. Fontconfig conflicts with the doc's plan to replace it with a custom Skia font manager. Removing it needs another CMakeLists patch (for example, adding a ZEROG branch or a custom SkFontMgr port file). The README.WebKit update procedure keeps WebKit's CMakeLists.txt and WebKitSkiaConfig.h across Skia updates, so these patches have to be carried in that file.

I tried to prove the reviewer wrong and couldn't. Every citation they gave matches the checkout at 31a83a39.

The doc claims a text stack of FreeType + HarfBuzz + a Skia font manager (embedded fonts or a font directory) instead of Fontconfig, with FreeType on every OS by default (ZeroG.md:242-247, 476). All the pieces exist in the tree, so the plan can work. But upstream WebKit's Skia path does not support it as shipped, in either the build files or WebCore. That makes the verdict PARTIAL, not CONFIRMED.

What holds up:
- WebCore's Skia text path does use HarfBuzz.
- FreeType is the Skia glyph backend on every non-Windows OS.
- Skia ships the custom font managers the doc needs: SkFontMgr_New_Custom_Directory, SkFontMgr_New_Custom_Data, SkFontMgr_New_Custom_Empty, plus an embedded-fonts variant.
- None of the custom managers are compiled by WebKit's Skia CMakeLists.

What does not hold without patches:
- Windows: the Skia CMake compiles only DirectWrite (no FreeType at all), and WebCore picks the DirectWrite font manager there.
- Every other OS except Android: Fontconfig is hard-required in three places: Skia's CMake (it also requires FreeType), WebCore's font-manager setup, and the whole system-fallback cache, which calls Fc* functions directly.
- PlayStation is not a precedent for dropping Fontconfig: its WebCore build skips the Skia-level lookup but still requires Fontconfig itself.

Problems I found that neither the doc nor the reviewer mentions:
1. **The reviewer's fallback fix won't work as stated.** They suggest reusing the Android/Windows branch, which calls matchFamilyStyleCharacter on the font manager. Skia's custom manager hard-returns nullptr from that function. Without more work, characters missing from the primary font would get no fallback at all. ZeroG must subclass SkFontMgr_Custom or write its own SkFontMgr with a real per-character fallback table (this is the "tabella di fallback propria" the doc mentions at :476).
2. **Generic family names are not mapped.** The custom manager matches families only by exact name; there is no alias for "serif", "sans-serif" or "monospace". WebCore turns -webkit-* generics into exactly those names. So bundled fonts need those aliases, or every page silently gets an empty, glyph-less font.
3. **Windows guards are inconsistent.** FontCacheSkia.cpp selects headers with PLATFORM(WIN) but selects code with OS(WINDOWS); FontCache.h also uses PLATFORM(WIN). A new PORT=ZeroG on Windows is OS(WINDOWS) but not PLATFORM(WIN), so it would include the Fontconfig header, call DirectWrite, and fail to compile. All of these guards need reworking for ZeroG.
4. **HarfBuzz's ICU integration (hb-icu) is a hard requirement.** Skia.cmake links HarfBuzz::ICU, and the Skia text path includes hb-icu.h and calls hb_icu_script_to_script. That conflicts with the doc's "HarfBuzz senza ICU" (ZeroG.md:460). ICU stays in WebCore regardless, but HarfBuzz must be built with its ICU support, or those calls must be replaced, for example with hb_script_from_iso15924_tag.
5. The Skia CMake has no SkFontMgr_custom* sources or flags anywhere, so ZeroG has to add them itself.
6. **WOFF2 is tied to the FreeType setup.** GTK and WPE call find_package(Freetype) themselves so WOFF2Checks can use FreeType's built-in WOFF2 support (HAVE_WOFF_SUPPORT). ZeroG's options file has to do the same, or keep the separate libwoff2.

macOS: SkFontMgr_mac_ct.cpp and the related CoreText helpers do exist in the vendored Skia tree. But Skia's CMake never compiles them, no Options*.cmake turns on USE_SKIA for Mac, and FontCacheSkia.cpp has no Apple/CoreText branch. Using CoreText would mean new CMake work and a new branch in WebCore. Possible, but not available today.

One nuance on the reviewer's evidence. The Windows IDWriteFontSetBuilder path does add extra font files, but only a hardcoded list of layout-test fonts, and only when the WEBKIT_TESTFONTS environment variable is set. Otherwise it returns early with a null collection, so Skia falls back to the system collection. The mechanism can be reused for embedded fonts, but it must be rewritten.

The mixed-guard gotcha is real and slightly worse than stated. FontCacheSkia.cpp uses PLATFORM(WIN) for its includes (else branch: fontconfig) and for the fallback/last-resort code. fontManager() uses OS(WINDOWS). createDWriteFactory is declared only under PLATFORM(WIN) && USE(SKIA). So a new PLATFORM(ZEROG) on Windows would include the fontconfig header, call an undeclared createDWriteFactory, and pull in the fontconfig-based SkiaSystemFallbackFontCache. It will not compile without fixing these guards.

The reviewer missed nothing that changes the verdict. My Glob for SkFontMgr_mac* returned nothing, but `ls` shows the file, so that was a tool quirk and not counter-evidence.

claims.evidence: Source/cmake/WOFF2Checks.cmake: if FreeType >= 2.10.2 is built with FT_CONFIG_OPTION_USE_BROTLI, HAVE_WOFF_SUPPORT is set. OptionsGTK.cmake:408-422 then turns USE_WOFF2 off ('Using FreeType's WOFF2 support'). FontCustomPlatformDataSkia.cpp:139 accepts woff2 `#if HAVE(WOFF_SUPPORT) || USE(WOFF2)`. Min FreeType 2.9.0 (skia/CMakeLists.txt:5).
claims.implication: Building FreeType with brotli removes the need for libwoff2 (one library fewer, and no C++ woff2 build), which contradicts 'FreeType: no brotli'. Pick one: FreeType+brotli, or libwoff2+brotli.

challenge.reasoning:
I could not show the reviewer wrong on the facts. The source tree confirms two separate ways to get WOFF2. (a) FreeType >= 2.10.2 built with FT_CONFIG_OPTION_USE_BROTLI sets HAVE_WOFF_SUPPORT, and the GTK and WPE ports then switch USE_WOFF2 off. (b) libwoff2dec through USE_WOFF2, which is what the Windows port does. Since the doc already keeps brotli for `Content-Encoding: br`, building FreeType with brotli adds no new library and would let ZeroG drop libwoff2, a C++ library.

Where the reviewer overstates: the doc's setup does not contradict itself. FreeType without brotli plus libwoff2+brotli is valid and builds; WebCore decodes WOFF1 itself with zlib and WOFF2 with libwoff2. So the claim is not wrong. It is a suboptimal choice that the doc does not explain, which makes PARTIAL correct.

The reviewer missed one point that favours the doc. With HAVE_WOFF_SUPPORT, WebCore stops decoding WOFF/WOFF2 itself: convertWOFFToSfntIfNecessary does nothing and the raw WOFF bytes go straight to Skia's fontManager().makeFromData(). That only works if Skia's font manager uses FreeType. The doc keeps the native font manager (DirectWrite/CoreText) as an option on Windows and macOS (ZeroG.md:247, 751). If that option is used, the FreeType-brotli route would break WOFF and WOFF2. The libwoff2 route works with any font manager. So the right fix is not simply to pick FreeType+brotli, but to tie the decision to the font-manager question: FreeType everywhere means FreeType+brotli without libwoff2; keeping native font managers as an option means libwoff2 plus WebCore's own zlib WOFF1 decoder, with FreeType built without brotli.

Other gotchas:
- The FreeType check only runs for FreeType >= 2.10.2 and is a compile-only test of FT_CONFIG_OPTIONS_H, so a vendored FreeType must export a matching ftoption.h.
- With USE_WOFF2, WebCore links WOFF2::dec, and FindWOFF2 looks for libwoff2common/dec through pkg-config, so a static vendored build must provide those imported targets.
- zlib is needed either way: inside FreeType for WOFF1 with HAVE_WOFF_SUPPORT, or in WOFFFileFormat.cpp without it.
- The doc's feature table (ZeroG.md:510) names only `USE_WOFF2`. HAVE_WOFF_SUPPORT is not a user option; the port's cmake has to detect it and expose it with SET_AND_EXPOSE_TO_BUILD.

Source/cmake/FindICU.cmake defers to CMake's built-in FindICU on non-Apple and uses system libicucore on Apple. There is no in-tree ICU (Source/WTF/icu holds only macOS headers, per its README) and no ICU data-filter support anywhere in Source/cmake (grep for ICU_DATA_FILTER finds nothing).

Converter data cannot be dropped wholesale: TextEncodingRegistry.cpp:274-275 always registers TextCodecICU, which serves ISO-8859-2/4/5/10/13/14/15/16, x-mac-*, EUC-TW and others (TextCodecICU.cpp:62-104). challenge.reasoning:
I tried to prove the reviewer wrong and could not. Their verdict holds, and one file path in their evidence needs correcting.

What the doc says (ZeroG.md:257, :435, :459): the build system applies the ICU data filter, with a "minimal" and a "full" profile chosen at compile time. ICU is linked statically, keeps the timezone data, and the converter data "can be cut a lot (to be verified)".

Upstream half, CONFIRMED: ICU comes from outside the tree. Every Options*.cmake calls find_package(ICU 70.1 REQUIRED COMPONENTS data i18n uc): Cocoa:256, GTK:20, JSCOnly:113, PlayStation:56, Win:46, WPE:16. Source/cmake/FindICU.cmake does two things. On Apple it uses libicucore. On every other platform it removes itself from the module path and calls CMake's built-in FindICU (lines 38-47). The tree contains no ICU sources. Source/WTF/icu/README says those headers are ICU 74.2 headers for macOS only, and that other platforms should use installed headers.

Data-filter half, NOT PRESENT upstream: WebKit has no ICU filter support. Searching Source/cmake for ICU_DATA_FILTER, filters.json and data_filter finds nothing. The one "ICU_DATA" hit is ICU_DATA_LIBRARY in FindICU.cmake, which is a library variable, not a filter. As a ZeroG design choice the plan is feasible: ICU's own build tooling supports data filtering (ICU_DATA_FILTER_FILE, ICU 64+). I know this from ICU, not from the checkout. ZeroG has to write all of it: build ICU from source as static libraries with a filter file per profile, then point ICU_ROOT at the result. So PARTIAL is right: the system-package part is accurate, and the filter part is entirely new work the upstream tree gives no help with.

Correction to the reviewer: TextEncodingRegistry.cpp and TextCodecICU.cpp live in Source/WebCore/PAL/pal/text/, not Source/WebCore/platform/text/. The line numbers they gave are correct.

Converter claim, checked and holds:
- extendTextCodecMaps() always registers TextCodecICU (TextEncodingRegistry.cpp:274-275). The encodingNames[] table in TextCodecICU.cpp:80-101 covers ISO-8859-2/4/5/10/13/14/15/16, KOI8-R, macintosh, windows-1250/1251/1254/1256/1258, x-mac-cyrillic/greek/centraleurroman/turkish and EUC-TW.
- TextCodecSingleByte does not take over these names. It registers a separate set: ISO-8859-3/6/7/8/8-I, windows-874 and others (TextCodecSingleByte.cpp:325-443).
- addToTextCodecMap uses HashMap::add (line 177), which keeps the first entry. So even if names overlapped, the ICU codec registered first would win.
- The filter must therefore keep the converter tables for every encoding in TextCodecICU.cpp, or ZeroG must patch those encodings out. That partly settles the doc's open "(da verificare)" point: the converter data can shrink, but not to nothing.

Gotchas the doc misses:
1. Upstream CMake has no U_STATIC_IMPLEMENTATION handling. On Windows, linking ICU statically needs that define on every consumer (WTF, JSC, WebCore, PAL), or the dllimport declarations break the link.
2. CMake's built-in FindICU looks for ICU library names, so a static ICU (for example with the "s" prefix on Windows) may need ICU_ROOT plus name overrides. This needs a build to confirm.
3. TextEncodingDetectorICU.cpp uses ICU charset detection (ucsdet).
4. JSC Intl and Date need the locale, collation and timezone (zoneinfo64) data that the doc already says to keep.
5. WebKit's Skia build compiles neither skunicode nor SkLoadICU.cpp, which loads icudtl.dat on Windows. So Skia adds no ICU data dependency, as long as ZeroG does not enable SkUnicode.

challenge.reasoning:
I tried to show the reviewer wrong and could not. Every point in their evidence checks out, and the checkout adds three things that make PARTIAL stronger.

(1) Windows: CONFIRMED in practice. WebKit's bundled Skia build compiles only the Ganesh GL backend, set up for GLES (SK_GL, SK_GANESH, SK_ASSUME_GL_ES=1). Its GL interface is EGL only. WebCore's Skia GPU glue (PlatformDisplaySkia) calls GrGLInterfaces::MakeEGL(), or MakeEpoxyEGL() when libepoxy is used. Windows has no native EGL, so with the existing WebCore code ANGLE's EGL/GLESv2 is effectively required for GPU Skia. The upstream Windows port hard-codes USE_ANGLE_EGL ON. One nuance: Skia's native D3D, Vulkan and Metal Ganesh sources are in the checkout (src/gpu/ganesh/d3d, vk, mtl), but WebKit's Skia CMakeLists never compiles them. So ANGLE is required unless ZeroG writes its own Skia build and glue code.

(2) Linux: CONFIRMED. GTK and WPE set USE_ANGLE=${ENABLE_WEBGL} and do not set USE_ANGLE_EGL, so Skia uses system EGL or libepoxy. ANGLE comes in only for WebGL, running on its GL backend over the system EGL.

(3) macOS: REFUTED as written. The doc says macOS needs ANGLE "only for WebGL", with Skia on Metal. But the in-tree Skia CMake builds no Metal sources, and the WebCore Skia glue is EGL/GLES only. macOS has no EGL. So the in-tree code only gives a GPU Skia path on macOS through ANGLE-Metal (EGL plus GLES), or through new work: adding the Skia ganesh/mtl sources to the build and writing a new PlatformDisplay/GLContext equivalent.

The reviewer's static-linking implication is correct, and it reaches further than they said:
- Windows: PlatformWin.cmake forces GLESv2 and EGL to SHARED. ZeroG has to override that back to STATIC and still compile D3D9.
- Apple: CMakeLists.txt forces ANGLE, GLESv2 and EGL to OBJECT libraries and merges them into ANGLE-shared.dylib, with an install name under WebCore.framework. ZeroG needs ANGLE-static instead, or its own target. ANGLE-static exists but is EXCLUDE_FROM_ALL and meant for tests.

The only correction to the reviewer: the line that D3D9 "will not compile without it" is just an upstream comment, not something verified.

I tried to prove the reviewer wrong and could not. Every point they made checks out in the checkout.

What is true in the claim:

- The SQLite cookie jar (CookieJarDB) is still in WebCore.
