challenge.reasoning:
I tried to break the reviewer's evidence and couldn't. WebKit never branches on BoringSSL. Outside ThirdParty, the only mention of BORINGSSL anywhere under Source/ is a CMake symbol probe (WEBKIT_CHECK_HAVE_SYMBOL) in OptionsWin.cmake and OptionsPlayStation.cmake. WebCore, WTF, JSC and WebKit have zero hits. BoringSSL reports OPENSSL_VERSION_NUMBER 0x1010107f, so NEED_OPENSSL_THREAD_SUPPORT is 0 and the EVP_KDF code behind the >= 0x30000000L guard is skipped. The SSL calls in CurlSSLVerifier (SSL_CTX_get_verify_mode, SSL_CTX_set1_sigalgs_list) exist in BoringSSL's ssl.h. So, at the header level, BoringSSL is a workable drop-in. Upstream does not test it, and only a real build will prove it. TLS 1.3 support and the static-linking fit are facts about the libraries outside the checkout, and they are plausible for both BoringSSL and OpenSSL 3.

The reviewer's framing of OpenSSL 3 is misleading, though. GTK and WPE call find_package(OpenSSL 3.0) only when USE_OPENSSL is ON. That is a PRIVATE option, OFF by default, described as "OpenSSL instead of libgcrypt as the crypto backend". It covers only the WebCrypto backend; GTK/WPE do their networking through libsoup, not curl. The OPENSSL_API_COMPAT=0x10100000L define likewise applies to the WebCrypto OpenSSL backend, which uses APIs that OpenSSL 3 deprecated.

The reviewer also missed which TLS library the curl ports actually use. The only upstream ports that use curl are Windows and PlayStation. Windows gets its dependencies from vcpkg.json, which pulls libressl and curl[http3,ipv6,libressl]. So the one upstream-tested curl TLS stack is LibreSSL, neither of the doc's two options. WebKit has LibreSSL-specific paths too: CurlSSLHandle.h:37 turns on thread-lock support for LibreSSL, and CurlSSLVerifier.cpp:46 skips sigalgs for it. Choosing BoringSSL or OpenSSL 3 for curl therefore means leaving the tested path.

Second gotcha: the BoringSSL copy in the checkout is the libwebrtc copy. libwebrtc's CMakeLists builds it with BORINGSSL_PREFIX=libwebrtc, which renames its symbols, so it is not a plain, unprefixed libssl/libcrypto that curl and WebCore can link against as-is. ZeroG should build its own BoringSSL. If WebRTC is ever turned on, the prefixed copy and ZeroG's copy will both be linked in.

Third: curl must use its OpenSSL-family backend built against the same BoringSSL (or OpenSSL 3), because WebKit casts the CURLOPT_SSL_CTX_FUNCTION void* straight to SSL_CTX*. The same applies to ngtcp2 if HTTP/3 is wanted.

Verdict stays PARTIAL. The headers are compatible, but upstream never exercises BoringSSL, the OpenSSL 3 precedent is WebCrypto-only, and the real upstream curl TLS library is LibreSSL.

challenge.reasoning:
I tried to prove the reviewer wrong and couldn't; their evidence holds. Every CurlHandle calls enableAcceptEncoding() in its constructor, and that sets CURLOPT_ACCEPT_ENCODING to "". Per the libcurl docs, "" means curl advertises and transparently decodes every content encoding it was built with: gzip/deflate via zlib, br via brotli, zstd via libzstd (zstd since curl 7.72). WebCore has no HTTP Content-Encoding decoder of its own, so response decompression depends only on how curl is built. The claim is functionally achievable. The doc is wrong in two ways, though, so PARTIAL is right:
(1) zstd is unaccounted for. The 'Tenere' rows in the Decisioni table are ICU, HarfBuzz, FreeType, Skia, curl, BoringSSL, nghttp2, libpsl, zlib, brotli, woff2, libpng, libjpeg-turbo, libwebp, libxml2 and SQLite. That is exactly 16, plus ANGLE makes 17, so zstd is not in the count. It is also missing from the license table (L544-554). Nothing in WebKit itself uses zstd: the only matches under Source/ are in ThirdParty (skia resources, libwebrtc, boringssl test vectors, ANGLE/mesa), none in WebCore, PAL, WTF or Source/cmake. Either add zstd as a curl-only dependency with its license and update the count, or drop it from the Stack table.

challenge.reasoning:
I tried to find code the first reviewer missed and found none, so their reading stands. The doc says the engine loads root CAs at startup: standard paths on Linux, CryptoAPI on Windows, Keychain on macOS, with an optional embedded bundle. This is a sound design, but upstream WebKit's curl layer covers only part of it.

- **Windows:** WebKit has no CryptoAPI code. It sets CURLSSLOPT_NATIVE_CA and libcurl reads the Windows store itself. From the curl docs, which I did not check in the tree: libcurl supports this with OpenSSL-family backends, including BoringSSL, on Windows since 7.71.0, and it links crypt32. So the Windows goal works, just not through engine code.
- **Linux and macOS:** there is no CurlSSLHandle::platformInitialize() implementation. Only Win and PlayStation provide one, and each is added to the build only by its own PlatformWin.cmake or PlatformPlayStation.cmake. A new ZeroG port must supply this function, or linking fails with an undefined symbol. That is a hard dependency the doc does not mention.
- **Keychain:** I found no SecTrustCopyAnchorCertificates or any other Keychain code in WebCore.
- **Embedded bundle:** the mechanism exists, via setCACertData into CURLOPT_CAINFO_BLOB. But the OS(WINDOWS) branch never reads getCACertInfo(), so a bundle set on Windows is silently ignored unless that code is patched.

One nuance the reviewer did not mention: if CURLOPT_CAINFO is never set, libcurl falls back to its compile-time default CA bundle/path. On Linux that default may happen to work. It is fragile for a statically linked binary that runs on many distros, so probing the path explicitly at runtime is still the right approach.

A second nuance, from memory of the curl docs: on Linux and macOS, CURLSSLOPT_NATIVE_CA is documented only for wolfSSL (and GnuTLS on some systems), not for OpenSSL or BoringSSL. That is why ZeroG must load the Keychain roots itself on macOS. Recent curl versions may offer Apple SecTrust verification for OpenSSL-family backends; check this against the curl version you pin.

challenge.reasoning:
I tried to refute the reviewer and could not. Their evidence holds, and I found more problems the doc does not mention.

1) The doc's threading model is accurate. CurlRequest does its transfers on a dedicated thread named "curlThread", started by CurlRequestScheduler. Every client callback is posted back to the main thread with ensureOnMainThread, and data arrives as separate curlDidReceiveData(Ref<SharedBuffer>) chunks. So "curl on the network thread, streamed to main in chunks" is correct.

2) Nothing in the tree works as a single-process LoaderStrategy for curl. WebKitLegacy, the only other implementation, is built only when ENABLE_WEBKIT_LEGACY is ON. That is set ON only in OptionsCocoa.cmake and OFF in Win, PlayStation and JSCOnly. Its WebResourceLoadScheduler also depends on ResourceHandle.

3) The doc misses a hard gotcha: under USE(SOUP) || USE(CURL), ResourceHandle is a set of ASSERT_NOT_REACHED stubs. That covers start, cancel, platformLoadResourceSynchronously and the auth callbacks. ResourceLoader::start() ends in ResourceHandle::create(...). So ZeroG's LoaderStrategy must not call ResourceLoader::start() for http(s) or app:// requests. It may call it only for data: URLs and archive loads, which start() handles before reaching ResourceHandle; this is the same as WebLoaderStrategy::startLocalLoad. Like WebKit2's WebResourceLoader, it must drive the ResourceLoader's public didReceiveResponse, didReceiveData/didReceiveBuffer, didFinishLoading and didFail directly from the CurlRequestClient callbacks (NetworkDataTaskCurl is the in-tree reference).

4) Synchronous loads: CurlRequest has no sync mode. runOnMainThread always calls ensureOnMainThread, and the callbacks start on curlThread, so they are always posted to the main thread. If loadResourceSynchronously blocks the main thread waiting for them, it deadlocks. ZeroG needs a separate sync path: a nested run loop that only handles that request's callbacks, or a blocking curl_easy call on another thread with direct handoff. The same is needed for CORS preflight sync checks. For app:// sync loads it should copy WebKit2, which calls handler->loadSynchronously directly.

5) The doc also skips registering custom schemes. app:// must be registered in LegacySchemeRegistry (registerURLSchemeAsSecure, registerURLSchemeAsCORSEnabled, registerURLSchemeAsHandledBySchemeHandler and so on). Without this, origin, fetch and CORS behaviour is wrong. blob: URLs also need their own handler, because in WebKit2 the network process serves them.

The design is sound, but most of the claim describes code ZeroG has to write from scratch with real traps, so PARTIAL is correct.

challenge.reasoning:
The PARTIAL verdict holds. The source actually makes the doc's claim weaker than the reviewer said: the reasoning it gives for each of the two registrations does not hold up as written.

1) Secure registration and crypto.subtle. `Crypto.subtle` is marked [SecureContext]. `Document::isSecureContext()` returns `m_isSecureContext`, which is computed by `computeIsSecureContext()`, which calls `isDocumentSecure()`, which calls `securityOrigin()->isPotentiallyTrustworthy()`. On non-Cocoa platforms (ZeroG), a non-special scheme like app:// gets an OPAQUE origin unless `schemeIsHandledBySchemeHandler(scheme)` is true. The opaque `SecurityOrigin()` constructor hard-sets `m_isPotentiallyTrustworthy{false}`, so the lazy `shouldTreatAsPotentiallyTrustworthy` check never runs. Result: `registerURLSchemeAsSecure("app")` by itself does NOT give app:// pages crypto.subtle. In the other direction, `registerURLSchemeAsHandledBySchemeHandler` by itself does: it makes the origin a real tuple origin, and SecurityOrigin.cpp:101 counts it as potentially trustworthy. So the "secure" flag is neither necessary nor sufficient for crypto.subtle. The flag still matters elsewhere. `SecurityOrigin::isSecure()` (L250) drives mixed-content checks: once app:// is a secure context, every app:// subresource counts as "mixed content" unless the scheme is also Secure. Today that is saved only by `shouldAllowConnectionWithPotentiallyInsecureProtocol`, which needs handled-by-scheme-handler and IsUpgradable::Yes. The flag is also used by the HTTPS-only check in CachedResourceLoader.cpp:1271 and the WebAuthn assert.

2) CORS-enabled and cross-origin fetch. `DocumentThreadableLoader::checkURLSchemeAsCORSEnabled` (L193-201) and CrossOriginAccessControl.cpp:197 check the TARGET (or redirect) URL's scheme, not the page's scheme. http and https are built in (LegacySchemeRegistry.cpp:275-279). So a fetch from an app:// page to an https API works whether or not app:// is CORS-enabled. The flag only matters for cross-origin requests TO app://, for example app://a to app://b, an http://localhost dev-mode page fetching app://, or any request made from an opaque-origin app:// document (opaque origins are never same-origin, so even fetching its own app:// assets is cross-origin and fails with "Cross origin requests are only supported for HTTP.").

3) The reviewer's key finding is correct. SecurityOriginData.cpp:193-232 makes app:// opaque unless it is handled by a scheme handler. `ScriptExecutionContext::canAccessResource` (L949-953) then returns No for an opaque origin, which blocks cookies, localStorage, IndexedDB and StorageManager. One correction to their citation: WebPage.cpp:1040 is the legacy custom-protocol path. The main WebKit2 path is `WebPage::registerURLSchemeHandler` (WebPage.cpp:9408-9412), which registers HandledBySchemeHandler + CORSEnabled. It does NOT register Secure.

Gotchas the doc misses:
(a) Do NOT register app:// as Local. `isOriginEquivalentToLocal` (ScriptExecutionContext.cpp:944-965) denies IndexedDB, LocalStorage and StorageManager to local origins.
(b) The `SecureContextChecksEnabled` setting (UnifiedWebPreferences.yaml:5552, default true) short-circuits `isSecureContext()` to true. It is an escape hatch, not the right fix.
(c) The registry must be filled before the first `SecurityOrigin` for that scheme is created. `isPotentiallyTrustworthy` is cached per origin, and origins are cached (for example blob origins).

Required set for app:// and every `zg_context_register_scheme` scheme: HandledBySchemeHandler (required) + CORSEnabled + Secure (for mixed-content correctness). Never Local.

challenge.reasoning:
I tried to refute the reviewer and could not. The doc says, at ZeroG.md:303 ("Cookie con il cookie jar su SQLite di WebCore") and :261 ("curl è già integrato in WebCore ... incluso il cookie jar su SQLite"), that WebCore has a SQLite cookie jar. That much is true: WebCore::CookieJarDB is in WebCore/platform/network/curl, built through Curl.cmake, and is backed by SQLiteDatabase. What the doc gets wrong is the suggestion that the jar comes already wired up. Inside WebCore, CookieJarDB is used only by its own .cpp file. Everything that connects it to page loading is WebKit2 code: NetworkStorageSession has moved out of WebCore (WebCore/platform/network now has only CookieStorageSession.h), and WebKit/Shared/NetworkStorageSession.h holds UniqueRef<CookieJarDB> under USE(CURL). On non-Cocoa platforms, every base CookieJar method is an ASSERT_NOT_REACHED stub. curl's own cookie engine is turned off, and the Cookie header for WebSocket handshakes is added by WebKit2's WebSocketTaskCurl. The storage engine can be reused as-is. The glue cannot: ZeroG has to supply its own CookieJar subclass (its methods are virtual, so this is possible), something equivalent to a storage session, and Cookie/Set-Cookie handling in its LoaderStrategy and WebSocket path. So PARTIAL is the right verdict.

Things the doc misses: (1) WebCore no longer has a NetworkStorageSession; ZeroG must port the CookieJarDB-related parts of WebKit/Shared/NetworkStorageSession.h and NetworkStorageSessionCurl.cpp (264 lines) or write its own. (2) CookieJarDB.cpp needs PublicSuffixStore (via libpsl or the platform's equivalent) when it checks cookie domains, so the doc's libpsl dependency (line 466) really is required. (3) getCookiesAsync defaults to completionHandler(std::nullopt), so the CookieStore API also needs a ZeroG implementation. (4) CookieJarDB's only open-file mode is the ":memory:" path, which is how ephemeral sessions are handled.

challenge.reasoning:
I tried to show the reviewer was wrong and couldn't. Their evidence checks out. The claim ("curl: only HTTP and HTTPS") is a build decision, and it can be done, but the WebCore curl code upstream does expect libcurl to support FILE as well, so PARTIAL is right.

1) CurlHandle::enableAllowedProtocols() sets CURLOPT_PROTOCOLS_STR to "file,http,https" (CurlContext.cpp:553-556). It runs on every CurlHandle (CurlContext.cpp:303).

2) The reviewer's wording undersells one point: libcurl actually reads the file:// body. CurlRequest::resume() (CurlRequest.cpp:116-119) only builds a fake 200 response with a MIME type taken from the path (invokeDidReceiveResponseForFile, CurlRequest.cpp:580-603). Its completion handler then calls startWithJobManager(), which hands the transfer to libcurl's FILE handler. CurlHandle::setURL also has a file-specific branch that strips the query (CurlContext.cpp:403-407). So with CURL_DISABLE_FILE, any file:// request through CurlRequest would fail with CURLE_UNSUPPORTED_PROTOCOL.

3) The point that weakens the reviewer's concern without overturning it: in this checkout the only user of CurlRequest is WebKit2's NetworkProcess (WebKit/NetworkProcess/curl/NetworkDataTaskCurl.cpp/.h). ZeroG drops WebKit2. Nothing in WebCore itself creates a CurlRequest, because the legacy curl ResourceHandle is gone. ZeroG's own loader therefore decides whether file:// ever reaches curl. Serving file:// (like app://) directly from the loader removes the problem, so this is a design caveat, not a blocker.

4) WebSocket works with HTTP-only curl: CurlStream rewrites ws/wss to http/https and uses CONNECT_ONLY (CurlStream.cpp:48-54), so curl's own WebSocket support is not needed.

5) If libcurl doesn't know the "file" name, curl_easy_setopt(CURLOPT_PROTOCOLS_STR, "file,http,https") may return an error. WebKit ignores the return value (CurlContext.cpp:555), so the default mask (every protocol compiled in, which would be http/https here) stays in place. I could not check this, because there is no curl source in the workspace and the result depends on how curl's setopt parses the list. It needs a build test.

Facts the doc leaves out: CurlContext RELEASE_ASSERTs that curl was built with CURL_VERSION_LARGEFILE (CurlContext.cpp:129), so a minimal curl build must keep large-file support. HTTP/3 is only turned on when curl has both HTTP3 and ALTSVC and is 8.5.0 or newer (CurlContext.cpp:130-135), so CURL_DISABLE_ALTSVC would silently turn HTTP/3 off. Existing ports require curl 7.85.0 or newer (OptionsPlayStation.cmake:105) or 7.87.0 or newer (OptionsWin.cmake:44); 7.85.0 is where CURLOPT_PROTOCOLS_STR appeared. Code paths depend on LIBCURL_VERSION_NUM (CurlRequest.cpp:282/357/384, CurlContext.cpp:507).

challenge.reasoning:
PARTIAL is still the right verdict, but the reviewer misread the preprocessor guards in EncodingTables.cpp, and that changes what they concluded. Only the *Reference tables* (jis0208Reference, jis0212Reference, big5Reference, eucKRDecodingIndexReference, gb18030Reference) and checkEncodingTableInvariants() sit inside `#if ASSERT_ENABLED`. The builder functions that call ucnv_open, jis0208(), jis0212(), big5(), eucKR() and gb18030(), are outside every guard and get compiled into Release builds too. So TextCodecCJK is not independent of ICU. It builds its decoding tables at runtime by sweeping the ICU converters "EUC-JP", "Big-5", "windows-949" and "gb18030" byte by byte, then patching in a few extras. The engine therefore needs that CJK converter data in production, not just in Debug. Those are also some of the largest .cnv files in ICU, which shrinks the doc's "reduce a lot" in practice.

What happens if the data is missing: for jis0208, jis0212, big5 and eucKR, the count check RELEASE_ASSERT_WITH_SECURITY_IMPLICATION(arrayIndex == N) will most likely crash even in Release, because invalid sequences are skipped and the count comes out wrong. For gb18030 there is no release count check, so the table silently fills with garbage. The way to remove this dependency is to patch the builders to use the Reference tables (from WHATWG) unconditionally. That adds roughly 60k pairs, about 250-300 KB, to the binary, and the in-file comment says upstream avoided this on purpose.

The rest of the reviewer's evidence checks out. TextCodecICU still owns about 20 single-byte encodings plus EUC-TW. It is registered unconditionally in extendTextCodecMaps, and registerCodecs only ASSERTs on failure, then skips via ASSERT_NOT_REACHED/continue. In Release, a missing converter means a registered name whose codec fails later in createICUConverter: ucnv_open returns null. TextEncodingDetectorICU uses ucsdet_*.

The claim is still partly true. TextCodecCJK implements Shift_JIS, ISO-2022-JP, EUC-KR and GBK on top of those four ICU-derived tables. So the EBCDIC, ibm-943, ISO-2022, HZ and similar converters can be dropped. Only PAL/text calls ucnv_* in WTF, JSC and WebCore.

Minimum ICU converter data to keep:
- cnvalias
- the TextCodecICU single-byte list
- EUC-TW
- EUC-JP, Big-5 (windows-950), windows-949 and gb18030, or patch EncodingTables.cpp to stop using them
- the ucsdet data, or patch out TextEncodingDetectorICU

challenge.reasoning:
I tried to refute the reviewer and couldn't. The main idea of the claim holds up: on Windows the engine's runtime dependencies look like OS-provided DLLs only, with the CRT linked statically. The specific list "kernel32, user32, d3d11, dxgi, crypt32, ws2_32" is the problem, because it leaves out several DLLs that the upstream Windows CMake files and sources actually link or load. The reviewer found iphlpapi, and that finding is correct. It is also only part of what is missing:

- WTF links DbgHelp, shlwapi, synchronization and winmm without any condition. winmm is really used: timeBeginPeriod/timeEndPeriod in CurrentTime.cpp.
- WTF RandomDevice calls CryptAcquireContext/CryptGenRandom, which come from advapi32.
- WebCore links usp10 (Uniscribe) without any condition. The Uniscribe sources themselves sit only in the USE_CAIRO block, so a Skia-only port could probably drop it, but the stock cmake lists it.
- WebCore links iphlpapi for NetworkStateNotifierWin, which is listed as an unconditional Windows source.
- Skia on Windows uses DirectWrite (SK_TYPEFACE_FACTORY_DIRECTWRITE). It loads DWriteCore.dll and then dwrite.dll at runtime with LoadLibraryExW.
- ANGLE loads d3d11.dll and dxgi.dll at runtime, and also d3dcompiler_47.dll for its HLSL compiler. That file is in System32 on Windows 10+, but it is not on the doc's list.

Two caveats. The parenthetical may have been meant as examples rather than a complete list, which is why this is PARTIAL and not REFUTED. And whether each DLL ends up as a load-time import depends on which sources ZeroG's own port compiles (iphlpapi and usp10 can be avoided), so the exact final import table can only be confirmed from a build (dumpbin /dependents).

Facts the doc misses:
(1) Upstream ANGLE on Windows is built as shared libraries: GLESv2_LIBRARY_TYPE SHARED and EGL_LIBRARY_TYPE SHARED. A fully static link has to override this, otherwise libGLESv2.dll and libEGL.dll ship next to the app.
(2) The ANGLE cmake still references d3d9 sources and links d3d9, but this checkout has no d3d9 backend directory. MSVC only records imports that are actually referenced, so this should be harmless, but the cmake needs cleaning up.
(3) BoringSSL and curl on Windows probably also bring in advapi32, bcrypt/bcryptprimitives and crypt32. This is outside the WebKit tree and was not checked here.

challenge.reasoning:
I tried to prove the reviewer wrong and couldn't. Their verdict holds, and the case against the doc is stronger than they made it.

1) WebCrypto is always compiled. Sources.txt:907-938 always lists crypto/*.cpp. ENABLE_WEB_CRYPTO appears nowhere in Source/WTF, Source/cmake, Source/WebCore/crypto or WebCore/CMakeLists.txt, so the flag was removed, not renamed. The algorithm classes declare platform* hooks (for example CryptoAlgorithmAESCBC.h:44-45 platformEncrypt/platformDecrypt, CryptoAlgorithmRegistry.cpp:42 platformRegisterAlgorithms) that only a backend defines. The tree has three backends: crypto/openssl (platform/OpenSSL.cmake), crypto/gcrypt (platform/GCrypt.cmake, which also needs Tasn1) and crypto/cocoa. Every CMake port includes one of them: Win, PlayStation, Haiku and GTK/WPE with USE_OPENSSL use OpenSSL, the rest use GCrypt. There is no stub backend. PAL's CryptoDigest likewise uses openssl, gcrypt or commoncrypto; PlatformWin.cmake:2 uses CryptoDigestOpenSSL.cpp. PAL/pal/crypto/win/CryptoDigestWin.cpp also exists but no cmake or txt file references it. That only removes the need for OpenSSL for PAL digests on Windows, not for WebCore's crypto. So BoringSSL's libcrypto is needed when WebCore is first linked in step 2, unless ZeroG writes about 20 stub platform* files of its own.

2) The reviewer missed something bigger: curl can't be deferred either, as long as only stock backends are used. ResourceRequest.h, ResourceResponse.h, ResourceError.h, CertificateInfo.h and AuthenticationChallenge.h are not in platform/network/. challenge.reasoning:
I tried to prove the reviewer wrong and couldn't. Their reading of the source is correct, and the one thing they left open I settled by running a test on this Windows 11 22621 machine.

1) WebKit never checks for ACG directly. I grepped Source/ (ThirdParty excluded) for ProhibitDynamicCode, ProcessDynamicCodePolicy, DynamicCodePolicy and PROCESS_MITIGATION and got no matches. So nothing in WebKit "detects" ACG. ZeroG would have to add that check itself.

2) JSC does fall back to the interpreter on its own, but only as a side effect of the JIT memory reservation failing. FixedVMPoolExecutableAllocator() calls initializeJITPageReservation(), which on Windows ends up in VirtualAlloc(MEM_RESERVE, PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE). If that fails, m_reservation is empty and isValid() returns false. enableAssembler() then returns false unless crashIfCantAllocateJITMemory is set (default false). After that, InitializeThreading sets useJIT=false and calls notifyOptionsChanged(). This path is silent. Nothing is logged unless verboseExecutablePoolAllocation is on.

3) The open question was whether ACG makes even a reserve-only RWX VirtualAlloc fail. I built a small mingw test (in a temp dir, outside the project) that calls SetProcessMitigationPolicy(ProcessDynamicCodePolicy, ProhibitDynamicCode=1). With ACG on:
- MEM_RESERVE with PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE returns NULL with error 1655 (ERROR_DYNAMIC_CODE_BLOCKED).
- MEM_RESERVE|MEM_COMMIT with RWX also fails with 1655.
- Committing RWX into a region reserved before ACG was turned on also fails with 1655.
- Committing PAGE_READWRITE into that region still works.

So if ACG is active before JSC initializes, the startup fallback to the interpreter really does happen. If ACG is turned on after init, the reservation already exists, and the next lazy RWX commit fails. OSAllocator::commit then calls CRASH(). That confirms the reviewer's caveat with a real test, not just by reading code.

Why PARTIAL: "switches to the interpreter" is effectively true when ACG is on before init. "Detects it at startup" is not something WebKit does; it is implicit. And there is no handling at all if ACG is enabled later, which ends in a hard crash.

Minor correction to the reviewer's line numbers: OSAllocator::commit is at OSAllocatorWin.cpp:92-97, not 88-93, and enableAssembler is at VM.cpp:208-224. One more point for ZeroG: enableAssembler() returns before any reservation when Options::useJIT() is already false (VM.cpp:210-211). So if ZeroG's "auto" mode calls GetProcessMitigationPolicy and sets useJIT=false before the first JSC init, no executable memory is ever reserved. That is the clean way to implement the doc's claim.

challenge.reasoning:
The reviewer's citations are all accurate, but PARTIAL is too cautious. The claim says that on Linux an SELinux execmem denial is detected at startup and the engine falls back to the interpreter. Upstream JSC already does exactly this on Linux, once per process, inside JSC::initialize(). ZeroG gets it without extra code.

1) The executable pool is reserved up front at initialization, not lazily. On Linux the "uncommitted" path still calls mmap with PROT_READ|PROT_WRITE|PROT_EXEC and MAP_NORESERVE. "Commit" afterwards is only madvise. So the one syscall where SELinux checks execmem is the startup reservation mmap. There is no later mprotect-to-exec step that could fail mid-run and crash, because MPROTECT_RX_TO_RWX is 0 and no port's CMake turns it on.

2) A failed reservation goes down a non-crashing path. isValid() returns false, enableAssembler() returns false (crashIfCantAllocateJITMemory defaults to false), canUseJIT becomes false, Options::useJIT() is set to false, and notifyOptionsChanged() calls disableAllJITOptions() and disableAllWasmJITOptions(). That leaves LLInt for JS and IPInt for Wasm.

3) The reviewer's open question was whether an execmem denial really makes an anonymous RWX mmap fail. That is kernel behaviour outside this tree, and I am citing it from memory rather than from source checked here. In security/selinux/hooks.c, file_map_prot_check() checks PROCESS__EXECMEM for any mapping with PROT_EXEC that is anonymous, or private and writable. This applies whenever default_noexec is set, which it is on any NX-capable CPU. If the check is denied, mmap returns EACCES. So with execmem denied in enforcing mode the failure is certain, not "policy-dependent".

The real caveats are these:
- A permissive domain only logs, so the JIT stays on.
- The fallback is silent. Nothing is logged unless verboseExecutablePoolAllocation is set, so ZeroG has to report the JIT state itself, for example from VM::canUseJIT or g_jscConfig.vm.canUseJIT.
- Detection is not a separate probe. It happens once (call_once) inside JSC::initialize(), so the zg_runtime_config `jit` option must be applied before that point:
  - "disabled": Options::useJIT=false, JSC_useJIT=0, or ExecutableAllocator::disableJIT(), which asserts that the allocator has not been created yet.
  - "always on": Options::crashIfCantAllocateJITMemory=true.
- The same fallback also triggers on non-SELinux failures, such as RLIMIT_AS or mmap failing on the large pool reservation.

The reviewer's security note is correct: on Linux and Windows the JIT pool is permanently RWX, because EXECUTABLE_POOL_WRITABLE is true and SEPARATED_WX_HEAP is 0 outside Cocoa ARM64. That supports the advice to turn the JIT off for untrusted content. Other PROT_EXEC users in JSC (PerfLog.cpp:182, ProfilerSupport.cpp:89) are file-backed marker mmaps that only run when profiling options are enabled, so they do not affect startup.

challenge.reasoning:
The claim is correct on both counts, so it should be CONFIRMED, not PARTIAL. The reviewer's facts are accurate. The one thing they got wrong is the reason they marked it down. They said the entitlement requirement is Apple policy that does not appear in the tree. It does appear: WebKit's own macOS JSC build script adds com.apple.security.cs.allow-jit to every JIT-using executable (jsc, testb3, testmasm and the others). DumpRenderTree carries the same entitlement. The JSC runtime checks for that exact string on Apple Silicon Macs in internal-SDK builds. MAP_JIT is added to every executable mapping on all Darwin builds. Apple's hardened-runtime docs say the same thing: MAP_JIT plus allow-jit is the supported way to run a JIT under hardened runtime.

Their conclusion mostly holds. In a public-SDK build with no entitlement, isJITEnabled() does not check entitlements. Reserving the JIT region then fails, ExecutableAllocator::isValid() returns false, and VM::enableAssembler() returns false. JSC keeps running on LLInt/CLoop instead of crashing, unless crashIfCantAllocateJITMemory is set. Only jsc.cpp:4216 sets that option, and it defaults to false.

Points the doc and the reviewer missed:
(1) ZeroG's 'jit: always on' setting must actually do something. Either set Options::crashIfCantAllocateJITMemory=true or check VM::canUseAssembler() and report an error. Otherwise 'always on' quietly behaves like 'auto'.
(2) Port macro gotcha. PlatformLegacy.h:49-58 defines PLATFORM(MAC), and through it PLATFORM(COCOA) at :80-81, on OS(MACOS) unless one of BUILDING_GTK__/HAIKU__/WPE__/JSCONLY__ is defined. A new ZeroG port macro needs its own #elif branch there, or the build inherits all the Cocoa code paths. That also changes HAVE_MAC_JIT_RESTRICTIONS (PlatformHave.h:634-635, needs PLATFORM(MAC) and ARM64). USE_PTHREAD_JIT_PERMISSIONS_API (PlatformUse.h:272-279) is keyed on OS(MACOS) on purpose, so W^X switching via pthread_jit_write_protect_np works either way.
(3) Without the entitlement, the YARR regex JIT and WebAssembly (BBQ/OMG) lose JIT as well. They share the same ExecutableAllocator.
(4) com.apple.security.cs.allow-unsigned-executable-memory also exists, but it is weaker. JSC does not need it because it always uses MAP_JIT.
(5) Private entitlements such as com.apple.private.verified-jit, com.apple.security.cs.single-jit and jit-write-allowlist are only added for WK_USE_RESTRICTED_ENTITLEMENTS (internal) builds. The reviewer's file and line citations are accurate. Their PARTIAL verdict, though, answers something the doc does not say. The section "Binding JavaScript dirette" (ZeroG.md:362) says natives are registered "direttamente nel contesto JSC della pagina, con l'API C di JavaScriptCore, senza IPC" ("directly in the page's JSC context, with JavaScriptCore's C API, without IPC"). WebCore already includes it in several files (LocalFrame.cpp:134, SerializedScriptValue.cpp:93). toGlobalRef itself is a trivial reinterpret_cast (APICast.h:201-204).

challenge.reasoning:
I tried to prove the reviewer wrong and could not. Their reading of the code is right, so PARTIAL stays.

1) The ctx passed to a JSC C API callback is the callee's realm, not the caller's. APICallbackFunction::callImpl sets `JSContextRef execRef = toRef(globalObject)`, where globalObject is the JSGlobalObject the host function was invoked with, which is the function's own realm. The C API gives you nothing to identify the caller. A same-origin iframe calling parent.App.fn() therefore shows up with the parent's ctx.

2) The callback runs inside `JSLock::DropAllLocks`, in both callImpl and constructImpl. Any C API call made inside it has to take the lock again, which adds cost to the binding latency metric.

3) Cross-origin frames are already stopped by WebCore before they ever reach `App`. JSDOMWindow's getOwnPropertySlot sends cross-origin access through BindingSecurity::shouldAllowAccessToDOMWindow and then to jsDOMWindowGetOwnPropertySlotRestrictedAccess, which only exposes the cross-origin allowlist.

4) A real per-call caller check is possible, just not through the public C API. WebCore already has the pieces: `incumbentDOMWindow(JSGlobalObject&)` uses `callerGlobalObject(fallback, vm.topCallFrame)`. callerGlobalObject skips the first frame (the host function) and returns the caller's codeBlock->globalObject(). DropAllLocks does not reset vm.topCallFrame. It only saves and restores the stack pointer and last stack top. So ZeroG's own C++ code can recover the caller's realm inside the callback, as long as it takes the JSLock again (JSLockHolder) before walking the stack. ZeroG links WebCore and JSC statically, so it has these internals. It could also skip the C API and register a JSC native host function (JSFunction plus NativeFunction). That gives it the CallFrame directly and avoids DropAllLocks completely.

The doc's goal is therefore achievable. But it does not follow from the doc's stated mechanism ("con l'API C di JavaScriptCore", line 362). Without engine internals, the only "per-call" check the C API can do is re-checking the origin of the callee realm's document. That mostly repeats the per-realm install filter. That is why the verdict is PARTIAL, not CONFIRMED or REFUTED.

Things the doc misses:
- Per-realm installation in the "window object cleared" callback is the main defence. The per-call check adds real value only for same-origin frame sharing, function references kept across frames, and document.domain or same-origin reuse of the window object.
- Doing a caller check needs WebCore-private APIs (incumbentDOMWindow, callerGlobalObject) or JSC-private host functions. That ties ZeroG to internals that change upstream.

challenge.reasoning:
Every piece of evidence the reviewer cited checks out. The design is buildable: JSObjectMakeDeferredPromise gives a promise plus resolve/reject functions, and a page's global object routes its microtasks to WebCore's WindowEventLoop queue, not to the VM's default queue. So when JSObjectCallAsFunction(resolve) releases the JSLock, the lock release drains only the default queue. It does not run the page's .then reactions, and the C API call never goes through JSExecState::didLeaveScriptContext either.

The reviewer missed one thing, and it makes their implication too strong. The reactions do not wait for "some later WebCore task". Putting a reaction job on WebCore's MicrotaskQueue calls an override, MicrotaskQueue::scheduleToRunIfNeeded. That calls EventLoop::scheduleToRunIfNeeded, then WindowEventLoop::scheduleToRun, which starts a 0-second one-shot WebCore Timer. When the timer fires, EventLoop::run does a microtask checkpoint even if no tasks are queued. So the .then reactions run on the next main RunLoop timer tick, through MainThreadSharedTimer. On non-CF, non-Windows ports that timer is a RunLoop::Timer, and Windows has its own MainThreadSharedTimerWin. They are delayed by one hop, not left pending.

This holds only if ZeroG's port implements the MainThreadSharedTimer/ThreadTimers path correctly and the page is not suspended. When the page is suspended, setMicrotaskRunnability is set to Suspended and the reactions are held back. One hop is still not spec-ideal: other timers, rAF or input events can run between the resolve and its reactions.

Recommendations still apply:
- Call resolve inside a task queued on the document's EventLoop (EventLoopTaskGroup::queueTask), or call eventLoop().performMicrotaskCheckpoint(vm) right after resolving.
- Hold resolve/reject with JSValueProtect until the promise settles.
- The doc's 'zg_promise_resolve runs on the main thread' is required. WebCore objects and the window event loop are main-thread-only (WindowEventLoop::isContextThread() returns isMainThread()).

Verdict: PARTIAL. The mechanism exists, but the doc does not mention event-loop integration, and the reviewer's 'may wait indefinitely' reading is overstated.

claims.implication: To get full arguments, stacks or worker logs, ZeroG needs a small WebCore patch (for example a ChromeClient hook that receives the whole Inspector::ConsoleMessage) or its own instrumentation. ZeroG must not use an ephemeral session, or it gets no console messages at all.

challenge.reasoning:
I tried to prove the reviewer wrong and could not. Every point they made checks out in the source tree.

What works: for main-frame/page console.log, console.warn and console.error, WebCore calls ChromeClient::addMessageToConsole with the source, the level, the message, the line, the column and the URL. For the basic case, that covers the "level, message, file, line" part of the claim. The class is FrameConsoleClient.

What breaks "every":
(1) Ephemeral sessions are blocked. Both FrameConsoleClient paths return early or skip when page->usesEphemeralSession() is true, which means m_sessionID.isEphemeral().
(2) Only the first argument is sent as text. getFirstArgumentAsString calls getArgumentAtIndexAsString(0). So console.log("a", obj, 3) reaches the host as just "a". Only the system-console printing path formats all arguments.
(3) MessageType is never passed. The ChromeClient signature has no type parameter, so table, trace, assert, dir and group all arrive looking like plain logs at a given level.
(4) No call stack is passed.
(5) A console.log() with zero arguments is skipped, because the call is guarded by arguments->argumentCount().
(6) console.count, countReset, time, timeLog, timeEnd, timeStamp, profile and takeHeapSnapshot only go to InspectorInstrumentation and never reach ChromeClient.
(7) Worker console messages, from both console API calls and WebCore-internal messages, only go to InspectorInstrumentation, plus the system console when a setting is on. They never reach ChromeClient.

Workaround that probably won't hold: replacing the JSC ConsoleClient on the global object. WebCore resets it to frame.console() on every window-proxy and navigation transition, so a ZeroG port cannot install its own ConsoleClient without patching WebCore.

Gap in the reviewer's suggestion: they proposed a WebCore patch, but there is another way. Connecting an in-process Inspector frontend channel gives full Console.messageAdded events, including type, all arguments, stack and worker messages, through the existing inspector machinery. That needs ENABLE inspector support and JSON handling, but no WebCore patch. Otherwise, a small patch is needed: for example, a ChromeClient hook that takes the const Inspector::ConsoleMessage&, plus forwarding from WorkerGlobalScope::addConsoleMessage.

The reviewer's implication is right: ZeroG must use a persistent (non-ephemeral) SessionID for its Page, or the host gets no console messages at all.

claims.claim: Unhandled JS errors and unhandled Promise rejections reach a dedicated callback with message and stack trace
claims.evidence: Uncaught exceptions: ScriptExecutionContext::reportException (dom/ScriptExecutionContext.cpp:546-564) logs to the console only if the error event was not handled. Rejections: RejectedPromiseTracker (dom/RejectedPromiseTracker.cpp:189-194) dispatches 'unhandledrejection', then reportUnhandledPromiseRejection (ScriptExecutionContext.cpp:566-622) builds an 'Unhandled Promise Rejection: ...' console message with a ScriptCallStack, gated by Settings unhandledPromiseRejectionToConsoleEnabled (default true, WebCore/page/Settings.yaml:337-339). ChromeClient never receives the call stack. JSDOMGlobalObject::addScriptErrorCallback (bindings/js/JSDOMGlobalObject.h:126-130) gives message/url/line/col only. JSGlobalContextSetUnhandledRejectionCallback (API/JSContextRefPrivate.h:164) does NOT work for page contexts: WebCore overrides promiseRejectionTracker (JSDOMGlobalObject.cpp:515-540), so VM::promiseRejected (JSGlobalObject.cpp:3724-3734 -> VM.cpp:1440-1457) never runs for them.
claims.implication: For stacks: install JS listeners for 'error' and 'unhandledrejection' at window-object-cleared time and forward error.stack, or patch WebCore to pass the ScriptCallStack. Do not rely on the JSC API's unhandled-rejection callback.

challenge.reasoning:
The doc line (ZeroG.md:408) says unhandled JS errors and unhandled Promise rejections reach "a dedicated callback with message and stack trace". This is a goal for ZeroG's own API, so the real question is whether WebCore already provides such a hook. I tried to show the reviewer was wrong and could not. WebCore does see both events, and it sometimes has a ScriptCallStack for them. But no port-facing hook delivers them with a stack:

1. Uncaught exceptions. reportException in JSDOMExceptionHandling.cpp first calls invokeScriptErrorCallbacks with message, url, line and column only (lines 143-151). It then calls ScriptExecutionContext::reportException (ScriptExecutionContext.cpp:545-564). That function logs to the console only when the error event was not handled (line 555-556), and goes through Document::logExceptionToConsole (Document.cpp:4835-4838) into FrameConsoleClient. FrameConsoleClient::addMessage (FrameConsoleClient.cpp:146-167) calls ChromeClient::addMessageToConsole(source, level, message, line, column, sourceID) (ChromeClient.h:266). That call carries no stack, so the stack is lost at the port boundary.

2. Rejections. The reviewer's chain is right. JSDOMGlobalObject::promiseRejectionTracker (JSDOMGlobalObject.cpp:515-539), installed in JSDOMWindowBase.cpp:104, JSWorkerGlobalScopeBase.cpp:66 and JSWorkletGlobalScopeBase.cpp:58, replaces JSC's default tracker. The default (JSGlobalObject.cpp:3724-3735) is the only path that calls vm.promiseRejected, so JSGlobalContextSetUnhandledRejectionCallback never fires for page contexts. RejectedPromiseTracker::reportUnhandledRejections dispatches 'unhandledrejection'. If the event is not default-prevented, it calls reportUnhandledPromiseRejection (ScriptExecutionContext.cpp:566-623). That function returns early if Settings::unhandledPromiseRejectionToConsoleEnabled is false (line 573). Otherwise it calls invokeScriptErrorCallbacks (url, line and column only, line 614) and builds an "Unhandled Promise Rejection: ..." ConsoleMessage, which reaches ChromeClient again without a stack.

Small corrections and additions to the reviewer:
(a) addScriptErrorCallback does not mean "unhandled". It fires before dispatchErrorEvent, so also for errors that page JS handles. It also fires for every console.error (FrameConsoleClient.cpp:226-227; WorkerConsoleClient.cpp:93). It is a raw, catch-everything error hook, and its only current user is WebKit/WebProcess/Extensions/Cocoa/WebExtensionControllerProxyCocoa.mm:107,141,178.
(b) Even inside WebCore, the stack for a rejection is often missing. createScriptCallStackFromReason (RejectedPromiseTracker.cpp ~98-110) captures one only if the reason equals vm.lastException() (a thrown value) or a debugger is attached. Promise.reject(new Error('x')) therefore gives a null ScriptCallStack, even though error.stack exists on the JS object.
(c) FrameConsoleClient::addMessage skips ChromeClient::addMessageToConsole entirely when page->usesEphemeralSession() is true (FrameConsoleClient.cpp:152; same check in messageWithTypeAndLevel). If ZeroG sets up its Page as ephemeral, it gets no console or error callbacks at all through ChromeClient.
(d) The reviewer's line numbers are off by one or two lines, which does not matter.

Conclusion: the feature can be built, but not with stock hooks. Either inject JS listeners for 'error' and 'unhandledrejection' that forward event.error.stack or event.reason.stack, or add a small WebCore patch or new ChromeClient hook that passes the ScriptCallStack or the JS reason value. PARTIAL stands.

claims.claim: Dev profile: start WebKit's remote inspector on a local port and open the frontend in a second window
claims.evidence: A non-GLib socket backend exists and builds on every platform: JavaScriptCore/inspector/remote/Socket.cmake (posix/RemoteInspectorSocketPOSIX.cpp on UNIX; win/RemoteInspectorSocketWin.cpp + ws2_32 on Windows). It is used by PlatformWin.cmake:10-11, PlatformPlayStation.cmake:1 and PlatformJSCOnly.cmake:31, with USE_INSPECTOR_SOCKET_SERVER (OptionsWin.cmake:130). JSRemoteInspectorServerStart(address, port) is public (API/JSRemoteInspectorServer.h:36). The server accepts one client and connects RemoteInspector::singleton() in-process (socket/RemoteInspectorServer.cpp:79-95), dispatching to RunLoop::mainSingleton() (socket/RemoteInspectorConnectionClient.cpp:73). Gaps: the page-level RemoteInspectionTarget (WebPageDebuggable) is WebKit2 UIProcess code (WebKit/UIProcess/Inspector/WebPageDebuggable.h), and WebCore has no PageDebuggable. The socket client and frontend host (WebKit/UIProcess/Inspector/socket/RemoteInspectorClient.cpp using RemoteWebInspectorUIProxy) are WebKit2-only. The server needs setBackendCommandsPath(InspectorBackendCommands.js) (WebProcessPoolWin.cpp:59-61). The protocol is WebKit-specific JSON over raw TCP: not CDP, not HTTP, no authentication.
claims.implication: Two options. (A) Remote: write ZeroG's own RemoteInspectionTarget per Page that forwards to page->inspectorController(), plus a frontend client that speaks the socket protocol. (B) Simpler, and enough for the 'second window': the in-process local frontend, as in WebKitLegacy (next claim), with no port at all. Either way, bind only to 127.0.0.1.

challenge.reasoning: The reviewer's verdict holds. The server side is real and works on every platform without GLib. The reviewer's evidence on the socket backend is accurate: the cmake wiring, the public start function, the one-client limit and the main-thread dispatch all check out. Their main gap overstates the problem, though. They say the only page-level RemoteInspectionTarget is WebKit2 UIProcess code (WebPageDebuggable) and that WebCore has none. The WebCore part is literally true, but they missed a single-process, non-WebKit2 page debuggable: Source/WebKitLegacy/WebCoreSupport/LegacyWebPageDebuggable.{h,cpp} together with LegacyWebPageInspectorController.{h,cpp}. It wraps a WebCore::Page directly, uses only JSC inspector headers plus WebCore/Page.h, and the JSC socket backend already handles its target type (Type::LegacyWebPage). The catch is that upstream only builds it for Cocoa (WebKitLegacy/PlatformCocoa.cmake:63, SourcesCMakeCocoa.txt:48), so ZeroG has to copy or adapt those two classes. That is a small port of existing code, not a from-scratch target. The frontend half really is missing: the socket client, the inspector:// protocol handler and RemoteWebInspectorUIProxy exist only in WebKit2 UIProcess. Opening the frontend in a second window that talks to the socket server means writing a ZeroG frontend host and client. The simpler route is to skip the port and attach the in-process local frontend, as WebKitLegacy does. Other needs the doc leaves out: ENABLE_REMOTE_INSPECTOR is OFF by default in OptionsJSCOnly.cmake:21, so the custom port must turn it on and set USE_INSPECTOR_SOCKET_SERVER the way OptionsWin.cmake:130 does. setBackendCommandsPath must point at InspectorBackendCommands.js. The bind address is whatever the caller passes to listenInet, so it should be fixed to 127.0.0.1 because there is no authentication. The protocol is WebKit's own JSON over raw TCP, not CDP.

claims.claim: Engine internal logs have configurable levels and go to the same host callback
claims.evidence: WTF/wtf/DataLog.h:35-37 setDataFile(std::unique_ptr<PrintStream>&&) redirects dataLog. Assertions.h:140-215 has WTFLogChannel / WTFSetLogChannelLevel / WTFLogWithLevel. RELEASE_LOG backends are per platform (not traced here).
claims.implication: dataLog can be redirected without patches; LOG/RELEASE_LOG need a port-level log sink.

challenge.reasoning:
The doc says (ZeroG.md:410) that engine internal logs have configurable levels and are routed to the same host callback, so the host decides where they go. I tried to show the reviewer was wrong and could not. PARTIAL stands, but their "needs a port-level log sink" understates the work. No port file can add the sink. It needs patches to WTF's own Assertions.h and Assertions.cpp. I found no WTFSetLogHandler, log callback or log hook in Source/WTF/wtf.

What holds up:
(1) Levels can be configured. WTFLogLevel {Always, Error, Warning, Info, Debug} exists. Per-channel state and level can be set with WTFSetLogChannelLevel. WTFInitializeLogChannelStatesFromString parses strings like "Channel=debug,-Other,all". LogChannels::initializeLogChannelsIfNecessary(std::optional<String>) accepts a string from code, so the host can set levels from the C API without environment variables.
(2) dataLog (used heavily by JSC) can be redirected without patches through setDataFile(std::unique_ptr<PrintStream>&&).
(3) Something the reviewer missed: WTF::Logger already has observer hooks, Logger::Observer::didLogMessage and Logger::MessageHandlerObserver::handleLogMessage. They only cover logging that goes through the Logger object (the ALWAYS_LOG/ERROR_LOG helpers, mostly media, WebRTC and MSE). Those messages still go to stderr as well.

What does not hold, so the "same callback" part needs patches:
(a) WTFLog, WTFLogVerbose, WTFLogWithLevel, WTFLogAlways and LOG_ERROR all end in logToStderr or vprintf_stderr_common. These write straight to stderr with fputs/vfprintf. They also call OutputDebugStringA on Windows when a debugger is attached. They never go through dataFile(), so setDataFile does not catch them.
(b) On a non-Cocoa, non-Android, non-journald build, RELEASE_LOG* is a header macro that inlines fprintf(stderr, ...) at every call site. Windows is such a build: OptionsWin.cmake turns ENABLE_RELEASE_LOG on, and ZeroG would likely do the same. So redirecting it means editing the generic WTF_RELEASE_LOG_SEND in Assertions.h. You cannot interpose one function.
(c) Logger::log also writes to stderr or the platform log before it notifies observers.
(d) The other way out is redirecting the process's stderr (fd 2). That is process-wide and would also capture the host application's own stderr, which conflicts with the doc's goal of living politely inside the host.

Gotchas the doc misses:
- LOG_DISABLED defaults to !ASSERT_ENABLED, which means it is on whenever NDEBUG is set. So LOG/LOG_VERBOSE/LOG_WITH_LEVEL compile to nothing in release builds. Only RELEASE_LOG survives, and only if ENABLE_RELEASE_LOG is on (default OFF in WebKitFeatures.cmake, ON in OptionsWin). Level control in shipped builds is therefore limited to RELEASE_LOG channels.
- With RELEASE_LOG off, Logger::logAlways is compiled out completely.
- Level names reach WebCore through WebCore::logLevelString(): the "WebCoreLogging" environment variable on Windows, and WTF::logLevelString() reads WEBKIT_DEBUG on Unix. The port will have to override these or pass the string explicitly.
- Generic RELEASE_LOG output passes the priority as a raw number ("[WebKit:Channel:4]"). It has no file or line, unlike the journald build, which records CODE_FILE/CODE_LINE. If the host callback is to get file and line as the doc promises, the patch must add them from __FILE__/__LINE__.

claims.claim: ENABLE_STATIC_JSC builds JSC non-shared (introduced for PlayStation)
claims.evidence: cmake/OptionsPlayStation.cmake:173 WEBKIT_OPTION_DEFINE(ENABLE_STATIC_JSC ... ON), :362-366 just sets JavaScriptCore_LIBRARY_TYPE OBJECT; OptionsJSCOnly.cmake:19, 52-56. It is a port-local CMake switch with no C++ effect.
claims.implication: The ZeroG port can just set *_LIBRARY_TYPE to OBJECT/STATIC in its Options file. The export macros are the real concern (see missing facts).

missing_facts: Windows static link: JS_EXPORT becomes __declspec(dllimport) for any consumer unless JS_NO_EXPORT or STATICALLY_LINKED_WITH_JavaScriptCore is defined (JavaScriptCore/API/JSBase.h:81-94). Inside the library it is dllexport, so a static exe would export all JSC C API symbols. Define JS_NO_EXPORT (and the equivalent for WTF_EXPORT_PRIVATE / JS_EXPORT_PRIVATE / WEBCORE_EXPORT) in the ZeroG port. cmake/WebKitMacros.cmake:914 shows the STATICALLY_LINKED_WITH_<target> convention.

New port on macOS: WTF/wtf/PlatformLegacy.h:49-77 sets PLATFORM(MAC), and therefore PLATFORM(COCOA), for any OS(MACOS) build unless BUILDING_GTK__/HAIKU/WPE/JSCONLY__ is defined. On Windows PLATFORM(WIN) is set automatically. ZeroG must add its own BUILDING_ZEROG__ branch (a small WTF patch) or Cocoa code paths get pulled in. OptionsJSCOnly.cmake:11 shows the pattern (add_definitions(-DBUILDING_JSCONLY__)).

JIT address-space reservation: 1 GB of virtual memory on x86_64 (ExecutableAllocator.cpp:101-102 fixedExecutableMemoryPoolSize = 1*GB), reserved at JSC init. Options::jitMemoryReservationSize (used at ExecutableAllocator.cpp:357-358) can shrink it for embedders. Worth exposing next to the heap limits.

JSC reads JSC_<option> environment variables in release builds on every non-Cocoa platform (Options.cpp:395-412 getenv in overrideOptionWithHeuristic; :1118-1129), plus 'JavaScriptCoreUseJIT' (VM.cpp:213-215). End users can change engine behavior (e.g. JSC_useJIT, dump options). The customization callback runs after env parsing (Options.cpp:1140-1141), so ZeroG must explicitly override any security-relevant option it cares about there.

Order of initialization: JSC::initialize is std::call_once (InitializeThreading.cpp:88-90), and WebCore calls plain JSC::initialize() from ScriptController::initializeMainThread (ScriptController.cpp:120-126), also reached from commonVMSlow (CommonVM.cpp:54-62). zg_runtime_create must call JSC::initialize(customizationLambda) before any WebCore object exists, or the JIT/Wasm/heap options are silently ignored.
Options freeze: the first VM::VM() calls Config::finalize() (VM.cpp:568), which makes g_jscConfig/WTF config pages read-only (WTFConfig.cpp:190-211). Any later Options::... write crashes.

No signal-based VM traps on Windows: ENABLE_SIGNAL_BASED_VM_TRAPS requires HAVE(MACHINE_CONTEXT) (PlatformEnable.h:969-971; PlatformHave.h:235-236 has no OS(WINDOWS)). Windows uses polling traps, which matters for watchdog/termination latency.

'Una sola VM JavaScript' holds only for main-thread pages (WebCore/bindings/js/CommonVM.cpp:54-90 commonVMSlow creates one HeapType::Large VM). Workers and worklets get their own VMs (workers/WorkerOrWorkletScriptController.cpp:81-95, 'm_vm != &commonVM()'), so memory limits and stats must sum several VMs.

The JSC C API callback runs under JSLock::DropAllLocks (API/APICallbackFunction.h:67-70), so every JSValue*/JSObject* call inside a native binding re-takes the API lock. For low-latency sync bindings, keep the number of C API calls per invocation small, or use internal JSC APIs in the generated dispatcher.

The doc's 'PageConsoleClient' / 'InspectorController' / 'InspectorClient' names are outdated at this revision: FrameConsoleClient (WebCore/page/FrameConsoleClient.cpp), PageInspectorController and InspectorBackendClient (WebCore/inspector/).

Console delivery is suppressed for ephemeral sessions (FrameConsoleClient.cpp:152, :238), and worker console output never reaches ChromeClient (WorkerGlobalScope.cpp:500-538). Both matter for the 'console in terminal in dev mode' feature.

Remote-inspector default: WEBKIT_OPTION_DEFINE(ENABLE_REMOTE_INSPECTOR ... ON) in cmake/WebKitFeatures.cmake:309, so the port must explicitly set it OFF for the minimal/standard profiles. On Win, PlatformWin.cmake:10-15 drops inspector/JSGlobalObjectInspectorController.cpp when it is off; check that the ZeroG Platform cmake does the same or still compiles.

challenge.reasoning: I tried to find a way around the Windows block and couldn't. The option is real and works on Linux and macOS. On Windows it is stopped at compile time by an unconditional #error, and nothing skips it. bmalloc is always added to the build. When the option is ON, bmalloc's CMake turns it into a -DUSE_SYSTEM_MALLOC=1 compile definition. BPlatform.h then sets BUSE_SYSTEM_MALLOC=1 and reaches the BOS(WINDOWS) #error. claims.claim: System malloc removes Gigacage, libpas/bmalloc heaps and isolated heaps
claims.evidence: BPlatform.h:398-417 sets BENABLE_LIBPAS and BUSE_LIBPAS to 0 when BUSE(SYSTEM_MALLOC), and :463-469 turns TZone off. GIGACAGE_ENABLED is still compiled as 1 on Linux/Darwin x86_64/arm64 (BPlatform.h:471-477, which only excludes MIMALLOC). At runtime it is disabled: Gigacage.cpp:270-282 shouldBeEnabled() returns early when Environment::shouldBmallocAllocateThroughSystemHeap() is true, and that function always returns true under BUSE(SYSTEM_MALLOC) (Environment.cpp:151-158, 200-202). The bmalloc library and the libpas sources are still compiled, but they are #if'd out. USE_MIMALLOC compiles Gigacage out entirely (GIGACAGE_ENABLED=0).

claims.claim: With system malloc there are no huge virtual memory reservations
claims.evidence: JSC reserves memory independently of malloc. jit/ExecutableAllocator.cpp:94-104 reserves a fixed executable pool: 1 GB on x86_64, 128/512 MB on arm64. heap/StructureAlignedMemoryAllocator.cpp:99-112 reserves the structure heap aligned, with fallbacks; it can be tuned with Options::structureHeapSizeInKB. Wasm fast memories reserve multi-GB regions when WebAssembly is on.
claims.implication: Expose JIT pool size and structure heap size through zg_runtime_config. With JIT off and Wasm off the reservations are much smaller, but not zero.

challenge.reasoning:
The claim is absolute: system malloc means no huge virtual memory reservations. The source says otherwise. The reviewer's evidence is correct, but they understated it. Their implication is also wrong: turning JIT and Wasm off still leaves a 4 GB reservation.

1) Gigacage part is true. With USE_SYSTEM_MALLOC, Gigacage's runtime check returns early, so the Gigacage reservation is never made. The compile-time GIGACAGE_ENABLED is still 1 on Linux and Darwin x86_64/arm64, because it only checks !BUSE(MIMALLOC). The runtime gate is what turns it off.

2) Structure heap: the reviewer missed the size and that it is unconditional. On every CPU(ADDRESS64) target, StructureMemoryManager reserves one aligned region. The default size is 4 GB on Linux, Windows, macOS and other desktop targets. It is 2 GB on arm64e iOS, 512 MB on older iOS/watchOS/tvOS, and 128 MB on PlayStation/QNX. This runs in JSC::initialize for every process, whatever the malloc choice and whether or not JIT is on. With system malloc it takes the m_useSystemHeap path and commits 16 KB blocks one at a time inside that reservation. The reservation itself is still made.

3) On Linux the reservation is not overcommit-neutral. tryReserveUncommitted maps memory read/write with MAP_NORESERVE, then calls madvise(DONTNEED). Under vm.overcommit_memory=2, Linux ignores MAP_NORESERVE and charges writable private mappings to the commit limit. So the doc's argument that system malloc removes the need for overcommit is also only half true. A tight RLIMIT_AS hits this too. If the reservation fails, the size is halved up to 8 times, down to about 16 MB. If even that fails, it is a RELEASE_ASSERT.

4) JIT executable pool: the reviewer's numbers are right. It is 1 GB on x86_64, 512 MB on arm64 with JUMP_ISLANDS (128 MB without), and 32 MB elsewhere. It is skipped when JIT is off: either Options::useJIT()=false before VM::computeCanUseJIT, or ExecutableAllocator::disableJIT() called before initialization. It can be resized with Options::jitMemoryReservationSize or with the FIXED_EXECUTABLE_MEMORY_POOL_SIZE_IN_MB compile define.

5) Wasm fast memory: these are made lazily, one per Wasm memory instance. Each is maxMemory32Bytes (4 GB) plus a redzone, up to maxNumWasmFastMemories (8 or 3). They can be turned off with useWasmFastMemory=false or ENABLE_WEBASSEMBLY=OFF.

Bottom line: system malloc removes only Gigacage. With default options, a JIT-on x86_64 desktop still reserves about 5 GB of virtual memory at startup: 4 GB structure heap plus 1 GB JIT pool. With JIT and Wasm off, 4 GB remains. The only way to shrink it is Options::structureHeapSizeInKB, which must be a power of two because of the RELEASE_ASSERT(hasOneBitSet). The doc should say that, and zg_runtime_config should expose structureHeapSizeInKB, jitMemoryReservationSize and the JIT/Wasm switches. These options have to be set before JSC::initialize, through the initializeWithOptionsCustomization callback.

So this is unbudgeted porting work, not an arithmetic error.

I correct the reviewer in two places.

claims.claim: ICU: keep; WebCore has its own codecs so ICU converter data can be cut a lot
claims.evidence: WTF links ICU::data/i18n/uc unconditionally (WTF/wtf/CMakeLists.txt:806-811), and WebCore links ICU::uc (WebCore/CMakeLists.txt:2264). Minimum version is 70.1 (OptionsWin.cmake:46, OptionsJSCOnly.cmake:113). TextCodecCJK and TextCodecSingleByte exist (PAL/pal/text). TextCodecICU is still registered (TextEncodingRegistry.cpp:274-275) and needs ucnv converters for about 20 encodings: ISO-8859-2/4/5/10/13/14/15/16, KOI8-R, macintosh, windows-1250/1251/1254/1256/1258, x-mac-cyrillic/greek/centraleurroman/turkish and EUC-TW (TextCodecICU.cpp:84-104). URL host IDNA uses ICU UTS46: WTF/URLParser.cpp:2673 `uidna_nameToASCII` and :3015 `uidna_openUTS46`.
claims.implication: In the ICU data filter, keep the converters for those encodings, uts46.nrm, normalization data, break iterators and time zones. Everything else in the converter data can go.

challenge.reasoning:
PARTIAL is still the right label for the doc claim, but the reviewer's evidence leaves out something important and their implication ("keep the ~20 TextCodecICU converters, everything else in the converter data can go") is wrong. If ZeroG followed it, the engine would crash in release builds.

The reviewer missed this: TextCodecCJK is not independent of ICU. Its decoding tables (jis0208, jis0212, big5, eucKR, gb18030) are built lazily at runtime, in release builds, by running ICU converters over every code point. Only the *Reference copies are inside #if ASSERT_ENABLED. The builders run outside that guard (the ASSERT_ENABLED blocks span EncodingTables.cpp lines 46-1016, 1107-1870, 1910-4238, 4933-7068 and 7104-8605). They call:
- ucnv_open("EUC-JP") for jis0208, used by EUC-JP, Shift_JIS and ISO-2022-JP
- ucnv_open("EUC-JP") for jis0212
- ucnv_open("Big-5") for Big5
- ucnv_open("windows-949") for EUC-KR
- ucnv_open("gb18030") for GBK/gb18030

Each builder (except gb18030) ends with RELEASE_ASSERT_WITH_SECURITY_IMPLICATION(arrayIndex == N). If that converter's data is filtered out, ucnv_open fails, the null-converter loop produces the wrong count, and the release assert crashes the process on the first Japanese, Chinese or Korean page. The gb18030 builder has no release assert, so it silently fills a table from a null converter, which gives corrupt decoding instead of a crash.

These CJK converters are also the largest part of ICU's converter data, so the "cut a lot" savings will be much smaller than the doc implies.

A second gap: TextCodecICU::registerCodecs calls ucnv_getCanonicalName(name, "IANA") (TextCodecICU.cpp:122). That needs the converter alias table (cnvalias.icu, a standard ICU data file) with the IANA standard kept. Without it, the code falls back to ucnv_open plus ucnv_getName. If that also fails, the encoding is silently skipped (`continue`), so it is not a crash.

What the reviewer got right:
- WTF links ICU::data/i18n/uc.
- WebCore links ICU::uc.
- TextCodecICU is registered in extendTextCodecMaps.
- The list of 20 encodings is accurate.
- UTS46 IDNA is in URLParser. It is also used in URL.cpp:460 and URLHelpers.cpp:672.

Charset auto-detection (TextEncodingDetectorICU, ucsdet) is ICU i18n code. It is called from TextResourceDecoder.cpp:580/612, so ucsdet must be kept in the build, but as far as I can tell it needs no converter data. It only includes ucnv.h and does not call ucnv_*.

The doc's premise ("WebCore has its own codecs, so ICU converter data can be cut a lot") is therefore only partly true. The single-byte codecs and the CJK state machines are WebCore's own code, but the CJK lookup tables come from ICU converter data at runtime. The doc's "(da verificare)" (to be verified) was justified.

Correct minimum converter set for the ICU data filter:
- the 20 TextCodecICU encodings (ISO-8859-2/4/5/10/13/14/15/16, KOI8-R, macintosh, windows-1250/1251/1254/1256/1258, x-mac-cyrillic/greek/centraleurroman/turkish, EUC-TW)
- EUC-JP, Big-5, windows-949 and gb18030
- cnvalias.icu with IANA names
- plus non-converter data: uts46.nrm, normalization data, break iterators, time zones, and the locale/Intl data JSC needs

Recommended follow-up: either keep these converters, or patch EncodingTables.cpp to use static tables (more binary size, which upstream explicitly avoided, see the "Allocate this at runtime" comments). Add a startup self-test that decodes one string in each of these encodings so a filtered-out converter is caught in CI.

claims.claim: HarfBuzz: build without GLib, ICU and Graphite
claims.evidence: WebCore/platform/Skia.cmake links `HarfBuzz::HarfBuzz HarfBuzz::ICU Skia::Skia`, and every port does `find_package(HarfBuzz ... REQUIRED COMPONENTS ICU)` (OptionsWin.cmake:45, OptionsWPE.cmake:15). The code calls hb_icu_script_to_script via <hb-icu.h> in skia/ComplexTextControllerSkia.cpp:35,265,270 and platform/text/LocaleICU.cpp:48,82.
claims.implication: Build HarfBuzz with ICU integration so it produces libharfbuzz-icu (you can still keep hb-ucd as the default Unicode funcs). The alternative is a small patch replacing hb_icu_script_to_script. Dropping GLib and Graphite is fine.

challenge.reasoning:
I tried to find a way around the reviewer's verdict and couldn't. Upstream WebCore needs HarfBuzz's ICU integration (the hb-icu.h header and the libharfbuzz-icu library) in three places: the CMake config, the Skia text shaper, and locale handling. No option or #if guard switches this off independently.
- The Skia platform file links HarfBuzz::ICU unconditionally.
- Every CMake port (GTK, WPE, Win, PlayStation) calls find_package(HarfBuzz ... REQUIRED COMPONENTS ICU). FindHarfBuzz.cmake fails configuration if harfbuzz-icu / hb-icu.h is not found once ICU is requested as a required component.
- In ComplexTextControllerSkia.cpp (listed in SourcesSkia.txt), the include of <hb-icu.h> and the calls to hb_icu_script_to_script are not behind any guard.
- In LocaleICU.cpp the include and the call are guarded only by USE(HARFBUZZ). That flag is always on for a Skia/HarfBuzz port, so it is not a separate switch.

So "build HarfBuzz without ICU" will not configure, or will not link, against unmodified WebCore. The parts about dropping GLib and Graphite are fine: WebCore has no hb-glib or hb-graphite usage. That makes the claim correct in two of its three parts. The ICU part is a hard blocker, though, so REFUTED is still the right overall verdict. PARTIAL would also be defensible.

Things that matter for implementation:
1. The simplest fix is to build HarfBuzz with ICU integration (-Dicu=enabled, or HB_HAVE_ICU in CMake). That produces harfbuzz-icu, and you can keep hb-ucd as the default Unicode functions. ZeroG ships ICU anyway, so this adds no new dependency.
2. The alternative is a small downstream patch. hb_icu_script_to_script(code) is essentially hb_script_from_string(uscript_getShortName(code), -1). Replacing it in the 2-3 call sites and dropping HarfBuzz::ICU from Skia.cmake and from the Options*.cmake find_package calls would remove the need for harfbuzz-icu.
3. If a ZeroG CMake port provides HarfBuzz as an in-tree static target instead of using find_package, it still has to define an imported or alias target named HarfBuzz::ICU, or edit Skia.cmake.
4. Skia's bundled HarfBuzz (ThirdParty/skia/third_party/harfbuzz/BUILD.gn:424-425) can compile hb-icu.cc. So the in-tree Skia HarfBuzz build can supply this if it is reused.
5. hb-ft (HarfBuzz's FreeType integration) is used only by the FreeType/Cairo code path, not the Skia path. The doc says nothing about FreeType here, and that is fine for Skia-only.

claims.claim: FreeType: keep, only zlib and libpng as deps
claims.evidence: Skia needs FreeType on non-Windows: skia/CMakeLists.txt:5 `find_package(Freetype 2.9.0 REQUIRED)` and :829-835. On WIN32 it uses DirectWrite (:815-827) with SK_TYPEFACE_FACTORY_DIRECTWRITE (:1089). Building FreeType with brotli would make libwoff2 unnecessary (WOFF2Checks.cmake).
claims.implication: On Linux/macOS FreeType is required. On Windows it is only needed if you change Skia's CMake to use FreeType for consistent embedded-font rendering.

challenge.reasoning:
I tried to show the reviewer was wrong and could not. Their line citations are accurate, and the PARTIAL verdict holds.

1) "Keep FreeType" is correct, and on non-Windows it is required. The in-tree Skia CMake has no font backend other than FreeType outside WIN32. That includes macOS: there is no CoreText path in this CMakeLists at all. On WIN32 it builds only the DirectWrite font sources and never compiles SkFontHost_FreeType*. So the doc's default of "FreeType everywhere" (ZeroG.md:247) means patching Skia's CMake on Windows to compile SkFontHost_FreeType*.cpp and set SK_TYPEFACE_FACTORY_FREETYPE instead of SK_TYPEFACE_FACTORY_DIRECTWRITE.

2) "Only zlib and libpng as deps" is a legitimate FreeType build choice. Every FreeType external dependency is optional, and nothing in the checkout forces bzip2 or HarfBuzz into FreeType.

3) "No brotli" works, but it sits awkwardly with the rest of the doc. Upstream GTK and WPE probe FreeType for FT_CONFIG_OPTION_USE_BROTLI. If it is there, they set HAVE_WOFF_SUPPORT and turn USE_WOFF2 off, so FreeType decodes WOFF/WOFF2 and libwoff2 is not needed. The doc keeps brotli anyway (row 468, for Content-Encoding: br). Turning off brotli in FreeType therefore saves no dependency and forces the libwoff2 path (USE_WOFF2 plus the woff2/decode.h include in WOFFFileFormat.cpp). Without HAVE_WOFF_SUPPORT, WebCore decodes WOFF1 itself through zlib, which is consistent with keeping zlib.

Important facts the doc misses:
(a) The in-tree Skia CMake hard-requires Fontconfig on every non-Windows, non-PlayStation build (find_package REQUIRED at :6, link at :852), and it uses SkFontMgr_fontconfig. WebCore's Skia fallback code also includes fontconfig/fontconfig.h directly. Row 476 of the doc ("replace Fontconfig with Skia's font manager") therefore needs CMake changes plus a rewrite of SkiaSystemFallbackFontCache. The replacement sources do exist in the checkout: SkFontMgr_custom_directory.cpp, _embedded.cpp and _empty.cpp under skia/src/ports.
(b) WebCore's platform/FreeType.cmake (FontCacheFreeType etc.) is used only by PlayStation. GTK/WPE/Win include only platform/Skia.cmake, so a Skia-based port does not need WebCore's FreeType font classes. FreeType.cmake also links Fontconfig.
(c) Skia's FreeType code compiles COLRv1 color-font support only on FreeType 2.11.1 or newer. libpng in FreeType matters only for PNG-embedded color bitmap glyphs (CBDT/sbix emoji). Inferred: without it, color emoji fonts of that kind will not render.

WebKit's Skia CMake builds only Ganesh GL (SK_GL, SK_GANESH, SK_ASSUME_GL_ES=1 at :1070-1086). challenge.reasoning:
I tried to show the reviewer was wrong and could not. Every point they made checks out in the source tree.

1. Skia is in the repo (CONFIRMED). It is vendored at Source/ThirdParty/skia. README.WebKit pins commit 588b550a4dd8af90dbe71c0554852806bd8f0b21. WebKit keeps its own CMakeLists.txt and WebKitSkiaConfig.h, which a Skia update restores with "git checkout".

2. "Build only the needed GPU backends" (PARTIAL). WebKit's CMake can build only one backend: Ganesh GL. The definitions are SK_GL, SK_GANESH and SK_GANESH_SMALL_PATH_DISTANCE_FIELD_ALWAYS (:1070-1074), plus SK_ASSUME_GL_ES=1 and SK_ASSUME_GL=0 (:1082-1086), with the comment "FIXME: Support other combinations." The only GPU sources it lists are under src/gpu/ganesh/{gl,glsl,ops,effects,geometry,image,gradients,mock,surface,tessellate,text}. No vk, mtl, d3d or graphite sources are listed, and SK_VULKAN, SK_METAL, SK_DIRECT3D and SK_GRAPHITE never appear. The GL interface is EGL only: either GrGLMakeNativeInterface_egl.cpp and GrGLMakeEGLInterface.cpp, or the Epoxy variant (:856-867). There is no WGL or CGL path. So picking backends is not a build option. Any backend other than GLES/EGL means adding sources and definitions to the CMake file yourself.

3. "No PDF" (REFUTED as a description of the current build; it would need a patch). The src/pdf/*.cpp files (21 of them, from :611) sit inside the main add_library(Skia STATIC ...) block that starts at :21. No closing ")" at column 0 appears between :21 and :640, and they are not under any if(). So PDF is always compiled. In WebKit, only the GTK printing code uses SkPDF/SkDocument (Source/WebKit/WebProcess/WebPage/gtk/WebPrintOperationGtk.cpp and .h), so dropping it is safe. It still requires editing the CMake file.

4. "No SVG" (CONFIRMED that it can be turned off). The Skia SVG module (modules/svg), skshaper, skresources, the xml sources and the SK_ENABLE_SVG definition are all inside if (USE_SKIA_OPENTYPE_SVG) (:888-970). That block needs EXPAT and HarfBuzz. Only GTK and WPE define the option (OptionsGTK.cmake:58, OptionsWPE.cmake:121, both default ON). A new port that does not define it gets no Skia SVG. This is unrelated to WebCore's own SVG engine. Note that turning it off also removes OpenType-SVG (colour emoji) font support.

5. "No Skottie" (trivially true). modules/skottie exists in the tree, but the CMake file never references it.

Gotchas the doc misses:
- USE_SKIA defaults OFF (WebKitFeatures.cmake:363). Only GTK, WPE and Win set it ON (OptionsGTK:159, OptionsWPE:154, OptionsWin:91), so a ZeroG port must set it explicitly. USE_SKIA_ENCODERS defaults ON (:364) and pulls in WebP::mux (:9-10, :869-879).
- Every non-WIN32, non-PlayStation build requires FreeType 2.9 and Fontconfig 2.13 (:4-7) and uses SkFontMgr_fontconfig (:845-852). That includes macOS, where SkFontMgr_mac_ct is never built. The font manager is hard-wired: Windows gets DirectWrite with SK_TYPEFACE_FACTORY_DIRECTWRITE, everything else FreeType. SkFontMgr_custom_directory, SkFontMgr_custom_embedded and SkFontMgr_custom_empty exist in src/ports but are not wired in.
- JPEG::JPEG and PNG::PNG are always linked (:972-975).
- The library is always STATIC (:21), which suits static linking.
- On Windows, OptionsWin with USE_SKIA also needs HarfBuzz with ICU (OptionsWin.cmake:166-171).

Overall: Skia being present, Skottie being absent and SVG being optional are all correct. "Build only the needed GPU backends" and "no PDF" are not true of the current build; they need ZeroG's own fork or patch of skia/CMakeLists.txt. The reviewer's PARTIAL verdict and their implication both stand.

claims.claim: BoringSSL for TLS and WebCrypto via WebCore's OpenSSL backend
claims.evidence: WebCore/platform/OpenSSL.cmake adds 21 crypto/openssl/*.cpp files. OptionsWin.cmake:134-139 checks OPENSSL_IS_BORINGSSL to set USE_BORINGSSL, but nothing in WebCore uses USE(BORINGSSL). There are BoringSSL accommodations in the code: CryptoAlgorithmHKDFOpenSSL.cpp:34 `__has_include(<openssl/hkdf.h>)`, and the OpenSSL-3-only code is gated by OPENSSL_VERSION_NUMBER >= 0x30000000L (OpenSSLCryptoUniquePtr.h:32,64). Uses AES_wrap_key and EVP_PKEY_HKDF.
claims.implication: Probably feasible, but a build is needed to confirm. Expect small patches. BoringSSL symbol prefixing (BORINGSSL_PREFIX) is a build-side task.

challenge.reasoning:
I could not show the PARTIAL verdict is wrong, so it stands. The design is plausible and the source tree already makes room for BoringSSL. Two ports, Win and PlayStation, check for it, and the crypto code avoids OpenSSL-3-only APIs. But no in-tree code branches on BoringSSL, no port is known to build it, and only a build can confirm it works. Several details in the reviewer's evidence are wrong or missing.

(1) With BoringSSL, HKDF does not go through EVP_PKEY_HKDF. CryptoAlgorithmHKDFOpenSSL.cpp:34 does `#if __has_include(<openssl/hkdf.h>)`. BoringSSL ships that header, so BoringSSL's own HKDF() is used. The EVP_PKEY_HKDF function at lines 40-75 is a fallback for plain OpenSSL only, as the comment on line 40 says.

(2) The OpenSSL-3 types (OsslParamBldPtr, OsslParamPtr, EVPKDFCtxPtr, EVPKDFPtr in OpenSSLCryptoUniquePtr.h:64-69) are guarded and not used anywhere in WebCore; a grep finds no users. BoringSSL reports OPENSSL_VERSION_NUMBER as 1.1.1, so this code drops out.

(3) USE_BORINGSSL is a real build define, not just a CMake variable. WEBKIT_CHECK_HAVE_SYMBOL (WebKitFeatures.cmake:683-686) calls SET_AND_EXPOSE_TO_BUILD. The reviewer is right that nothing in WebCore, WTF or JSC reads USE(BORINGSSL); it is only used inside ThirdParty/libwebrtc.

(4) AES-CFB is written by hand on top of AES_encrypt (CryptoAlgorithmAESCFBOpenSSL.cpp:39-68), so BoringSSL's libdecrepit CFB ciphers are not needed.

(5) The rest of the APIs used are in BoringSSL's mainline API: AES_wrap_key, RSA_*_set0/get0, EVP_PKEY_new_raw_*, ED25519/X25519 keygen, and EVP_PKEY_CTX_set0_rsa_oaep_label called with uint8_t* and size_t. This is from my knowledge of BoringSSL, not checked against its headers.

Things the doc misses:
(a) WebCore's curl layer calls the TLS library directly. CurlContext.cpp:694 sets CURLOPT_SSL_CTX_FUNCTION, CurlSSLVerifier.cpp casts to SSL_CTX* and calls SSL_CTX_set_verify and SSL_CTX_set1_sigalgs_list, and OpenSSLHelper.cpp uses X509, BIO, PEM, ASN1_TIME fields and SSL_get_peer_cert_chain. So curl and WebCore must link the same single BoringSSL, with the same BORINGSSL_PREFIX if prefixing is used.
(b) CurlContext.cpp:809 returns nothing unless info->backend == CURLSSLBACKEND_OPENSSL. In curl.h, CURLSSLBACKEND_BORINGSSL is an alias with the same value, so this should work; that is external knowledge, not verified here. curl must be built with its OpenSSL-family backend, not schannel or mbedTLS.
(c) On Windows, CurlContext.cpp:346-347 sets CURLSSLOPT_NATIVE_CA, which loads system certificates through curl. On Linux and macOS a CA bundle or path is needed, because BoringSSL has no system trust store.
(d) WTF/wtf/Platform.h:160-162 defines HAVE_OPENSSL_OKP for USE(OPENSSL) on every platform except PlayStation. A new ZeroG PLATFORM gets it, so the Ed25519/X25519 OpenSSL code compiles in and BoringSSL must provide raw-key EVP_PKEY support, which it does.
(e) PlatformGTK.cmake:8-15 is the model for choosing between OpenSSL and GCrypt: it includes OpenSSL.cmake, links OpenSSL::Crypto and sets OPENSSL_API_COMPAT. PlatformWin.cmake:6 includes OpenSSL.cmake with no condition. The ZeroG port needs USE_OPENSSL ON, find_package(OpenSSL) pointed at BoringSSL, and include(platform/OpenSSL.cmake). No libgcrypt is needed.
